items.name: Lavender plant
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining soil mixed with grit or sand to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Prune annually in late August after flowering by cutting back green stems but never into old wood.
Water newly planted lavender weekly in spring then stop watering once established in UK ground.
Grow with companion plants like rosemary or thyme that share the same love for poor dry soil.
Choose English cultivars like Hidcote or Munstead for the best frost hardiness in UK climates.
items.description: Lavandula angustifolia, formerly L. officinalis, is a flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, native to the Mediterranean basin. Its common names include lavender, true lavender and English lavender ; also garden lavender, common lavender and narrow-leaved lavender.

items.name: Lavandula stoechas
items.growersTips:
Prune immediately after the first flush of flowers in June to encourage a second late-summer bloom.
Plant in a raised bed or terracotta pot using a fifty-fifty mix of peat-free compost and horticultural grit.
Protect from wet UK winters by placing pots against a south-facing house wall under the eaves.
Water newly planted lavender weekly in summer, then stop watering entirely once established in autumn.
Avoid pruning back into old wood as French lavender will not regenerate from bare brown stems.
items.description: Lavandula stoechas, the Spanish lavender or topped lavender (U.S.) or French lavender (U.K.), is a species of lavender native to the Mediterranean Basin.

items.name: Lavandula ×intermedia
items.growersTips:
Prune hard in late August after flowering, cutting into current year growth but never old wood.
Plant in full sun in gritty, free-draining soil, raising the bed or adding gravel to avoid rot.
Water newly planted Grosso or Dutch Group sparingly, then leave mature plants entirely rain-fed.
Space plants eighty centimetres apart to ensure the excellent air circulation needed in UK damp.
Protect young plants from winter wet by mulching with grit or gravel rather than organic compost.

items.name: Blue sage
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Cut back faded flower spikes to the ground in July to trigger a second flush of blooms in autumn.
Leave dead stems intact over winter to protect the crown from frost, then clear them in March.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain plant vigour and flower size.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, using beer traps or grit barriers.
items.description: Salvia nemorosa, the woodland sage, Balkan clary, blue sage or wild sage, is a hardy herbaceous perennial plant native to a wide area of central Europe and Western Asia.

items.name: Salvia officinalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil in full sun to prevent root rot during wet UK winters.
Prune hard in April by cutting back to just above new growth shoots to prevent the wood from splaying.
Water newly planted sage weekly in summer but leave established plants dry to concentrate essential oils.
Grow near cabbages and carrots to deter pests like cabbage white butterflies with its strong scent.
Take semi-ripe cuttings in August to propagate and replace woody, unproductive five-year-old plants.
items.description: Salvia officinalis, common sage or sage, is a perennial, evergreen subshrub, with woody stems, grayish leaves, and blue to purplish flowers. It is a member of the mint family (Lamiaceae) and native to the Mediterranean region, though it has been naturalized in many places throughout the world. It has a long history of culinary use, and in modern times it has been used as an ornamental garden plant. The common name "sage" is also used for closely related species and cultivars.

items.name: Rosmarinus officinalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil with added horticultural grit to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Prune immediately after spring flowering by cutting back green stems by a third to prevent woodiness.
Grow in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to radiate heat and shelter from cold UK winds.
Water newly planted rosemary weekly in summer, then leave established plants entirely to UK rainfall.
Choose the cultivar Miss Jessopps Upright for tight spaces or Prostratus to cascade over dry walls.
items.description: Salvia rosmarinus, synonym Rosmarinus officinalis, commonly known as rosemary, is a shrub with fragrant, evergreen, needle-like leaves and purple or sometimes white, pink, or blue flowers. It is a member of the mint family, Lamiaceae. The species is native to the Mediterranean region. It has numerous cultivars, and its leaves are commonly used as a flavoring.

items.name: Faassen's catnip
items.growersTips:
Cut back to the ground in March to make way for fresh green shoots and prevent woody center rot.
Shear the entire plant by half in late July after the first flush of flowers to trigger a rebloom.
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay and waterlogged beds.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and neighborhood cats who will roll on and crush the stems.
Divide the root clump every three years in autumn to maintain vigor and prevent the center dying out.
items.description: Nepeta × faassenii, a flowering plant also known as catmint and Faassen's catnip, is a primary hybrid of garden origin. The parent species are Nepeta racemosa and Nepeta nepetella.

items.name: Stachys byzantina
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Divide congested clumps every three springs to maintain vigour and prevent center die-out.
Cut back rain-damaged sodden mushy leaves in late autumn to prevent fungal rot at the crown.
Grow the non-flowering cultivar Silver Carpet to avoid messy flower spikes in damp summers.
Position in full sun next to lavender or rosemary to match their low-water requirements.
items.description: Stachys byzantina, the lamb's-ear Monty plant or woolly hedgenettle, is a species of flowering plant in the mint family Lamiaceae, native to Armenia, Iran, and Turkey. It is cultivated throughout much of the temperate world as an ornamental plant, and is naturalised in some locations as an escapee from gardens. Plants are very often found under the synonym Stachys lanata or Stachys olympica.

items.name: Wild thyme
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural grit to prevent winter wet root rot.
Water newly planted plugs weekly until established, then rely solely on natural UK rainfall.
Prune lightly with shears immediately after flowering in late summer to prevent woody leggy stems.
Plant alongside rosemary or sage in full sun to naturally deter common UK garden pests like aphids.
Grow the pink chintz cultivar in shallow gaps between paving slabs to withstand light foot traffic.
items.description: Thymus serpyllum, known by the common names of Breckland thyme, Breckland wild thyme, wild thyme, creeping thyme, or elfin thyme, is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae. It is a low, usually prostrate subshrub forming creeping stems up to 10 cm (4 in) tall. The oval evergreen leaves are up to 8 mm. The strongly scented flowers are either lilac, pink-purple, magenta, up to 6 mm long and produced in clusters.

items.name: Oregano
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil or add horticultural grit to compost to survive wet UK winters.
Cut back hard in late summer after flowering to encourage a fresh flush of tasty leaves before frost.
Water only during prolonged dry spells as established oregano thrives on neglect and dry conditions.
Grow in full sun, ideally in a terracotta pot which helps prevent the roots from rotting in winter.
Propagate by dividing the root clump in spring to maintain plant vigour and prevent woody centres.
items.description: Oregano is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae. It was native to the Mediterranean region, but widely naturalised elsewhere in the temperate Northern Hemisphere.

items.name: Spearmint
items.growersTips:
Grow this vigorous spreader in a submerged 30cm pot to stop invasive roots choking your UK borders.
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on the leaves.
Cut stems back to ground level in autumn and mulch with compost to protect roots from wet UK winters.
Plant near carrots to deter carrot rust fly but keep mint in its own pot to avoid root competition.
Divide the root clump every three years in spring to rejuvenate growth and maintain strong flavour.
items.description: Spearmint, also known as garden mint, common mint, lamb mint and mackerel mint, is native to Europe and southern temperate Asia, extending from Ireland in the west to southern China in the east. It is naturalized in many other temperate parts of the world, including northern and southern Africa, North America, and South America. It is used as a flavouring in food and herbal teas. The aromatic oil, called oil of spearmint, is also used as a flavoring and sometimes as a scent.

items.name: Mentha piperita
items.growersTips:
Grow this vigorous spreader in a submerged 30cm pot to stop invasive runners overtaking UK borders.
Water daily in dry British summers to keep the compost damp, as dry soil triggers early flowering.
Cut stems back to the ground in October then mulch with compost to protect roots from winter rot.
Check the undersides of leaves in spring for orange rust pustules and destroy any infected stems.
Plant near cabbages to repel pests, but keep away from chamomile which stunts peppermint growth.
items.description: Peppermint is a hybrid species of mint, a cross between watermint and spearmint. Indigenous to Europe and the Middle East, the plant is now widely spread and cultivated in many regions of the world. It is occasionally found in the wild with its parent species.

items.name: Scarlet beebalm, Oswego tea
items.growersTips:
Plant Monarda didyma in moisture-retentive soil enriched with garden compost to prevent powdery mildew
Water deeply at the base weekly during dry UK summers rather than spraying foliage from above
Divide the congested root clumps every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour
Cut stems back to ground level in autumn and clear away fallen leaves to remove overwintering spores
Plant alongside Alliums or Nepeta to help deter aphids and mask the bare lower stems in summer
items.description: Monarda didyma, the crimson beebalm, scarlet beebalm, scarlet monarda, Eau-de-Cologne plant, Oswego tea, or bergamot, is a North American aromatic herb in the family Lamiaceae.

items.name: Perovskia atriplicifolia
items.growersTips:
Cut back hard to 15cm from the ground in April to promote strong new stems and prevent floppiness.
Plant in poor well-drained soil; wet winter clay will rot the roots of this Mediterranean native.
Position in maximum all-day sun to prevent the silvery stems from flopping and seeking light.
Water newly planted specimens weekly in summer, but leave established plants entirely to rainfall.
Partner with drought-tolerant Echinacea or Sedum spectabile for a classic UK late-summer display.
items.description: Salvia yangii, previously known as Perovskia atriplicifolia, and commonly called Russian sage, is a flowering herbaceous perennial plant and subshrub. Although not previously a member of Salvia, the genus widely known as sage, since 2017 it has been included within them. It has an upright habit, typically reaching 0.5–1.2 metres tall, with square stems and gray-green leaves that yield a distinctive odor when crushed. It is best known for its flowers. Its flowering season extends from mid-summer to late October, with blue to violet blossoms arranged into showy, branched panicles.

items.name: Common sunflower
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in April indoors in pots at two centimeters deep to protect young shoots from UK slugs.
Plant out in late May in a spot receiving at least six hours of direct British summer sun daily.
Stake tall cultivars like Russian Giant early using sturdy bamboo canes and soft twine ties.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Leave faded flower heads intact through autumn to provide essential winter seeds for local birds.
items.description: The common sunflower is a large annual forb in the daisy family Asteraceae. The domesticated form of common sunflower is harvested for its edible seeds, which come in two types: oil and confectionary seeds. Oilseed sunflowers are widely grown globally and represent the fourth most used vegetable oil in the world. They also are used widely as bird food or as food for livestock. In contrast, confectionary sunflowers are often eaten as a snack food or in baking. There also are horticultural sunflower varieties that are used as plantings in domestic gardens for aesthetics. items.name: Garden cosmos
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April, then plant out in late May after the final UK frost to avoid damage.
Plant in poor, well-drained soil because rich soil produces excess foliage instead of flowers.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are fifteen centimetres tall to encourage bushy growth.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly down to the next leaf node to prolong flowering until autumn frosts.
Stake taller varieties like Sensation in June to protect brittle stems from strong UK summer winds.
items.description: Cosmos bipinnatus, commonly called the garden cosmos, Mexican aster or cosmea, is a medium-sized flowering herbaceous plant in the daisy family Asteraceae, native to the Americas. The species and its varieties and cultivars are popular as ornamental plants in temperate climate gardens.

items.name: Cosmos sulphureus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 3mm deep, then plant out in late May after the final frost.
Grow in poor, well-drained soil because rich soil produces excess foliage instead of orange blooms.
Water young plants weekly, but leave established cosmos to dry out to prevent root rot in wet clay.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach 20cm high to encourage a bushy habit and more flowers.
Deadhead faded orange blooms weekly until October to prolong the flowering season in UK summers.
items.description: Cosmos sulphureus is a species of flowering plant in the sunflower family Asteraceae, also known as sulfur cosmos and yellow cosmos. It is native to Mexico, Central America, and northern South America, and naturalized in other parts of North and South America as well as in Europe, Asia, and Australia.

items.name: Purple coneflower
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass as they need light and a cold spell to germinate in the UK.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers rather than daily light sprinkling to build deep roots.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut stems back to ground level in late autumn to prevent rot in wet British winter soils.
Plant alongside Rudbeckia or ornamental grasses in gritty, free-draining soil to avoid winter wet.
items.description: Echinacea purpurea, the eastern purple coneflower, purple coneflower, hedgehog coneflower, or Echinacea, is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is native to parts of eastern North America and present to some extent in the wild in much of the eastern, southeastern and midwestern United States, as well as in the Canadian Province of Ontario. It is most common in the Ozarks, the Mississippi Valley, and the Ohio Valley. Its habitats include dry open woods, prairies, and barrens.

items.name: Rudbeckia fulgida
items.growersTips:
Plant Goldsturm in heavy UK clay improved with grit to prevent winter crown rot in wet soils.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers rather than daily light sprinkling to establish roots.
Cut back faded stems to the ground in March to protect the crown from frost and provide winter seeds.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent powdery mildew.
Combine with Calamagrostis Karl Foerster to create a classic UK late-summer prairie planting scheme.
items.description: Rudbeckia fulgida, the orange coneflower or perennial coneflower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, native to eastern North America.

items.name: Black-eyed Susan
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 2mm depth using a heated propagator to beat the cool UK spring.
Plant out in late May after frosts in free-draining soil enriched with grit to prevent root rot.
Water deeply at the base once a week in dry summer spells to avoid powdery mildew on the foliage.
Deadhead faded blooms weekly until October to stimulate continuous flowering before first frosts.
Protect young spring transplants from slugs using organic wool pellets or beer traps.
items.description: Rudbeckia hirta, commonly called black-eyed Susan and yellow coneflower, is a North American flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It grows to 1 metre tall with daisy-like yellow flower heads. There are numerous cultivars. It was used medicinally by Native Americans, and is the state flower of Maryland.

items.name: French marigold 'Dainty Marietta'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 5mm deep then transplant out in late May after the last UK frosts.
Pinch out the growing tips when seedlings are 10cm tall to encourage a bushy, floriferous habit.
Plant next to greenhouse tomatoes to deter whitefly with their strong-scented foliage.
Water at the base in the morning to prevent botrytis and powdery mildew in damp UK summers.
Deadhead spent single yellow-and-maroon blooms weekly to prolong flowering right up to first frost.
items.description: Tagetes patula, the French marigold, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, native to Mexico and Guatemala with several naturalised populations in many other countries. It is widely cultivated as an easily grown bedding plant with hundreds of cultivars, which often have bright yellow to orange flowers.

items.name: Aztec mariwanol relagantus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at five millimetres deep to beat the cool wet British spring weather.
Plant out in late May after the last frost into free-draining soil to prevent root rot in wet clay.
Water deeply at the base once a week rather than daily sprinkles to encourage deep drought-proof roots.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are fifteen centimetres tall to force bushy side-branching.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly down to the next leaf node to prolong the flowering display until frost.
items.description: Tagetes erecta, the Aztec marigold, Mexican marigold, big marigold, cempaxochitl or cempasúchil, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Tagetes native to Mexico and Central America. Despite being native to the Americas, it is often called the African marigold. In Mexico, this plant is found in the wild in the states of México, Michoacán, Puebla, Veracruz and Guerrero.

items.name: Pot marigold
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors from March to May at a depth of one centimetre in well-drained soil.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly in summer to prolong the flowering season well into autumn.
Plant next to tomatoes or potatoes to deter aphids and attract beneficial hoverflies.
Water only at the base of the plant in the morning to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK summers.
Sow a second batch in September for early spring blooms that survive mild UK winters.
items.description: Calendula officinalis, Mary's gold, common marigold, the pot marigold, Scotch marigold, or ruddles, is a flowering plant in the daisy family, Asteraceae. It is probably native to southern Europe, but its long history of cultivation makes its precise origin unknown, and it is widely naturalised. The florets are edible and the plant has historically been used as medicine.

items.name: Garden aster
items.growersTips:
Plant Aster amellus in free-draining chalky or gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Position in full sun to maximize late-summer blooms and reduce the risk of powdery mildew infection.
Cut stems back to the ground in early spring rather than autumn to protect the crown from UK frosts.
Divide the congested root clumps every three years in spring to maintain plant vigor and flowering.
Water deeply at the base during dry summer spells, keeping foliage dry to stop fungal diseases.
items.description: Aster amellus, the European Michaelmas daisy, is a perennial herbaceous plant and the type species of the genus Aster and the family Asteraceae.

items.name: New York aster
items.growersTips:
Divide clumps every third spring to maintain vigour and prevent powdery mildew in damp UK weather.
Cut stems back by half in late May to encourage bushier growth and more autumn flowers.
Water at the base rather than overhead to stop fungal leaf spot during humid British summers.
Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive soil with compost to prevent the roots from drying out.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots and protect them with organic pellets.
items.description: Symphyotrichum novi-belgii, commonly called New York aster, is a species of flowering plant. It is the type species for Symphyotrichum, a genus in the family Asteraceae, whose species were once considered to be part of the genus Aster. Plants in both these genera are popularly known as Michaelmas daisy because they bloom around September 29, St. Michael’s Day.

items.name: Common yarrow
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly on the surface in spring as they need light to germinate in the UK climate.
Grow in poor well-drained soil to prevent floppy stems and avoid adding rich compost or manure.
Deadhead faded flowers in July to encourage a second flush of blooms before the autumn frosts.
Divide established clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent center rot.
Avoid overwatering once established as this native wildflower is highly drought-tolerant in summer.
items.description: Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. Growing to 1 metre tall, it is characterized by small whitish flowers, a tall stem of fernlike leaves, and a pungent odor.

items.name: Leucanthemum ×superbum
items.growersTips:
Divide clumps every three springs to maintain vigour and prevent the centre of the plant dying out.
Deadhead spent blooms down to the next lateral bud to trigger a second flush of late summer flowers.
Plant in free-draining soil with grit to prevent winter wet from rotting the crown in UK winters.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in spring, keeping it clear of the emerging stems.
Watch for aphids and earwigs on young buds, especially during damp British spring mornings.
items.description: Leucanthemum × superbum, the Shasta daisy, is a commonly grown flowering herbaceous perennial plant with the classic daisy appearance of white petals around a yellow disc, similar to the oxeye daisy Leucanthemum vulgare Lam, but larger.

items.name: Large-flowered tickseed
items.growersTips:
Divide clumps every two to three years in early spring to maintain vigor in damp UK winter soils.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly from June to October to stimulate continuous new flower bud production.
Plant in free-draining soil with grit added to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Cut the entire plant back to ground level in late autumn after the first hard frost hits.
Sow seeds indoors in March at a depth of two millimeters before transplanting out after May frosts.
items.description: Coreopsis grandiflora is a North American species of perennial plant in the family Asteraceae. The common name is large-flowered tickseed. It is found in eastern Canada and much of the United States, especially the south-central part of the country. The species is widely cultivated in China and naturalized there.

items.name: D. pinnata
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers 10cm deep in mid-May after the last frosts, ensuring the old stem points upwards.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily sprinkling to encourage deep, drought-resistant roots.
Apply organic slug pellets or beer traps in spring to protect vulnerable emerging shoots.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach 40cm high to promote bushy growth and more blooms.
Lift tubers in November after the first frost blackens foliage, then store them in dry compost.
items.description: Dahlia pinnata is a species in the genus Dahlia, family Asteraceae, with the common name garden dahlia. It is the type species of the genus and is widely cultivated.

items.name: Chrysanthemum morifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant rooted cuttings in late May after frosts, spacing them 45cm apart at the same depth as their pot.
Pinch out the growing tips in early June to encourage bushy growth and maximize autumn flower buds.
Water deeply at the base weekly during dry summer spells, keeping foliage dry to prevent rust disease.
Apply a high-potassium liquid feed every fortnight from midsummer until the flower buds begin to open.
Lift stools in November, cut stems to 10cm, and store in dry compost in a frost-free UK greenhouse.
items.description: Chrysanthemum × morifolium is a hybrid species of perennial plant in the genus Chrysanthemum of the family Asteraceae.

items.name: Rugosa rose
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn or winter at the same depth as the pot to establish roots before the spring dry spell.
Prune in late winter by cutting back one-third of old stems to the base to encourage fresh growth.
Avoid chemical sprays as Rugosa foliage is highly sensitive and will yellow and drop if treated.
Grow in sandy or acidic soils as they tolerate coastal salt spray and wind better than other roses.
Leave late summer blooms on the shrub to allow the large orange-red hips to develop for winter birds.
items.description: Rosa rugosa is a species of rose native to eastern Asia, in northeastern China, Japan, Korea and southeastern Siberia, where it grows on beach coasts, often on sand dunes. It is naturalized in much of Europe and parts of the United States and Canada. It should not be confused with Rosa multiflora, which is also known as "Japanese rose". The Latin word "rugosa" means "wrinkled", referring to the wrinkled leaves. Often used as an ornamental plant, it has become invasive in parts of Europe, North America and South America.

items.name: Dog rose
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root dog rose in November at the same depth it was previously grown to establish roots.
Prune in late winter by removing one-third of old stems to the base to encourage fresh hip growth.
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall.
Grow in heavy clay or poor soil but avoid waterlogged spots where root rot can kill the shrub.
Underplant with wild garlic to naturally deter aphids and blackspot in damp British spring weather.
items.description: Rosa canina, the dog rose, is a variable climbing, wild rose species native to Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia.

items.name: Geum chiloense
items.growersTips:
Divide Geum chiloense every three years in spring to prevent the woody crown from rotting in UK rain.
Plant crowns level with the soil surface in fertile, moisture-retentive but free-draining loam.
Deadhead faded stems down to the basal leaves weekly from May to August to trigger a second flush.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on the foliage.
Grow alongside Nepeta or Salvia to support the heavy flower stems and mask dying post-bloom leaves.
items.description: Geum quellyon, commonly called scarlet avens, Chilean avens or Grecian rose, is a perennial herb in the family Rosaceae. It is native to the central and southern regions of Chile. G. quellyon has been introduced to other countries including Belgium, Bolivia, and the United Kingdom, where it was first planted in 1826.

items.name: Water Avens
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, mimicking UK bog gardens or damp woodland edges.
Water consistently during dry summer spells to keep the soil constantly damp but not waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Cut back faded flower stems to the base in midsummer to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Plant alongside Astilbe or Candelabra Primulas which thrive in the same cool, damp UK soil conditions.
items.description: Geum rivale, the water avens, is a flowering plant in the genus Geum within the family Rosaceae. Other names of the plant are nodding avens, drooping avens, cure-all, water flower and Indian chocolate. It is native to the temperate regions of Europe, Central Asia and parts of North America, where it is known as the purple avens. It grows in bogs and damp meadows, and produces nodding red flowers from May to September.

items.name: Alchemilla mollis
items.growersTips:
Cut back faded foliage and spent flower stems to ground level in August to trigger fresh new growth.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring by lifting and splitting with a sharp spade.
Plant bare-root divisions with the crown sitting exactly level with the soil surface in autumn.
Shake dried seedheads into a bucket in late summer to prevent aggressive self-seeding in borders.
Position in partial shade alongside hardy geraniums to prevent leaves from scorching in dry summers.
items.description: Alchemilla mollis, the garden lady's-mantle or lady's-mantle, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. This herbaceous perennial plant is native to Southern Europe and grown throughout the world as an ornamental garden plant. It grows 30 to 45 cm tall, with leaves that are palmately veined, with a scalloped and serrated margin. The stipules are noteworthy in that they are fused together and leaf like. The chartreuse yellow flowers are held in dense clusters above the foliage. A. mollis has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. The plant self-seeds freel

items.name: Mead wort
items.growersTips:
Grow in moist, boggy soil or pond edges, mimicking UK fens, and never let the roots dry out.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames, as they require winter chilling to break dormancy in the UK.
Cut back the flower stems to ground level in late autumn to keep the clump tidy and prevent mildew.
Plant alongside moisture-loving UK natives like Marsh Marigold and Purple Loosestrife in partial shade.
Watch for powdery mildew in dry summers; improve airflow and water the soil directly, not the leaves.
items.description: Filipendula ulmaria, commonly known as meadowsweet or mead wort, is a perennial herbaceous plant in the family Rosaceae that grows in damp meadows. It is native throughout most of Europe and Western Asia. It has been introduced and naturalised in North America.

items.name: Shrubby Cinquefoil
items.growersTips:
Prune hard in early spring by cutting stems back to fifteen centimetres to boost summer flowering.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile well-drained soil as rich soils produce lush leaves but few buds.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry UK summers until established then leave to dry out.
Plant yellow cultivars in full sun but place pink or red types in partial shade to prevent fading.
Avoid heavy clay sites by digging in plenty of grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
items.description: Dasiphora fruticosa is a species of hardy deciduous flowering shrub in the family Rosaceae, native to the cool temperate and subarctic regions of the northern hemisphere, often growing at high elevations in mountains. Dasiphora fruticosa is still widely referenced in the horticultural literature under its synonym Potentilla fruticosa. Common names include shrubby cinquefoil, golden hardhack, bush cinquefoil, shrubby five-finger, widdy, kuril tea and tundra rose.

items.name: Common laurel
items.growersTips:
Prune in late spring or late summer using secateurs to avoid cutting leaves in half and causing rot
Water deeply once a week during the first dry summer to establish roots in heavy UK clay soils
Plant with the root flare level with the soil surface to prevent stem rot in damp UK winters
Watch for shothole disease in wet springs and prune out affected branches to improve air flow
Incorporate well-rotted manure to enrich sandy or chalky soils before planting this hungry shrub
items.description: Prunus laurocerasus, also known as cherry laurel, common laurel and sometimes English laurel in North America, is an evergreen species of cherry (Prunus), native to regions bordering the Black Sea in southwestern Asia and southeastern Europe, from Albania and Bulgaria east through Turkey to the Caucasus Mountains and northern Iran.

items.name: Wild cherry
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root whips between November and March in deep, moist, well-drained loam to aid rooting.
Prune strictly in midsummer to prevent silver leaf disease and bacterial canker infections.
Water deeply every fortnight during the first dry summer to establish the shallow root system.
Apply a thick mulch of composted bark in spring, keeping it clear of the collar to prevent rot.
Watch for black cherry aphid in May and encourage ladybirds or lacewings as a natural control.
items.description: Prunus avium, commonly called wild cherry, sweet cherry or gean, is a species of cherry, a flowering plant in the rose family, Rosaceae. It is native to western Eurasia and naturalized elsewhere. It is an ancestor of P. cerasus.

items.name: Scarlet firethorn
items.growersTips:
Prune in late spring after flowering to retain berries and shape the shrub against a UK wall.
Plant in well-drained soil with the root ball level with the ground to prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells until the root system is fully established.
Inspect leaves in spring for pyracantha scab and woolly aphid, common in damp UK climates.
Train young shoots onto horizontal support wires spaced thirty centimetres apart on garden fences.
items.description: Pyracantha coccinea, the scarlet firethorn is the European species of firethorn or red firethorn that has been cultivated in gardens since the late 16th century. The tree has small white flowers. It produces small, bright red berries. Its leaves are slightly toothed and grow opposite to one another. The fruit is bitter and astringent, making it inedible when raw. The fruit can be cooked to make jellies, jams, sauces and marmalade. It ranges from southern Europe to western Asia. It has been introduced to North America and cultivated there as an ornamental plant since the 18th century.

items.name: Helleborus orientalis
items.growersTips:
Cut back all old leathery foliage in late January to reveal new buds and prevent black spot disease.
Plant crowns shallowly with the bud just below the soil surface to prevent rot in wet UK winters.
Incorporate well-rotted leafmould or manure to mimic their native damp, alkaline woodland soils.
Apply a thick mulch of organic matter annually in autumn to keep roots cool and retain moisture.
Watch for hellebore aphid in spring, washing them off with water before they distort the flowers.
items.description: Helleborus orientalis, or the Lenten rose, is a perennial flowering plant and species of hellebore in the buttercup family, Ranunculaceae, native to Greece and Turkey.

items.name: Black hellebore
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained alkaline soil enriched with well-rotted leafmould to mimic forest floors.
Position in dappled shade sheltered from cold winds to protect the delicate midwinter white blooms.
Snip off old tattered leaves in December to expose emerging flower buds and prevent black spot fungus.
Apply an annual top-dressing of grit around the crown in autumn to prevent wet winter crown rot.
Water deeply during dry summer months when the plant is setting its flower buds underground.
items.description:
Helleborus niger, commonly called Christmas rose or black hellebore, is an evergreen perennial flowering plant in the buttercup family, Ranunculaceae. It is one of about 20 species from the genus Helleborus.
It is a poisonous cottage garden favourite because it flowers in the depths of winter.

items.name: Stinking hellebore
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained chalky or alkaline soil to mimic its native UK limestone woodland habitat
Prune the faded flowering stems right back to the base in May to encourage fresh healthy new foliage
Wear gloves when handling to avoid skin irritation from its toxic sap and watch out for aphids in spring
Sow fresh seeds in pots outdoors in late summer as they require winter cold to germinate naturally
Position in dappled shade under deciduous trees to protect the evergreen leaves from harsh summer sun
items.description: Helleborus foetidus, known variously as stinking hellebore, dungwort, setterwort and bear's foot, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to the mountainous regions of Central and Southern Europe and Asia Minor. It is found wild in many parts of England, especially on limestone soil.

items.name: Common columbine
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in late summer, barely covering them as they need light to germinate in UK soil.
Water young plants weekly until established, then only during dry spells to prevent powdery mildew.
Cut flower stems to the ground in July to stop self-seeding and encourage a fresh flush of leaves.
Watch for the Aquilegia sawfly larvae in May, handpicking them immediately to prevent defoliation.
Plant alongside hostas or ferns in partial shade to hide dying foliage after the spring bloom.
items.description: Aquilegia vulgaris is a species of perennial flowering plant of the genus Aquilegia (columbine) in the family Ranunculaceae. Commonly called the common columbine, European crowfoot, and granny's bonnet, it presently possesses the most expansive range and greatest morphological variability in its genus. The current wild range of A. vulgaris includes its native range in Europe as well as introduced populations in Asia, Oceania, North America, and South America.

items.name: Winter windflower
items.growersTips:
Soak the shrivelled tubers in tepid water for twenty-four hours before planting in autumn.
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in moist, well-drained soil under deciduous trees or shrubs.
In heavy UK clay, mix grit into the planting hole to prevent winter waterlogging and tuber rot.
Leave the dying foliage to wither naturally in late spring to feed the tubers for next year.
Associate with snowdrops and early daffodils for a layered spring display in partial shade.
items.description: Anemonoides blanda, syn. Anemone blanda, the Balkan anemone, Grecian windflower, or winter windflower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. The species is native to southeastern Europe and the Middle East. The specific epithet blanda means "mild" or "charming". The genus name is derived from the Greek word anemos, or wind.

items.name: Anemone ×hybrida
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to prevent the roots from drying out.
Mulch annually in late autumn with well-rotted manure to protect young crowns from severe UK frosts.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late winter while the plant is dormant to avoid transplant shock.
Cut flowered stems down to the ground in late autumn to keep the clump tidy and encourage fresh growth.
Plant alongside Hostas or Astilbes to mask the scruffy post-flowering foliage in late summer.
items.description: Eriocapitella × hybrida is a hybrid of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae. The parents of the hybrid are E. japonica and E. vitifolia. Cultivars of the hybrid are commonly known as Japanese anemone hybrids.

items.name: Indian virgin's bower
items.growersTips:
Plant the root ball 8cm deep in moist, alkaline to neutral soil to prevent clematis wilt disease.
Prune immediately after flowering in June by cutting back overlong shoots to a strong side bud.
Shade the roots with flat stones or low-growing companion plants like hardy geraniums in summer.
Water deeply once a week during dry spring spells to support the rapid burst of early May blooms.
Watch for earwig damage on young petals and trap them overnight using upturned straw-filled pots.
items.description: Clematis montana, the mountain clematis, also Himalayan clematis or anemone clematis, is a flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae. A vigorous deciduous climber, in late spring it is covered with a mass of small blooms for a period of about four weeks. The odorous flowers are white or pink, four-petalled, with prominent yellow anthers. It is native to mountain areas of Asia from Afghanistan to Taiwan.

items.name: Clematis viticella
items.growersTips:
Plant your viticella clematis deep with the root crown five to ten centimetres below the soil level.
Hard prune all stems down to thirty centimetres above ground level every year in late February.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to keep the roots cool and damp.
Mulch the base in spring with compost and plant low shrubs to shade the roots from direct midday sun.
Watch for earwigs chewing the delicate flowers in July and trap them using upturned straw-filled pots.
items.description: Clematis viticella, the Italian leather flower, purple clematis, or virgin's bower, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to Southern Europe and Western Asia, from the Italic Peninsula to Iran. This deciduous climber was the first clematis imported into English gardens, where it was already being grown in 1569 by Hugh Morgan, apothecary to Elizabeth I. By 1597, when it was already being called "virgin's bower", there were two varieties in English gardens, a blue and a red.

items.name: Delphinium elatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep rich moisture-retentive soil in spring adding garden compost and grit for drainage.
Stake young stems in April using sturdy canes or grow-through rings to prevent wind damage in summer.
Apply organic slug pellets or beer traps in early spring as new shoots emerge to stop slug damage.
Cut faded flower spikes down to the ground in July and feed with liquid fertiliser for a second flush.
Propagate by taking basal cuttings in spring rather than dividing the woody crown to prevent rot.
items.description: Delphinium elatum is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, known by the common names alpine delphinium, bee larkspur, or candle larkspur. It is native to temperate Asia and Europe, it is an erect herbaceous perennial growing to 1.8 m (5.9 ft), with deeply divided leaves. It produces spikes of blue or purple flowers in summer.

items.name: Wolf's bane
items.growersTips:
Wear thick gloves and long sleeves when handling to avoid absorbing its highly toxic alkaloids.
Plant tubers five centimetres deep in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial woodland shade.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut faded flower spikes to the ground in autumn to encourage healthy regrowth the following spring.
Watch for delphinium moth caterpillars and treat infestations by hand-picking with sturdy gloves.
items.description: Aconitum napellus, monkshood, aconite, Venus' chariot or wolfsbane, is a species of highly toxic flowering plants in the genus Aconitum of the family Ranunculaceae, native and endemic to western and central Europe. A perennial plant, it is herbaceous and grows to 1 m tall, with hairless stems and leaves. The leaves are rounded, 5–10 cm (2.0–3.9 in) diameter, palmately divided into five to seven deeply lobed segments. The flowers are dark purple to bluish-purple, narrow oblong helmet-shaped, 1–2 cm (0.39–0.79 in) tall. Plants native to Asia and North America formerly listed as A. napellus are n

items.name: Tall buttercup
items.growersTips:
Grow in moist heavy clay or loam in a wildflower meadow or bog garden to mimic its damp UK habitat.
Sow seeds in autumn directly onto the soil surface as they require winter cold stratification to germ.
Wear gloves when weeding or dividing in spring to avoid skin irritation from the toxic sap ranunculin.
Control spreading by deadheading faded yellow flowers in midsummer before they self-seed aggressively.
Plant alongside damp-loving native companions like Ragged Robin and Cuckoo Flower in partial shade.
items.description: Ranunculus acris is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, and is one of the more common buttercups across Europe and temperate Eurasia. Common names include meadow buttercup, tall buttercup, common buttercup and giant buttercup.

items.name: Sweet pea 'Millennium'
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in deep pots during October or February to accommodate their long, active root systems.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants reach about ten centimetres tall to encourage bushy growth.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells to prevent bud drop in the British summer.
Tie stems regularly to a sturdy support frame to keep the heavy, multi-flowered stems upright.
Cut flowers every two days to prevent seed pod formation and prolong the summer blooming period.
items.description: The sweet pea, Lathyrus odoratus, is a flowering plant in the genus Lathyrus in the family Fabaceae (legumes), native to Sicily, southern Italy and the Aegean Islands.

items.name: Bigleaf Lupine
items.growersTips:
Plant crown level with the soil in deep, fertile, acidic to neutral ground to prevent root rot.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to keep the deep taproot hydrated.
Search for and handpick giant lupin aphids from stems in May before they ruin the flower spikes.
Cut spent flower spikes down to the base in July to encourage a second flush of late-summer blooms.
Sow seeds in pots in autumn and overwinter in a cold frame to plant out after the spring frosts.
items.description: Lupinus polyphyllus, the large-leaved lupine, big-leaved lupine, many-leaved lupine, blue-pod lupine, or, primarily in cultivation, garden lupin, is a species of lupine (lupin) native to western North America from southern Alaska and British Columbia and western Wyoming, and south to Utah and California. It commonly grows along streams and creeks, preferring moist habitats.

items.name: Wisteria sinensis
items.growersTips:
Prune twice a year in July or August to five buds and again in January or February to two buds.
Plant grafted wisteria with the graft union at least five centimetres above the soil level.
Water newly planted wisteria deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells to establish roots.
Grow in fertile well drained soil against a sunny south or west facing wall to ripen flowering wood.
Train main stems horizontally along sturdy wires spaced thirty centimetres apart to encourage blooms.
items.description: Wisteria sinensis, commonly known as the Chinese wisteria, is a species of flowering plant in the pea family, native to China, in the provinces of Guangxi, Guizhou, Hebei, Henan, Hubei, Shaanxi, and Yunnan. Growing 20–30 m (66–98 ft) tall, it is a deciduous vine. It is widely cultivated in temperate regions for its twisting stems and masses of scented flowers in hanging racemes, in spring.

items.name: White clover
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 5mm into firm, weed-free soil for high germination rates in UK rain.
Inoculate seeds with Rhizobium bacteria before sowing in poor soils to boost nitrogen fixation.
Mow white clover lawns to 5cm in late summer to encourage dense, low-growing winter ground cover.
Sow Abercrest or Pipolina micro-clover cultivars for a tidier, less invasive UK garden lawn mix.
Grow clover alongside heavy-feeding brassicas to naturally supply nitrogen and deter cabbage root fly.
items.description: Trifolium repens, the white clover, is a herbaceous perennial plant in the bean family, Fabaceae.

items.name: Tic bean
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds five centimetres deep in late autumn to establish strong roots before the winter frosts.
Support the heavy stems with hazel twigs or pea sticks in spring to prevent wind damage on wet soil.
Pinch out the growing tips in May to deter black bean aphid attacks and encourage pod development.
Water deeply once a week during flowering and pod set if the UK summer weather becomes dry.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into heavy clay soils before planting to improve drainage and tilth.
items.description: Vicia faba, commonly known as the broad bean, fava bean, or faba bean, is a species of vetch, a flowering plant in the pea and bean family Fabaceae. It is widely cultivated as a crop for human consumption, and also as a cover crop. Varieties with smaller, harder seeds that are fed to horses or other animals are called field bean, tic bean or tick bean. This legume is commonly consumed in many national and regional cuisines.

items.name: Bearded iris
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to the UK sun to bake and ensure reliable flowering.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils to prevent winter rot in wet British conditions.
Cut foliage back to a clean five-inch fan in autumn to reduce wind rock and prevent leaf spot.
Divide congested clumps every three years in late summer after flowering to maintain plant vigour.
Watch for iris sawfly larvae in spring and handpick them to prevent rapid defoliation of leaves.
items.description: Iris × germanica is the accepted name for a species of flowering plants in the family Iridaceae commonly known as the bearded iris or the German bearded iris. It is of hybrid origin. Varieties include I. × g. var. florentina.

items.name: Iris reticulata
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres to protect them from severe UK winter frosts.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils to prevent bulb rot during wet British autumn and winter months.
Apply a high-potash liquid feed after flowering to help the bulbs build energy for next spring.
Plant alongside low-growing sedums to cover the untidy, dying foliage as it yellows in late spring.
Grow in terracotta pots to easily move them under cover and keep them dry during summer dormancy.
items.description: Iris reticulata, the snow iris, netted iris, or golden netted iris, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae.

items.name: Iris sibirica
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes just below the soil surface in autumn, keeping them moist but well-drained.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to ensure robust flowering in the UK's early summer.
Cut the foliage back to the ground in late autumn after it turns yellow to prevent pests.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early autumn to maintain plant vigour.
Grow in moisture-retentive, slightly acidic soil alongside primulas or astilbes in damp borders.
items.description: Iris sibirica, commonly known as Siberian iris or Siberian flag, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae. It is a rhizomatous herbaceous perennial, from Europe and Central Asia. It has long green grass-like leaves, tall stem, 2–5 violet-blue, to blue, and occasionally white flowers. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant in temperate regions.

items.name: Giant crocus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm to protect them from winter frosts and foraging squirrels.
Plant in well-drained soil as wet UK winter clay will rot the bulbs; add grit to the planting hole.
Protect emerging spring buds from birds by placing physical barriers or black cotton thread nearby.
Let the foliage die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before mowing lawns with crocuses.
Divide congested clumps in late spring after flowering to maintain vigorous blooms in future years.
items.description: Crocus vernus is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae, native to the Alps, the Pyrenees, and the Balkans. Its cultivars and those of Crocus flavus are used as ornamental plants. The Dutch crocuses are larger than the other cultivated crocus species. Depending on the year, Crocus vernus starts flowering about the same time or up to 2 weeks after Crocus chrysanthus starts flowering. Height: 4–6 inches (10–15 cm).

items.name: Early crocus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in September or October at a depth of 8cm to 10cm to protect them from winter frosts.
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent the bulbs from rotting during wet UK winters.
Protect newly planted bulbs from squirrels by laying wire mesh just under the soil surface.
Mow lawns only after the foliage has naturally died back in late spring to ensure blooms next year.
Plant under deciduous trees or shrubs to ensure they get full sun before the canopy leaves emerge.
items.description: Crocus tommasinianus, the woodland crocus, early crocus, or Tommasini's crocus, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae. It is named after the botanist Muzio G. Spirito de Tommasini (1794–1879). It is native to Bulgaria, Hungary, Albania, and the former Yugoslavia. It is often referred to as the early or snow crocus, but these terms are shared with several other species, although C. tommasinianus is amongst the first to bloom. Multiple plants are often called tommies in the horticultural trade.

items.name: Didier's tulip
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in late November to avoid tulip fire disease, placing them 15cm deep in sandy, grit soil.
Water container-grown bulbs sparingly in winter, only when the top 5cm of compost feels dry.
Snip off faded flower heads in May but leave the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks.
Lift bulbs in July after leaves yellow, store in a dry shed, and replant in autumn to ensure blooms.
Plant alongside forget-me-nots to mask yellowing tulip leaves and deter aphids in spring.
items.description: Tulipa gesneriana, the Didier's tulip or garden tulip, is a species of plant in the lily family, cultivated as an ornamental in many countries because of its large, showy flowers. This tall, late-blooming species has a single blooming flower and linear or broadly lanceolate leaves. This is a complex hybridized neo-species, and can also be called Tulipa × gesneriana. Most of the cultivars of tulip are derived from Tulipa gesneriana. It has become naturalised in parts of central and southern Europe and scattered locations in North America.

items.name: Common daffodil
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10 to 15cm in moist but well-drained soil to prevent basal rot.
Leave foliage intact for six weeks after spring flowering to build energy for next year's blooms.
Watch for the narcissus bulb fly in May and firm the soil around dying leaves to block egg laying.
Rejuvenate congested clumps by lifting and dividing them in late summer while the bulbs are dormant.
Grow in dappled shade under deciduous trees to mimic their natural UK woodland habitat.
items.description: Narcissus pseudonarcissus, commonly named the wild daffodil or Lent lily, is a perennial flowering plant.

items.name: Poet's daffodil
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres to prevent them drying out in UK summers.
Grow in damp heavy clay soil or poorly drained lawns as this species dislikes dry summer earth.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before mowing UK lawns.
Plant alongside snake head fritillaries which thrive in the same damp British spring conditions.
Watch for the narcissus bulb fly in May and firm the soil around stems to block egg laying.
items.description: Narcissus poeticus, the poet's daffodil, poet's narcissus, nargis, pheasant's eye, findern flower or pinkster lily, was one of the first daffodils to be cultivated, and is frequently identified as the narcissus of ancient times. It is also often associated with the Greek legend of Narcissus. It is the type species of the genus Narcissus.

items.name: Galanthus nivalis
items.growersTips:
Plant Galanthus nivalis bulbs in green during spring rather than dry bulbs in autumn for success.
Incorporate leaf mould into heavy clay or sandy UK soil to mimic their natural deciduous woodland.
Plant bulbs at a depth of three times their height, roughly 10cm deep, to prevent drying out.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering in March while the leaves are still green.
Position under deciduous shrubs to ensure winter sun and essential summer shade while dormant.
items.description: Galanthus nivalis, the snowdrop or common snowdrop, is the best-known and most widespread of the 20 species in its genus, Galanthus. Snowdrops are among the first bulbs to bloom in spring and can form impressive carpets of white in areas where they are native or have been naturalised. They should not be confused with the snowflakes, in the genera Leucojum and Acis.

items.name: Wood bell
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimeters in moist, well-drained soil under deciduous shade.
Water during dry spring periods but keep soil relatively dry during their summer dormant phase.
Avoid planting near Spanish bluebells to prevent hybridization and preserve the native UK species.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before clearing the leaves.
Divide congested clumps in late summer by lifting and replanting bulbs immediately to boost blooms.
items.description: Hyacinthoides non-scripta is a bulbous perennial plant found in Atlantic areas from the north-western part of the Iberian Peninsula to the British Isles, and also frequently used as a garden plant. It is known in English as the common bluebell, English bluebell or simply bluebell, a name which is used in Scotland to refer to the harebell, Campanula rotundifolia. In spring, H. non-scripta produces a nodding, one-sided inflorescence of 5–12 tubular, sweet-scented violet–blue flowers, with strongly recurved tepals, and 3–6 long, linear, basal leaves.

items.name: Lilium regale
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at least fifteen to twenty centimetres deep to protect them from UK winter frost.
Place grit at the base of the planting hole to prevent bulb rot in wet UK clay soils.
Apply organic mulch in spring to keep the root zone cool while the stems grow into full UK sun.
Handpick red lily beetles and their larvae from leaves daily from April to prevent total defoliation.
Stake the heavy flower stems early in summer to prevent wind damage from sudden UK rainstorms.
items.description: Lilium regale, called the regal lily, royal lily, king's lily,or, in New Zealand, the Christmas lily, is a species of flowering plant in the lily family Liliaceae, with trumpet-shaped flowers. It is native to the western part of Sichuan Province in southwestern China, and cultivated elsewhere as an ornamental. It was introduced to England in 1903 by Ernest Henry Wilson.

items.name: Martagon lily
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15-20cm deep in autumn in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil with added leaf mould.
Position in dappled shade or woodland edges, as they dislike the hot afternoon UK summer sun.
Keep soil moist but never waterlogged, watering deeply during dry spring spells before flowering.
Hand-pick red lily beetles and their grubs from April onwards to prevent total foliage ruin.
Leave the faded flower stems to die back naturally in autumn to feed the bulb for next summer.
items.description: Lilium martagon, the martagon lily or Turk's cap lily, is a Eurasian species of lily. It has a widespread native region extending from Portugal east through Europe and Asia as far east as Mongolia.

items.name: Allium giganteum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn 15cm deep in free-draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Position in full sun sheltered from strong winds that snap the tall 1.5-metre flower stems.
Plant behind mid-height perennials like hardy geraniums to hide the ugly, yellowing foliage.
Avoid watering once the foliage dies back in summer to let the bulb ripen in dry soil.
Leave the architectural dried seed heads intact for winter structure and frost interest.
items.description: Allium giganteum, common name giant onion or giant leek, is an Asian species of onion in the amaryllis family (Amaryllidaceae), subfamily Allioideae, native to central and southwestern Asia but cultivated in many countries as a flowering garden plant. It is the tallest species of Allium in common cultivation, growing to 1.5 metres (4.9 ft).

items.name: Purple Sensation
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in October or November at a depth of fifteen centimetres to prevent winter frost damage.
Choose a south-facing spot with free-draining soil to prevent bulb rot during wet UK winters.
Hide the unsightly yellowing foliage by planting them among hardy geraniums or herbaceous peonies.
Avoid watering once the flowers fade in July to let the bulbs bake and dry out in the summer soil.
Leave the dried seed heads intact over winter to provide structural interest and food for UK birds.
items.description: Allium hollandicum, the Persian onion or Dutch garlic, is a species of flowering plant native to Iran and Kyrgyzstan but widely cultivated as an ornamental because of its umbels of attractive purple flowers. It is reportedly naturalized in Saint Louis County, Minnesota.

items.name: Fritillaria meleagris
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 10cm deep in autumn, placing them on their sides to prevent water collecting in the crown.
Grow in damp, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking their native UK wet meadow habitat.
Never let the soil dry out during spring, but ensure it remains moist and cool even in summer.
Leave foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering to feed the bulb for next year.
Protect emerging spring shoots from lily beetles, which will quickly strip the delicate foliage.
items.description: Fritillaria meleagris is a Eurasian species of flowering plant in the lily family Liliaceae. Its common names include snake's head fritillary, snake's head, chess flower, frog-cup, guinea-hen flower, guinea flower, leper lily, Lazarus bell, chequered lily, chequered daffodil, drooping tulip or, in the British Isles, simply fritillary. The plant is a bulbous perennial native to the flood river plains of Europe where it grows in abundance.

items.name: Common hyacinth
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm to 15cm to protect them from severe UK winter frosts.
Wear gloves when handling bulbs to prevent skin irritation caused by calcium oxalate crystals.
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch in November to insulate bulbs against wet UK winter rot.
Cut faded flower spikes to the base in spring but leave foliage to die back naturally for six weeks.
Grow in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent bulb rot during damp British autumn and winter months.
items.description: Hyacinthus orientalis, the common hyacinth, garden hyacinth or Dutch hyacinth, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, subfamily Scilloideae. It is native to western Asia, from southern Turkey, through Syria and Lebanon to northern Israel. It was introduced to Europe in the 16th century. It is widely cultivated everywhere in the temperate world for its strongly fragrant flowers which appear exceptionally early in the season, and frequently forced to flower at Christmas time.

items.name: Tomato
items.growersTips:
Plant cordon varieties deep up to their first leaves in May to encourage a strong, deep root system.
Pinch out side shoots of indeterminate types weekly in summer to focus energy on fruit production.
Water consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot, avoiding wetting the leaves in damp UK weather.
Remove lower leaves up to the first truss in August to improve air circulation and prevent late blight.
Underplant with French marigolds to deter whitefly and glasshouse pests common in UK gardens.
items.description: The tomato is a plant whose fruit is an edible berry that is eaten as a vegetable. The tomato is a member of the nightshade family that includes tobacco, potato, and chili peppers. It originated from western South America, and may have been domesticated there, in Mexico, or in Central America. The Spanish introduced tomatoes to Eurasia in the Columbian exchange in the 16th century.

items.name: Potato
items.growersTips:
Chit seed tubers in a cool, bright frost-free room from February to give crops a head start.
Plant tubers 12cm deep in mid-spring, spacing rows 60cm apart to allow room for earthing up.
Draw soil up around growing stems to block light, preventing green toxic tubers and frost damage.
Water tubers deeply once they reach marble size in June to prevent common scab and boost yields.
Watch for potato blight in warm, wet summer weather and cut infected foliage to ground level.
items.description: The potato is a starchy tuberous vegetable native to the Americas that is consumed as a staple food in many parts of the world. Potatoes are underground stem tubers of the plant Solanum tuberosum, a perennial in the nightshade family Solanaceae.

items.name: Capsicum annuum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in February or March using a heated propagator to offset the cool UK spring.
Pot on into peat-free compost once the first true leaves appear, burying the stem up to those leaves.
Move plants to a greenhouse or sunny patio only after late May frosts have completely passed.
Pinch out the growing tip when plants reach twenty centimetres high to encourage a bushy habit.
Water consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot, avoiding wetting the foliage.
items.description: Capsicum annuum is a flowering plant in the family Solanaceae (nightshades), native to the northern regions of South America and to southwestern North America. The plant produces berries of many colors including red, green, and yellow, often with pungent taste. It is one of the oldest cultivated crops, with domestication dating back to around 6,000 years ago in regions of Mexico. The genus Capsicum has over 30 species but Capsicum annuum is the primary species in its genus, as it has been widely cultivated for human consumption for a substantial amount of time and has spread across the world.

items.name: Eggplant
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in warm propagators by early March to ensure a long enough growing season in the UK.
Grow plants in a greenhouse or polytunnel as UK outdoor summers are rarely warm enough for success.
Pinch out the main growing tip when the plant reaches thirty centimetres to encourage bushy growth.
Limit each plant to four or five fruits and remove later flowers to ensure the remaining crop ripens.
Water the compost consistently to keep it moist and mist the foliage daily to deter red spider mites.
items.description: Eggplant, aubergine, brinjal, or baigan is a plant species in the nightshade family Solanaceae. Solanum melongena is grown worldwide for its edible fruit, typically used as a vegetable in cooking.

items.name: Petunia × hybrida
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 18C on the soil surface without covering them as they need light.
Water at the base in the morning to keep foliage dry and prevent botrytis grey mould in wet summers.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are 10cm tall to promote bushy growth and more UK blooms.
Deadhead weekly by snapping off the spent flower and the green seed capsule behind it to prolong UK flowering.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato fertiliser from July to September to sustain heavy blooming.
items.description: Petunia × atkinsiana is a Petunia plant "nothospecies" (hybrid), which encompasses all hybrid species of petunia between P. axillaris and P. integrifolia. Most of the petunias sold for cultivation in home gardens are this type and belong to this nothospecies. It is said to have originated with the Quaker plantsman James Atkins at his nursery at Painshill in 1834 but did not spread around the world until the 1990s.

items.name: Nicotiana sylvestris
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in March as they need light to germinate before planting out in May.
Space plants at least sixty centimetres apart in rich moist soil to allow the huge leaves to expand.
Stake the tall flower spikes early in windy UK gardens to prevent them snapping in summer storms.
Water deeply at the base during dry summer spells to support the massive foliage and prevent wilting.
Treat as a half-hardy annual in the UK or mulch heavily to protect the crown from wet winter rot.
items.description: Nicotiana sylvestris is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae, known by the common names woodland tobacco, flowering tobacco, and South American tobacco. It is a biennial or short-lived perennial plant in the tobacco genus Nicotiana, native to the Andes region in Argentina and Bolivia, in South America.

items.name: Parsley
items.growersTips:
Pour boiling water over the soil before sowing in spring to speed up notoriously slow germination.
Sow in deep pots or root trainers to avoid disturbing the sensitive taproot when transplanting.
Water the soil around the base in the morning, keeping leaves dry to prevent septoria leaf spot.
Keep plants in light shade during hot UK summers to stop them bolting and going to seed prematurely.
In autumn cover plants with a cloche to harvest fresh leaves through the damp British winter.
items.description: Parsley, or garden parsley, is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae that is native to the Balkans. It has been introduced and naturalized in Europe and elsewhere in the world with suitable climates, and is widely cultivated as a herb and a vegetable.

items.name: Coriander
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly into final pots or beds as coriander taproots hate transplanting shock in spring.
Sow seeds in shallow drills one centimetre deep from April to July for a continuous summer harvest.
Water the soil consistently at the base to prevent premature bolting during dry UK summer spells.
Grow slow-bolting cultivars like Calypso or Leisure which cope best with unpredictable UK weather.
Sow in partial shade during midsummer to mimic cooler conditions and delay the plant going to seed.
items.description: Coriander, or Coriandrum sativum, is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae. The leaves are known as cilantro in the US. Most people perceive the leaves as having a fresh, slightly citrus taste. Due to variations in the gene OR6A2, some people perceive its flavor to be more soaplike or rotten.

items.name: Dill
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from April to July as dill has a taproot and hates transplant shock.
Sow in a sunny, sheltered spot to prevent the tall, hollow stems from blowing over in UK wind.
Water the soil consistently at the base to prevent powdery mildew in humid British summers.
Sow in small batches every three weeks for a continuous supply of fresh leaves until the first frost.
Plant near cabbages to repel pests but keep away from fennel to prevent cross-pollination.
items.description: Dill is an annual herb in the celery family Apiaceae. Native to North Africa and West Asia, dill is grown widely in Eurasia, where its leaves and seeds are used as a herb or spice for flavouring food.

items.name: Fennel
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly in late spring 1cm deep as taproots hate transplanting in wet UK soils.
Plant away from dill and coriander to prevent cross-pollination and stunted growth of neighbours.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers rather than light daily sprinkles to prevent bolting.
Cut dead stems back to ground level in autumn and mulch the crown to survive wet British winters.
Watch for the bright green shield bug and handpick them off the feathery foliage in midsummer.
items.description: Fennel is a flowering plant species in the carrot family. It is a hardy, perennial herb with yellow flowers and feathery leaves. It is indigenous to the shores of the Mediterranean but has become widely naturalized in many parts of the world, especially on dry soils near the sea coast and on riverbanks.

items.name: Daucus carota sativus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from April to July at a depth of 1cm to avoid transplant shock in cool UK soil.
Sow alongside spring onions or rosemary to mask the scent and deter the destructive carrot root fly.
Grow under a fine insect mesh barrier at least 60cm high to physically block low-flying female flies.
Grow in stone-free sandy soil or deep containers to prevent the taproots from splitting and fanning.
Water deeply once a week rather than daily to encourage the taproots to grow straight and downward.
items.description: The carrot is a root vegetable in the umbellifer family Apiaceae. Carrots are typically orange in colour due to their beta-carotene content, which makes them a rich source of vitamin A. Heirloom variants may be white, yellow, red, purple, or black. They are biennial plants.

items.name: Great masterwort
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam enriched with garden compost to prevent soil drying out.
Position in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges, as full sun scorches the delicate bracts.
Cut faded flower stems back to ground level in July to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Protect fresh spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and flower size.
items.description: Astrantia major, the great masterwort, is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae, native to central and eastern Europe. Growing up to 90 cm (35 in) tall by 45 cm (18 in) broad, it is an herbaceous perennial, much used in gardens.

items.name: Eryngium giganteum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining, poor to moderately fertile soil in full sun to prevent winter root rot.
Sow seeds in autumn in cold frames as they require a period of winter cold to trigger germination.
Leave the architectural seed heads intact over winter to feed birds and provide structural frost interest.
Wear thick leather gloves when handling or weeding around this plant to protect against sharp spines.
Plant alongside purple-flowered Salvia or lavender to contrast with the silver-blue bracts.
items.description: Eryngium giganteum, with the common name Miss Willmott's ghost, is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae.

items.name: Field pumpkin
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep in 9cm pots, keeping them at 20C before planting out in June.
Dig a 30cm deep hole in May, fill with rotted manure, and plant your pumpkin on top of this mound.
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry spells, keeping the leaves dry to prevent powdery mildew.
Elevate developing fruits onto bricks or wooden boards in August to prevent rot from damp UK soil.
Cut the vine tips in late August to redirect all plant energy into ripening the existing pumpkins.
items.description: Cucurbita pepo is a cultivated plant of the genus Cucurbita. It yields varieties of winter squash and pumpkin, but the most widespread varieties belong to the subspecies Cucurbita pepo subsp. pepo, called summer squash.

items.name: Cucurbita maxima
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April 1.5cm deep on their sides in 9cm pots to prevent rotting in wet UK soil.
Plant out in late May after frosts, burying the stem up to the first leaves to encourage extra roots.
Water deeply at the base, not the leaves, to prevent powdery mildew in humid UK summer weather.
Place a slate or tile under developing pumpkins in August to stop them rotting on damp British soil.
Pinch out growing tips in late August so the plant puts all energy into ripening existing fruits.
items.description: Cucurbita maxima, one of at least five species of cultivated squash, is one of the most diverse domesticated species. This species originated in South America from the wild subspecies Cucurbita maxima subsp. andreana over 4,000 years ago. Cucurbita maxima, known for modern varieties as Hubbard, Delicious, Marblehead, Boston Marrow, and Turks Turban, originated in northern Argentina near the Andes or in certain Andean valleys. Secondary centers of diversity include India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, and the southern Appalachians.

items.name: Cucumber
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on their edge 2cm deep in April indoors to prevent rotting in damp UK spring compost.
Water the soil around the base daily, never the leaves, to prevent powdery mildew in humid weather.
Grow all-female greenhouse varieties like Carmen to avoid bitter fruits caused by cross-pollination.
Pinch out the main growing tip at the top of the support to encourage heavy-fruiting side shoots.
Plant alongside dill or marigolds to deter aphids and attract pollinators to your outdoor crops.
items.description: The cucumber is a widely-cultivated creeping vine plant in the family Cucurbitaceae that bears cylindrical to spherical fruits, used as culinary vegetables. Considered an annual plant, there are three main types: slicing, pickling, and seedless.

items.name: Cucurbita moschata
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep on their sides in 9cm pots to prevent rotting in cold UK soil.
Plant out in late May after frosts into soil enriched with a bucket of well-rotted manure per plant.
Water deeply at the base not the leaves, aiming for 10 litres per plant weekly during dry summer spells.
Pinch out the main growing tip at 2 metres long in July to force energy into developing female flowers.
Elevate swelling fruits onto bricks or tiles by August to stop damp UK soil from rotting the skins.
items.description: Cucurbita moschata is a species originating in the tropical Americas which is cultivated for edible flesh, flowers, greens, and seeds. It includes cultivars known in English as squash or pumpkin. Cultivars of C. moschata are generally more tolerant of hot, humid weather than squash of other domesticated species. C. moschata also exhibit a greater resistance to certain disease and insects, notably including to the squash vine borer. Commercially-made pumpkin pie mix is most often made from varieties of C. moschata.

items.name: Wild cabbage
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring at a depth of 1.5cm in firm, alkaline soil to prevent clubroot disease.
Net plants with 7mm mesh from May to October to block cabbage white butterflies and wood pigeons.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to prevent premature bolting to seed.
Plant mint or sage nearby to mask the brassica scent and deter destructive flea beetles.
Apply a high-nitrogen organic mulch in early spring to boost leafy growth in damp UK weather.
items.description: Brassica oleracea, also known as wild cabbage in its uncultivated form, is a plant of the family Brassicaceae.

items.name: Lobularia maritima
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in April at a depth of just two millimetres as they need light to germinate.
Water container-grown plants only when the top two centimetres of compost feels dry to the touch.
Shear back the foliage by half in midsummer after the first flush of flowers to trigger new blooms.
Watch for flea beetles in dry spring weather and use fine insect netting to protect young seedlings.
Plant alongside brassicas like cabbages to attract hoverflies that naturally control aphid pests.
