items.description: Lobularia maritima is a species of low-growing flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae. Its common name is sweet alyssum or sweet Alison, also commonly referred to as just alyssum.

items.name: Cheiranthus cheiri L.
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in June or July for strong bare-root plants ready to transplant into autumn beds.
Plant out in October in free-draining chalky or alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot.
Pinch out the growing tips in spring to encourage bushy growth and more fragrant flowers.
Watch for cabbage white butterfly caterpillars and clubroot disease as they are brassicas.
Remove spent flower spikes in July to encourage a potential second flush of blooms.
items.description: Erysimum cheiri, syn. Cheiranthus cheiri, the wallflower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae (Cruciferae), native to Greece, but widespread as an introduced species elsewhere. It is also treated as a hybrid under the name Erysimum × cheiri. It is widely cultivated as a garden plant.

items.name: Rogue's gillyflower
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds outdoors in May or June at five millimetres deep for strong biennial roots before winter.
Grow in moist well-drained soil with garden lime to raise pH and prevent Brassicaceae clubroot.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry summer spells to stop powdery mildew on leaves.
Cut back faded flowering stems to ground level in July to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Inspect leaves weekly for caterpillars of the small white butterfly and handpick them off immediately.
items.description: Hesperis matronalis is an herbaceous flowering plant species in the family Brassicaceae. It has numerous common names, including dame's rocket, damask-violet, dame's-violet, dames-wort, dame's gilliflower, night-scented gilliflower, queen's gilliflower, rogue's gilliflower, sweet rocket, and mother-of-the-evening.

items.name: Sweet William
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in June or July for strong biennial roots that survive wet British winters to flower next May.
Plant in free-draining alkaline soil to prevent winter crown rot caused by heavy UK clay and rain.
Deadhead spent blooms in July to encourage a second flush and prevent messy self-seeding in borders.
Space plants twenty centimetres apart in full sun to prevent rust fungus in damp British summers.
Support taller cultivars like Holborn Glory with brushwood twigs before heavy spring rain bows stems.
items.description: Dianthus barbatus, the sweet William, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae, native to southern Europe and parts of Asia. It has become a popular ornamental garden plant. It is a herbaceous biennial or short-lived perennial plant growing to 13–92 cm tall, with flowers in a dense cluster of up to 30 at the top of the stems. Each flower is 2–3 cm diameter with five petals displaying serrated edges. Wild plants produce red flowers with a white base, but colours in cultivars range from white, pink, red, and purple to variegated patterns. The exact origin of its English comm

items.name: Clove pink
items.growersTips:
Incorporate plenty of grit to ensure sharp drainage in heavy UK clay to prevent winter root rot.
Water only at the base when the soil is dry to touch, keeping foliage dry to avoid rust disease.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in spring to encourage a bushy habit and more flowers.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly down to the next lateral bud to prolong the summer flowering period.
Propagate by taking heel cuttings or layering non-flowering shoots in July or August.
items.description: Dianthus caryophyllus, commonly known as carnation or clove pink, is a species of Dianthus native to the Mediterranean region. While its exact natural range is uncertain due to extensive cultivation over the last 2,000 years, wild carnations are most common in the Mediterranean region. Carnations are prized for their wide variety of colors, delicate fringed petals, and fragrance, often described as spicy, clove-like, or reminiscent of a combination of cinnamon and nutmeg, hence the common name "clove pink". This aroma has made carnations a popular choice for use in perfumes, potpourri, and sce

items.name: Lychnis coronaria
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn or spring directly where they are to flower in well-drained soil.
Grow in poor, dry soil in full sun to prevent floppy growth and keep the silver foliage vibrant.
Deadhead spent blooms in August to prolong flowering and control its prolific self-seeding habit.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially during damp UK April weather.
Divide established clumps in early spring every three years to maintain plant vigour and health.
items.description: Silene coronaria, the rose campion, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae, native to Eurasia. Other common names include dusty miller, mullein-pink and bloody William. In the United Kingdom it is still widely referenced under its synonym Lychnis coronaria.

items.name: Red catchfly
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn at a shallow depth of two millimetres to mimic natural UK self-seeding cycles.
Grow in moist but well-drained soil with a neutral to alkaline pH to prevent winter root rot.
Shear back the stems to ground level in mid-July to encourage a second flush of late-summer blooms.
Plant alongside wild garlic or bluebells in dappled shade to recreate a classic British woodland.
Watch for campion smut fungus in humid summers and immediately remove infected black-tipped buds.
items.description: Silene dioica, known as red campion and red catchfly, is a herbaceous flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae, native to Europe and introduced to the Americas.

items.name: Bergenia cordifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in shallow holes with the stout rhizomes sitting right at the soil surface to prevent rot.
Water newly planted bergenia weekly during dry UK spring spells until their roots are established.
Handpick vine weevil grubs from the roots and adult beetles from the notched leaves in autumn.
Cut away tattered winter-damaged leaves right at the base in April to encourage fresh green growth.
Grow in heavy clay or poor soil in partial shade to trigger the best bronze winter foliage colour.
items.description: Bergenia crassifolia is a species of flowering plant of the genus Bergenia in the family Saxifragaceae. Common names for the species include heart-leaved bergenia, heartleaf bergenia, leather bergenia, winter-blooming bergenia, elephant-ears, elephant's ears, Korean elephant-ear, badan, pigsqueak, Siberian tea, and Mongolian tea.

items.name: Heuchera micrantha
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using well-drained soil enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot.
Gently firm soil around the crown but keep it just above the surface to avoid rot in wet winters.
Divide the woody crown every three years in early autumn to prevent the plant from lifting out.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn and drench the soil with nematodes to protect the roots.
Cut back tattered winter foliage in early spring to encourage fresh, colorful new leaf growth.
items.description: Heuchera micrantha is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family known by the common name crevice alumroot, or small-flowered alumroot.

items.name: Pulmonaria officinalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive humus-rich soil in partial to full shade to mimic UK woodland edges.
Divide clumps every three years in autumn after flowering to maintain vigor and prevent center rot.
Cut back hard to ground level in midsummer after flowering to stimulate fresh mildew-free foliage.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent powdery mildew on the hairy leaves.
Plant alongside early spring bulbs like snowdrops and daffodils to hide their dying foliage later.
items.description: Pulmonaria officinalis, common names lungwort, common lungwort, Mary's tears or Our Lady's milk drops, is a herbaceous rhizomatous evergreen perennial plant of the genus Pulmonaria, belonging to the family Boraginaceae.

items.name: Brunnera macrophylla
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil in partial shade to prevent the delicate leaves from scorching.
Water young plants regularly in summer to establish a deep root system in damp UK woodland borders.
Cut back faded flower stems in summer to encourage a fresh flush of attractive heart-shaped foliage.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps in damp weather.
Divide congested clumps in early autumn or spring to propagate and maintain vigorous growth.
items.description: Brunnera macrophylla, the Siberian bugloss, great forget-me-not, largeleaf brunnera or heartleaf, is a species of flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae, native to the Caucasus. It is a hardy, rhizomatous, herbaceous perennial, that can reach from 12 to 18 inches in height, and carries basal, simple cordate leaves on slender stems. Sprays of small blue flowers, similar to those seen in the related forget-me-nots, are borne from mid-Spring, and bloom for eight to ten weeks.

items.name: Borage
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors from April to June at a depth of one centimetre to avoid root damage.
Grow borage next to strawberries in UK clay soil to improve fruit yield and attract pollinators.
Water young plants weekly until established, then only during dry British summer spells.
Cut the plant back by half in July to encourage a second flush of fresh leaves and edible flowers.
Deadhead spent blooms promptly to prevent aggressive self-seeding across your vegetable beds.
items.description: Borage, also known as starflower, is an annual herb in the flowering plant family Boraginaceae native to the Mediterranean region. Although the plant contains small amounts of pyrrolizidine alkaloids, some parts are edible and its seeds provide oil.

items.name: Fall phlox
items.growersTips:
Space plants 60cm apart in moist, fertile soil to prevent powdery mildew in damp UK summers.
Water deeply at the base weekly rather than overhead to keep the dense foliage dry and disease-free.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in March to retain moisture and feed these hungry feeders.
Cut stems back by half in May using the Chelsea chop to delay flowering and create bushier plants.
Divide congested clumps every three years in autumn to maintain vigor and prevent center dieback.
items.description: Phlox paniculata is a species of flowering plant in the phlox family (Polemoniaceae). It is native to parts of the eastern and central United States. It is extensively cultivated in temperate regions as an ornamental plant and has become established in the wild in scattered locales in other regions. Common names include fall phlox, garden phlox, perennial phlox, summer phlox, and panicled phlox.

items.name: Phlox subulata
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Shear back by half immediately after flowering in June to maintain a neat cushion and boost growth.
Water newly planted divisions weekly during dry spring spells, then leave to rely on natural rain.
Combine with Aubrieta and Thymus in rock gardens or atop dry stone walls for a classic spring show.
Watch for stem eelworm damage in humid summers, discarding distorted plants to stop it spreading.
items.description: Phlox subulata the creeping phlox, moss phlox, moss pink or mountain phlox, is a species of flowering plant in the family Polemoniaceae, native to the eastern and central United States, and widely cultivated.

items.name: Pontic rhododendron
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, keeping the root ball level with the soil surface.
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer spells to ensure next spring's flower buds develop.
Prune immediately after flowering in June to control size before the plant sets next year's buds.
Watch for vine weevil larvae eating roots and adult beetles notch-chewing the leaf margins.
Grow alongside acid-loving UK companions like heather, pieris, or vaccinium in partial shade.
items.description: Rhododendron ponticum, called common rhododendron or pontic rhododendron, is a species of flowering plant in the Rhododendron genus of the heath family Ericaceae. It is native to the Iberian Peninsula in southwest Europe and the Caucasus region in northern West Asia.

items.name: Camellia japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in ericaceous compost and position in sheltered partial shade to prevent morning sun scorch.
Water deeply with rainwater from July to September to ensure next springs flower buds develop fully.
Prune immediately after flowering in late spring to avoid cutting off the newly forming buds.
Protect early blooms from frost damage by covering the shrub with horticultural fleece overnight.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating roots and scale insects on the undersides of the glossy leaves.
items.description: Camellia japonica, known as common camellia, or Japanese camellia, is a species of flowering plant from the genus Camellia in the tea family Theaceae. It is native to China and Japan, and grows naturally in forests at altitudes of around 300–1,100 metres (980–3,600 ft).

items.name: Spring heath
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral soil, adding composted pine needles to lower pH if your soil is alkaline.
Prune immediately after flowering in late spring by shearing faded spikes to keep the shrub bushy.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water during dry summer spells to prevent chlorosis.
Space plants thirty centimetres apart in full sun to prevent damp-induced fungal root rot in winter.
Plant alongside dwarf conifers or pieris which share the same acidic soil and moisture needs.
items.description: Erica carnea, the winter heath, winter-flowering heather, spring heath or alpine heath, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ericaceae, native to mountainous areas of central, eastern and southern Europe, where it grows in coniferous woodlands or stony slopes.

items.name: Calluna vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic, peat-free ericaceous compost mixed with grit to ensure the essential sharp drainage.
Water with stored rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil pH below five point five.
Prune annually in early spring by cutting back dead flower spikes to just below the spent blooms.
Space plants thirty centimetres apart in full sun to prevent damp-induced powdery mildew and rot.
Grow alongside Erica carnea and dwarf conifers to provide year-round structure and acidic soil cover.
items.description: Calluna vulgaris, common heather, ling, or simply heather, is the sole species in the genus Calluna in the flowering plant family Ericaceae. It is a low-growing evergreen shrub growing to 20 to 50 centimetres tall, or rarely to 1 metre (40 in) and taller, and is found widely in Europe and Asia Minor on acidic soils in open sunny situations and in moderate shade.

items.name: Pieris japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, adding composted pine needles or ericaceous compost.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to keep the soil acidic and prevent leaf yellowing.
Protect young spring growth from late UK frosts using horticultural fleece on cold nights in April.
Prune lightly immediately after flowering in late spring to avoid cutting off next year's buds.
Watch for lacebug damage in dry summers, spraying the leaf undersides with organic fatty acids.
items.description: Pieris japonica, the Japanese andromeda or Japanese pieris, is a species of flowering plant in the heath family Ericaceae. It is native to eastern China, Taiwan, and Japan, where it grows in mountain thickets. This medium-sized evergreen shrub or tree is widely cultivated in gardens.

items.name: Penny mac
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to prevent afternoon leaf scorch.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry UK summers to support its repeat-blooming habit.
Apply a thick mulch of composted bark in spring to retain soil moisture and protect shallow roots.
Prune in late winter by removing only dead wood and old flower heads, as it blooms on new wood too.
Add sulfur-based ericaceous fertiliser in March to turn flowers blue in neutral UK garden soils.
items.description: Hydrangea macrophylla is a species of flowering plant in the family Hydrangeaceae, native and endemic to Japan. It is a deciduous shrub growing to 3 m (10 ft) tall by 2.5 m (8 ft) or more broad with large heads of pink or blue flowers in summer and autumn. It is currently treated as monotypic, with no subspecies or varieties. Common names include bigleaf hydrangea, and, for particular cultivar groups, the names lacecap hydrangea, mophead hydrangea, and hortensia. It is widely cultivated in many parts of the world in many climates. It is not to be confused with H. aspera 'Macrophylla'.

items.name: Hydrangea paniculata
items.growersTips:
Prune hard in early March down to a low framework of buds to guarantee massive current-season blooms.
Water deeply twice a week during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy.
Plant in full sun to partial shade in moisture-retentive soil enriched with well-rotted manure.
Mulch annually in spring with compost to retain moisture and protect roots from drying out.
Select Limelight for strong upright stems that will not flop under heavy British summer rain.
items.description: Hydrangea paniculata, or panicled hydrangea, is a species of flowering plant in the family Hydrangeaceae native to southern and eastern China, Korea, Japan and Russia (Sakhalin). It was first formally described by Philipp Franz von Siebold in 1829.

items.name: Hydrangea arborescens
items.growersTips:
Prune hard to 30cm in March to encourage massive new-wood blooms on cultivars like Annabelle.
Plant in moisture-retentive soil enriched with well-rotted manure to prevent summer wilting.
Provide sturdy support rings in May to stop heavy flowerheads flopping during wet UK summers.
Water deeply at the base twice a week during dry spells rather than spraying the foliage.
Grow in dappled shade to protect the delicate white bracts from scorching in midday sun.
items.description: Hydrangea arborescens, commonly known as smooth hydrangea or sevenbark, is a species of flowering plant in the family Hydrangeaceae. It is a small- to medium-sized, multi-stemmed, deciduous shrub up to 2 m (7 ft) tall that is native to the eastern United States.

items.name: Hog weed
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn directly onto weed-free soil as they require winter cold to trigger germination.
Water seedlings weekly in dry UK spring weather until their deep taproot establishes in the soil.
Cut flowering stems to the ground in late summer before seeds disperse to prevent aggressive spread.
Plant alongside campion and foxglove in sandy, well-drained soil to mimic British wildflower banks.
Wear gloves when weeding to avoid skin irritation from the sap when handling bruised foliage.
items.description: Oenothera biennis, the common evening-primrose, is a species of flowering plant in the family Onagraceae, native to eastern and central North America, from Newfoundland west to Alberta, southeast to Florida, and southwest to Texas, and widely naturalized elsewhere in temperate and subtropical regions. Evening primrose oil is produced from the plant.

items.name: Fuchsia magellanica
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at least 5cm deeper than the pot level to protect the crown from deep UK frosts.
Prune hard to ground level in early spring once new growth appears at the base of the stems.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the soil consistently moist but not wet.
In cold northern UK regions, mulch the root zone with 10cm of bark chippings before winter starts.
Grow alongside shade-tolerant hostas and ferns in moist, well-drained soil with partial shade.
items.description: Fuchsia magellanica – commonly known as the hummingbird fuchsia, hardy fuchsia or chilco – is a species of flowering plant in the evening primrose family Onagraceae, native to the lower Southern Cone of southern South America.

items.name: Cardamindum majus Moench
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in May at a depth of two centimetres after the last frost of spring.
Grow in poor well-drained soil to encourage abundant flowers rather than excessive leafy growth.
Plant next to brassicas as a sacrificial trap crop to lure away cabbage white butterfly larvae.
Water young plants weekly until established then only during prolonged dry summer spells in the UK.
Protect from autumn frosts by taking stem cuttings in late August to overwinter indoors on a sill.
items.description: Tropaeolum majus, the garden nasturtium, nasturtium, Indian cress or monk's cress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Tropaeolaceae. An annual or a short-lived perennial with disc-shaped leaves and brilliant yellow, orange or red flowers, it is of cultivated, probably hybrid origin. It is not closely related to the genus Nasturtium.

items.name: Meadow Geranium
items.growersTips:
Cut back faded stems to ground level in July to stimulate a fresh flush of foliage and autumn flowers.
Plant bare roots in autumn at a depth where the crown sits just two centimetres below the soil surface.
Grow in moist but well-drained neutral to alkaline soil to prevent winter crown rot in wet UK climates.
Check leaves in damp British summers for powdery mildew and prune affected foliage immediately to ground.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigour and propagate new plants.
items.description: Geranium pratense, the meadow crane's-bill or meadow geranium, is a species of flowering plant in the family Geraniaceae, native to Europe and Asia. Forming a clump up to 1 m (3.3 ft) broad, it is a herbaceous perennial with hairy stems and lax saucer-shaped blooms of pale violet. It is extremely hardy to at least −20 °C (−4 °F), reflecting its origins in the Altai Mountains of central Asia.

items.name: Geranium sanguineum
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky or sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Shear foliage to the ground after the first summer flush to trigger fresh leaves and autumn blooms.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn or dividing the woody crown in early spring.
Position in full sun to maximise the vibrant magenta flower density and tight hummock growth habit.
Space plants forty centimetres apart to allow the sprawling rhizomatous stems to form weed cover.
items.description: Geranium sanguineum, common name bloody crane's-bill or bloody geranium, is a species of hardy flowering herbaceous perennial plant in the cranesbill family Geraniaceae. It is the county flower of Northumberland.

items.name: Pelargonium ×hortorum
items.growersTips:
Overwinter plants indoors before the first frost by cutting back by half and keeping compost dry.
Water only when the top two inches of compost are dry to prevent root rot in damp UK summers.
Deadhead regularly by snapping the entire flower stem off at the base to trigger new blooms.
Pinch out the growing tips of young plants in March to encourage a bushy habit and more flowers.
Plant in free-draining peat-free compost mixed with twenty percent grit to survive wet spells.
items.description: Pelargonium × hortorum, commonly called zonal geranium, or garden geranium, is a nothospecies of Pelargonium most commonly used as an ornamental plant. It is a hybrid between Pelargonium zonale and Pelargonium inquinans. They are the group of Pelargonium cultivars, with leaves marked with a brown annular zone and inflorescence in the form of large balls of tight flowers, usually red, pink, or white. These are the most common geraniums of garden centers and florists, sold in pots for windowsills and balconies or planted in flowerbeds.

items.name: Papaver orientale
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, gritty, alkaline to neutral soil to accommodate the long taproot and prevent winter rot.
Cut the entire plant back to ground level in July after flowering to stimulate fresh new foliage.
Propagate by taking three-inch root cuttings in late autumn or winter when the plant is dormant.
Support heavy flower stems in May using hazel twigs or metal hoops before the blooms open and flop.
Plant alongside late-summer perennials like dahlias to mask the unsightly yellowing summer foliage.
items.description: Papaver orientale, the Oriental poppy, is a perennial flowering plant native to the Caucasus, northeastern Turkey, and northern Iran.

items.name: Red poppy
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly onto finely raked soil in spring or autumn as they need light to germinate.
Thin seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart in spring to prevent mildew in damp UK weather.
Grow in poor well drained soil in full sun to prevent floppy stems and encourage more blooms.
Deadhead faded flowers weekly to prolong blooming or leave seedheads to self sow for next year.
Sow alongside cornflowers and chamomile in autumn for a classic British cottage garden display.
items.description: Papaver rhoeas, with common names including common poppy, corn poppy, corn rose, field poppy, Flanders poppy, red poppy, and Odai, is an annual herbaceous species of flowering plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae. It is native to north Africa and temperate Eurasia and is introduced into temperate areas on all other continents except Antarctica.

items.name: Eschscholzia californica
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in April at five millimetres deep as they dislike root disturbance.
Grow in poor well-drained soil in full sun to prevent lush leaf growth at the expense of flowers.
Avoid watering established plants in the UK summer except during prolonged periods of severe drought.
Deadhead regularly to prolong the blooms and prevent aggressive self-seeding across your borders.
Leave some late seed heads intact to allow the plant to self-sow naturally for the following spring.
items.description: Eschscholzia californica, the California poppy, golden poppy, Mexican poppy, California sunlight or cup of gold, is a species of flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae, native to the United States and Mexico. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant flowering in summer, with showy flowers in brilliant shades of red, orange and yellow. It is also used as food or a garnish. It had various uses in indigenous herbalism. It became the official state flower of California in 1903.

items.name: Digitalis purpurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds thinly on the surface of damp peat-free compost in June, as they need light to germinate.
Plant out young rosettes by autumn in moist, humus-rich soil, spaced thirty centimetres apart.
Water young plants weekly during dry summer spells to establish strong roots before winter wet.
Cut spent flower spikes to the ground in July to encourage a second flush of late-summer blooms.
Leave some seed heads intact in autumn to self-seed naturally in shady borders or woodland edges.
items.description: Digitalis purpurea, the foxglove or common foxglove, is a toxic species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae, native to and widespread throughout most of temperate Europe. It has also naturalized in parts of North America, as well as some other temperate regions. The plant is a popular garden subject, with many cultivars available. It is the original source of the heart medicine digoxin. This biennial plant grows as a rosette of leaves in the first year after sowing, before flowering and then dying in the second year. It generally produces enough seeds so that new plants wi

items.name: Yellow foxglove
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds on the soil surface in late spring as they need light to germinate in UK conditions.
Grow in moist but well-drained humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic their native woodland edge.
Cut back the faded flower spikes in August to encourage a second flush of blooms and prevent self-seeding.
Watch for foxglove aphids in May and squash them by hand to protect the emerging flower buds.
Plant alongside ferns and hostas which thrive in the same damp shade and mask the fading lower leaves.
items.description: Digitalis grandiflora, the yellow foxglove, big-flowered foxglove, or large yellow foxglove, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Digitalis, family Plantaginaceae. It is native to southern Europe and Asia. In mountains it grows on warm, bushy slopes or areas left after logging. The Latin specific epithet grandiflora means "large flowered".

items.name: Antirrhinum majus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March on the surface of damp compost as they need light to germinate in the UK.
Pinch out the growing tips when plants are ten centimetres tall to encourage bushier multi-stem growth.
Water deeply at the base in the morning to prevent rust disease which thrives in damp UK summers.
Deadhead faded flower spikes weekly to stimulate a continuous display of blooms until the first frost.
Grow as a hardy annual in the UK by planting out in late spring after the last frost has passed.
items.description: Antirrhinum majus, the common snapdragon, is a species of flowering plant belonging to the genus Antirrhinum. The plant was placed in the family Plantaginaceae following a revision of its prior classical family, Scrophulariaceae.

items.name: Penstemon barbatus
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Sow seeds shallowly in spring under glass, barely covering with compost, for blooms the next year.
Cut spent flower spikes back to the base in August to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide congested clumps every three years in April to maintain plant vigour and flower quality.
items.description: Penstemon barbatus, known by the common names golden-beard penstemon, and beardlip penstemon, is a flowering plant native to the western United States.

items.name: Great mullein
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring on the soil surface without covering as they need light to germinate in the UK.
Grow in poor, sharply drained chalky or sandy soil to prevent winter wet from rotting the roots.
Water young plants sparingly and stop watering entirely once established to suit their drought tolerance.
Cut the spent flower spike down to the base in autumn to prevent excessive self-seeding in your garden.
Watch for the mullein moth caterpillars in June and handpick them off to protect the large leaves.
items.description: Verbascum thapsus, the great mullein, greater mullein or common mullein, is a species of mullein native to Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, and introduced in the Americas, Australia and New Zealand.

items.name: Sedum spectabile
items.growersTips:
Do the Chelsea chop in late May to reduce the height of stems and prevent the heavy clumps splaying.
Plant crowns level with the soil surface in free-draining grit to prevent winter wet crown rot.
Water only during severe summer droughts as wet UK soil causes floppy growth and root rot.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating the roots in autumn and slugs damaging new spring shoots.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
items.description: Hylotelephium spectabile is a species of flowering plant in the stonecrop family Crassulaceae, native to China and Korea. Its common names include showy stonecrop, iceplant, and butterfly stonecrop.

items.name: Hylotelephium telephium
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Do the Chelsea chop in late May to keep stems sturdy and prevent them from flopping.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this succulent thrives on neglect.
Leave faded flower heads intact over winter to provide structural frost interest and feed birds.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating the roots and protect young spring shoots from slugs.
items.description: Hylotelephium telephium, known as orpine, livelong, frog's-stomach, harping Johnny, life-everlasting, live-forever, midsummer-men, Orphan John, witch's moneybags, and garden stonecrop is a succulent perennial plant of the family Crassulaceae native to Eurasia. The flowers are held in dense heads and can be reddish or yellowish-white. A number of cultivars, often with purplish leaves, are grown in gardens as well as hybrids between this species and the related Hylotelephium spectabile (iceplant), especially the popular 'Herbstfreude'. Occasionally garden plants may escape and naturalise as has

items.name: Sempervivum tectorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a 50 percent grit and peat-free compost mix to survive wet UK winters without rotting.
Position in full south-facing sun as British overcast skies will cause rosettes to lose color.
Water only when the soil is bone dry from spring to autumn and keep completely dry during winter.
Gently pull away dead outer leaves in late spring to prevent dampness and deter slugs and snails.
Propagate by snipping off offsets in summer and pressing them shallowly into gritty soil to root.
items.description: Sempervivum tectorum, the common houseleek, is a species of flowering plant in the family Crassulaceae, native to the mountains of southern Europe, cultivated in the whole of Europe for its appearance and a Roman-era tradition claiming that it protects buildings against lightning strikes.

items.name: Common box
items.growersTips:
Plant box in well-drained soil with a handful of grit to prevent waterlogging in wet UK winters.
Trim Buxus on a dry, overcast day in late May or June to prevent sun scorch on newly cut leaves.
Check weekly from April to October for green box moth caterpillars and web-like silk in the foliage.
Water deeply at the base rather than overhead to keep leaves dry and reduce the risk of box blight.
Grow dwarf Suffolk Blue or Faulkner cultivars for better natural resistance to common UK diseases.
items.description: Buxus sempervirens, the common box, European box, or boxwood, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Buxus, native to western and southern Europe, northwest Africa, and southwest Asia, from southern England south to northern Morocco, and east through the northern Mediterranean region to Turkey. Buxus colchica of western Caucasus and B. hyrcana of northern Iran and eastern Caucasus are commonly treated as synonyms of B. sempervirens.

items.name: Common holly
items.growersTips:
Plant male and female cultivars like Golden King together for autumn berries in the UK climate.
Prune in late spring after frosts to shape the shrub and prevent winter dieback on cut stems.
Apply a thick mulch of composted bark in spring to maintain the moist acidic soil holly prefers.
Watch for the holly leaf miner insect in summer and remove affected leaves to stop the spread.
Plant container-grown holly in autumn at the same depth as the pot to avoid root rot in wet winters.
items.description: Ilex aquifolium, the holly, common holly, English holly, European holly, or occasionally Christmas holly, is a species of flowering plant in the family Aquifoliaceae, native to western and southern Europe, northwest Africa, and southwest Asia. It is regarded as the type species of the genus Ilex, which by association is also called holly. It is an evergreen tree or shrub found, for example, in shady areas of forests of oak and in beech hedges. In the British Isles it is one of very few native hardwood evergreen trees. It has a great capacity to adapt to different conditions and is a pioneer sp

items.name: Verbena bonariensis
items.growersTips:
Cut stems to the ground in April after winter frosts pass to protect the crown from UK wet-cold.
Plant in free-draining soil with added grit to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Leave seedheads intact over winter to encourage self-seeding in gravel paths and sunny borders.
Grow alongside Echinacea or Rudbeckia to provide structural support for its tall, wiry stems.
Propagate via softwood cuttings in May if your garden soil is heavy clay and plants die in winter.
items.description: Verbena bonariensis, commonly known as the purpletop vervain, clustertop vervain, Argentinian vervain, tall verbena or pretty verbena, is a member of the verbena family cultivated as a flowering annual or herbaceous perennial plant. In United States horticulture, it is also known by the ambiguous names purpletop and South American vervain. For the misapplication "Brazilian verbena" see below.

items.name: Verbena ×hybrida
items.growersTips:
Plant out after the last May frosts, spacing them thirty centimetres apart in full UK sunshine.
Deadhead faded flower clusters weekly in summer to stimulate continuous blooming until first frost.
Water deeply at the base once a week during dry spells, keeping foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew.
Overwinter tender cultivars indoors as cuttings, as they rarely survive wet UK winters in the ground.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils before planting to ensure the sharp drainage they require.

items.name: Purple loosestrife
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive soil or bog gardens at a depth where the crown sits just at ground level
Water deeply twice a week in dry UK summers to mimic its natural damp canal-side habitat
Cut stems back to the ground in late winter before new spring shoots emerge to maintain a tidy clump
Deadhead spent flower spikes in August to prevent heavy self-seeding in nearby damp garden borders
Grow alongside moisture-loving UK native companions like Marsh Marigold and Yellow Iris in wet soil
items.description: Lythrum salicaria or purple-loosestrife is a flowering plant belonging to the family Lythraceae. It should not be confused with other plants sharing the name loosestrife that are members of the genus Lysimachia in the family Primulaceae. This herbaceous perennial plant is native to temperate regions of Europe, Asia, northern Africa, and eastern Australia.

items.name: Common garden peony
items.growersTips:
Plant eyes no deeper than two centimetres below soil level to ensure they flower in UK climates.
Stake stems in April using metal grid supports before heavy blooms collapse in wet British spring rain.
Water deeply at the base during dry May spells to support bud development, keeping foliage dry.
Cut all foliage back to ground level in autumn and burn or discard it to prevent peony blight.
Incorporate well-rotted manure deep below the roots when planting, keeping it away from the crown.
items.description: Paeonia lactiflora is a species of herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Paeoniaceae, native to central and eastern Asia from eastern Tibet across northern China to eastern Siberia.

items.name: Garden peony
items.growersTips:
Plant Paeonia officinalis eyes no deeper than two centimeters below soil level to ensure UK flowering.
In wet UK autumns, cut stems to ground level to prevent the spread of botrytis peony blight fungus.
Apply a thick layer of well-rotted manure in early spring, keeping it clear of the central crown.
Stake the heavy double-flowered varieties in April before the foliage grows too tall to support.
Water deeply at the base during dry May spells to support bud development in sandy UK soils.
items.description: Paeonia officinalis, the common peony, or garden peony, is a species of flowering plant in the family Paeoniaceae, native to mainly mountainous areas of Southern Europe and introduced in Central and Western Europe and North America.

items.name: Strelitzia reginae
items.growersTips:
Bring indoors before first frost and overwinter in a bright conservatory or heated greenhouse.
Pot in a heavy loam-based compost like John Innes No 3 mixed with grit to support the top-heavy plant.
Water deeply when the top five centimetres of soil dry out, but keep almost dry during winter.
Keep the roots tightly bound in a small pot to encourage flowering rather than leaf growth.
Wipe the broad leaves monthly with a damp cloth to prevent red spider mite and mealybug build-up.
items.description: Strelitzia reginae, commonly known as the crane flower, bird of paradise, or isigude in Nguni, is a species of flowering plant native to the Cape Provinces and KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa. An evergreen perennial, it is widely cultivated for its dramatic flowers. In temperate areas it is a popular houseplant.

items.name: Phalaenopsis amabilis
items.growersTips:
Position on a north or east-facing UK windowsill to prevent leaf scorch from direct summer sun.
Water weekly by submerging the inner pot in tepid rainwater, draining fully to prevent root rot.
Repot every two years in coarse pine bark rather than soil to maintain essential root aeration.
Maintain a minimum winter indoor temperature of twelve degrees Celsius to prevent bud drop.
Prune spent flower spikes down to the third node to stimulate a secondary autumn flush.
items.description: Phalaenopsis amabilis, commonly known as moon orchid, moth orchid, or mariposa orchid, is a species of flowering plant in the orchid family Orchidaceae. It is widely cultivated as a decorative houseplant. It is an epiphytic or lithophytic herb with long, thick roots, between two and eight thick, fleshy leaves with their bases hiding the stem and nearly flat, white, long-lasting flowers on a branching flowering stem with up to ten flowers on each branch.

items.name: Cymbidium hybridum
items.growersTips:
Grow in a chunky bark-based orchid compost, never standard soil, keeping the pseudobulbs above mix.
Stand pots outdoors in semi-shade from June to September to trigger autumn flower spikes with cool air.
Water weekly in summer with rainwater, but keep nearly dry in winter to prevent root rot in UK cold.
Feed with high-nitrogen fertilizer in spring, switching to high-potash in late summer for blooms.
Watch for red spider mite in dry indoor winter air and wipe leaves with a damp cloth to deter them.

items.name: Noble Dendrobium
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining coarse bark medium in small pots, never in standard UK multipurpose compost.
Position on a cool, bright windowsill but move away from glass in winter to avoid frost damage.
Water weekly in summer, then stop watering completely from November to February to trigger blooms.
Provide a cold autumn drop to 10C for six weeks to stimulate flower buds instead of leafy keikis.
Watch for mealybugs in leaf axils and wipe them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
items.description: Dendrobium nobile, also known as the noble dendrobium, is a member of the family Orchidaceae. It is one of the most widespread ornamental members of the orchid family. It is the state flower of the Indian state of Sikkim.

items.name: Strawberry
items.growersTips:
Plant crowns level with the soil surface in spring to prevent rot in wet UK weather.
Water heavily at the base during fruit swell, keeping foliage dry to avoid grey mould.
Tuck barley straw under developing berries in May to lift them off damp soil and deter slugs.
Cut back all foliage to five centimetres after the final harvest in August to stimulate new growth.
Plant alongside garlic or chives to naturally deter aphids and red spider mites in humid summers.
items.description: The garden strawberry is a widely grown hybrid plant cultivated worldwide for its fruit. The genus Fragaria, the strawberries, is in the rose family, Rosaceae. The fruit is appreciated for its aroma, bright red colour, juicy texture, and sweetness. It is eaten either fresh or in prepared foods such as jam, ice cream, and chocolates. Artificial strawberry flavourings and aromas are widely used in commercial products. Botanically, the strawberry is not a berry, but an aggregate accessory fruit. Each apparent 'seed' on the outside of the strawberry is actually an achene, a botanical fruit with a

items.name: Red raspberry
items.growersTips:
Prune summer-fruiting canes to the ground in autumn, but cut autumn-fruiting ones down in February.
Plant bare-root canes between November and March at the same depth they were previously growing.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in March to retain moisture in sandy or chalky UK soils.
Net the ripening fruit in summer to protect your harvest from hungry blackbirds and thrushes.
Grow in slightly acidic to neutral soil, avoiding wet clay areas to prevent Phytophthora root rot.
items.description: Rubus idaeus is a red-fruited species of Rubus native to Eurasia and commonly cultivated in other temperate regions.

items.name: Blackcurrant
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root bushes in late autumn 5cm deeper than the nursery mark to encourage strong new stems.
Prune in winter by removing one-third of the oldest dark wood at the base to stimulate new growth.
Water newly planted bushes weekly during dry spring spells to ensure fruit swells in June and July.
Mulch annually in March with well-rotted manure to keep the shallow root system cool and damp.
Net bushes in early summer to protect ripening berries from bullfinches and blackbirds.
items.description: The blackcurrant, black currant or cassis is a deciduous shrub in the family Grossulariaceae grown for its edible berries. It is native to temperate parts of central and northern Europe and northern Asia, where it prefers damp fertile soils. It is widely cultivated both commercially and domestically.

items.name: High blueberry
items.growersTips:
Plant in ericaceous compost with pine needles to keep the soil pH strictly between 4.5 and 5.2.
Water only with stored rainwater because UK tap water contains calcium that raises soil pH.
Prune in late winter by removing wood older than three years to stimulate productive new stems.
Cover bushes with fine netting in July to prevent UK blackbirds from stripping the ripening fruit.
Grow two different cultivars like Duke and Bluecrop nearby to ensure successful cross-pollination.
items.description: Vaccinium corymbosum is a North American species of blueberry that became commonly cultivated as a fresh fruit crop in the 20th century. Dozens of commercial cultivars exist.

items.name: Basil
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 5mm depth using a heated propagator to combat cool UK spring nights.
Water basil only in the morning at the base of the stem to prevent damp-off and grey mould.
Pinch out the central growing tip above the second set of leaves to encourage a bushy growth habit.
Keep pots on a south-facing windowsill or in a greenhouse as UK outdoor nights are often too cold.
Harvest the top leaves regularly to delay flowering and extend the lifespan of this tender plant.
items.description: Basil, also called great basil, is a culinary herb of the family Lamiaceae (mints). It is a tender plant, and is used in cuisines worldwide. In Western cuisine, the generic term "basil" refers to the variety also known as Genovese basil or sweet basil. Basil is native to tropical regions from Central Africa to Southeast Asia. In temperate climates basil is treated as an annual plant, but it can be grown as a short-lived perennial or biennial in warmer horticultural zones with tropical or Mediterranean climates.

items.name: Peppermint
items.growersTips:
Grow this vigorous spreader in a submerged 30cm pot to stop invasive runners overtaking UK borders.
Water daily in dry British summers to keep the compost damp, as dry soil triggers early flowering.
Cut stems back to the ground in October then mulch with compost to protect roots from winter rot.
Check the undersides of leaves in spring for orange rust pustules and destroy any infected stems.
Plant near cabbages to repel pests, but keep away from chamomile which stunts peppermint growth.
items.description: Peppermint is a hybrid species of mint, a cross between watermint and spearmint. Indigenous to Europe and the Middle East, the plant is now widely spread and cultivated in many regions of the world. It is occasionally found in the wild with its parent species.

items.name: Astilbe chinensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam enriched with leafmould to prevent the soil drying out.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent leaf scorch, keeping the soil constantly damp.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and size.
Plant alongside Hostas or Rodgersia in partial shade to create a self-shading damp-loving canopy.
Leave faded bronze flower heads intact over winter to provide structural interest in frosty gardens.
items.description: Astilbe chinensis, commonly known as false goat's beard, tall false-buck's-beard or Chinese astilbe, is a species of flowering plant in the saxifrage family, Saxifragaceae. It is a perennial herb that grows near shaded streams and rivers. It is also commonly grown in shade gardens.

items.name: Astilbe × arendsii
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil, incorporating well-rotted manure to prevent drying out.
Position in partial shade to protect the delicate feathery plumes from the drying UK midday sun.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent the foliage from crisping and browning at the edges.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and bloom.
Leave the spent flower heads over winter to provide structural interest and protect the crown from frost.

items.name: Largest masterwort
items.growersTips:
Plant Astrantia maxima in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking UK woodland edges.
Water consistently during dry UK summers to keep the soil damp, as this species cannot tolerate drought.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in midsummer to encourage a second flush of pink blooms.
Protect fresh spring shoots from slugs and snails, which thrive in damp UK gardens and target them.
Propagate by division in spring or autumn every three years to maintain plant vigour and flower size.
items.description: Astrantia maxima,, is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae.

items.name: Hosta plantaginea
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun to partial shade to trigger the highly fragrant late summer white blooms in the UK
Water deeply at the base weekly during dry summer spells to keep the large thin leaves from scorching
Apply a thick layer of organic mulch in spring to retain moisture in free-draining UK garden soils
Surround the plant with copper tape or beer traps in spring to protect emerging shoots from slugs
Cut back dead foliage to the ground in late autumn after the first frost to prevent overwintering pests
items.description: Hosta plantaginea, the fragrant plantain lily or August lily, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to southeast and south-central China, and a garden escapee in scattered locations worldwide. This species and cultivars and hybrids derived from it are the only fragrant hostas. As a wild plant, it is typically found growing in the herb layer of mountain forests, below 2000 m.

items.name: Hosta fortunei
items.growersTips:
Plant crown level with soil in moisture-retentive, organic-rich loam to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply at the base once a week in dry UK summers, keeping leaves dry to avoid fungal spots.
Apply organic wool pellets or copper tape around the base in early spring to deter slugs and snails.
Cut faded flower spikes to the base in August to redirect energy into next year's leaf production.
Divide overcrowded clumps in early spring just as the sharp nose-like shoots begin to break soil.
items.description: Hosta sieboldiana, Siebold's plantain lily, is a species of hosta native to Japan. A putative variety, Hosta sieboldiana var. elegans, has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, as has a putative variety of its synonym; Hosta fortunei var. aureomarginata, the gold-edged plantain lily. The cultivars 'Blue Angel', 'Blue Mammoth', and 'Olive Bailey Langdon' have also gained the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Hosta sieboldiana
items.growersTips:
Plant this giant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral clay or loam enriched with leafmould.
Position in deep or partial shade to prevent the blue-grey waxy leaf coating from melting in sun.
Surround crowns with sharp grit or copper tape in wet UK springs to deter slugs and snails.
Water deeply at the base weekly during dry summer spells, keeping the large foliage dry.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as the pointed buds begin to push through the soil.
items.description: Hosta sieboldiana, Siebold's plantain lily, is a species of hosta native to Japan. A putative variety, Hosta sieboldiana var. elegans, has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, as has a putative variety of its synonym; Hosta fortunei var. aureomarginata, the gold-edged plantain lily. The cultivars 'Blue Angel', 'Blue Mammoth', and 'Olive Bailey Langdon' have also gained the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Heuchera sanguinea
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining neutral soil with compost to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Keep the crown exactly level with the soil surface to prevent stem rot in damp British weather.
Divide every three years in autumn to prevent the woody central stem from lifting out of the ground.
Drench the soil with parasitic nematodes in August to kill devastating vine weevil larvae.
Cut back tattered winter foliage in March to encourage fresh new leaves and summer flower spikes.
items.description: Heuchera sanguinea, called coral bells, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Heuchera, native to the US states of Arizona and New Mexico, and to northern Mexico. A number of cultivars are commercially available. The Latin specific epithet sanguinea means blood-red, in reference to the color of the flowers. Flowers are deep pink to red, sweetly fragrant, and bell-shaped. Heuchera sanguinea is a perennial herb. The plant attracts bees and hummingbirds.

items.name: Heucherella ×tiarelloides
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade using humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil to prevent UK winter root rot.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent leaf scorch, keeping the crown just above soil level.
Divide the woody crowns every three years in early autumn to maintain vigour and prevent center dieback.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which chew the roots and cause the foliage to suddenly collapse.
Pair with hostas and ferns in damp woodland borders to highlight their semi-evergreen winter foliage.
items.description: × Heucherella is an evergreen perennial flowering plant in the family Saxifragaceae. A hybrid of garden origin, it is the result of a cross between two distinct genera, Heuchera and Tiarella, and shows similarities to both parents. This type of intergeneric hybrid is quite rare, and is indicated by a multiplication symbol before the name. The name Heucherella is an example of a portmanteau word, a combination of the two parents' names.

items.name: Tiarella cordifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade under trees
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the shallow fibrous root system from drying out completely
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigour and leaf colour
Watch for vine weevil larvae eating roots in patio pots and apply biological nematodes in autumn
Plant alongside hostas and ferns to create a slug-resistant groundcover in damp woodland borders
items.description: Tiarella cordifolia, the heart-leaved foamflower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Saxifragaceae. The specific name cordifolia means "with heart-shaped leaves", a characteristic shared by all taxa of Tiarella in eastern North America. It is also referred to as Allegheny foamflower, false miterwort, and coolwort.

items.name: Oyster plant
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained soil as wet UK winters will rot the fleshy roots of Acanthus mollis.
Control spread in small gardens by planting inside a deep root barrier to restrict invasive runners.
Cut flower spikes to the base in October and clear dead foliage to prevent overwintering snails.
Grow in partial shade to prevent the large leaves from wilting during dry UK summer spells.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn when the plant enters its winter dormant phase.
items.description: Acanthus mollis, commonly known as bear's breeches, sea dock, bear's foot plant, sea holly, gator plant or oyster plant, is a species of plant in the family Acanthaceae and is native to the Mediterranean region. It is a leafy, clump-forming perennial herb, with a rosette of relatively large, lobed or toothed leaves, and purplish and white flowers on an erect spike.

items.name: Spine acanthus
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, well-drained soil as their taproots hate wet winter clay common in UK gardens.
Position in full sun or partial shade, allowing plenty of space as they easily crowd out neighbours.
Cut flower spikes to the base in late summer to prevent prolific self-seeding across your borders.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in winter when the plant is dormant to guarantee new stock.
items.description: Acanthus spinosus, the spiny bear's breech, is a species of flowering plant in the family Acanthaceae, native to southern Europe, from Italy to western Turkey. It is an herbaceous perennial growing to 150 cm (59 in) tall by 60–90 cm (24–35 in) wide. The deeply cut leaves have spiny margins, and in early summer it bears erect, 1 m (3 ft) long racemes of white flowers with maroon bracts.

items.name: Hubei Anemone
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to prevent the roots from drying out.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to stop foliage crisping, keeping soil consistently damp.
Cut flowered stems down to the ground in late autumn and mulch the crown to protect from hard frosts.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late winter when the plant is dormant to expand your stock.
Watch for caterpillars and slugs on young spring shoots, protecting them with beer traps or grit.
items.description: Eriocapitella hupehensis, a species of flowering plant in the Ranunculaceae family of plants and has an extensive native distribution across a large area of Asia. The plant was previously known as Anemone hupehensis and is often still referred to as such. Together with several closely related species and hybrids between these species, in horticulture these plants are often referred to as Japanese anemones.

items.name: Smell fox
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes horizontally in autumn five centimetres deep in leaf-mould-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water only during dry spring spells to keep soil damp, then leave completely dry during summer dormancy.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Propagate by dividing the brittle rhizomes in late summer once the foliage has completely died back.
Plant alongside wild garlic and primroses to mimic natural UK woodland communities and extend color.
items.description: Anemonoides nemorosa, the wood anemone, is an early-spring flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to Europe. Other common names include windflower, European thimbleweed, and smell fox, an allusion to the musky smell of the leaves. It is a perennial herbaceous plant growing 5–15 cm (2–6 in) tall.

items.name: Anemone cyanea Risso
items.growersTips:
Soak the claw-like tubers in tepid water for twelve hours before planting to kickstart UK growth.
Plant tubers five centimetres deep with the pointed ends facing downwards in autumn or early spring.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soils to prevent winter rot in wet British garden borders.
Apply a thick mulch of bracken or leaf mould in November to protect tubers from hard UK frosts.
Grow alongside early flowering dwarf narcissi to mask the anemone foliage as it dies back in June.
items.description: Anemone coronaria, the poppy anemone, Spanish marigold, or windflower, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to the Mediterranean region.

items.name: Golden columbine
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late winter on the surface of damp compost as they need light and cold to germinate.
Plant in moist, well-drained soil enriched with leafmould to mimic their native woodland habitat.
Cut back faded flower stems to the ground in July to prevent self-seeding and promote fresh leaves.
Check leaves weekly in May for green sawfly larvae and handpick them to prevent total defoliation.
Grow alongside hostas or ferns in partial shade to hide the Aquilegia foliage as it dies back.
items.description: Aquilegia chrysantha, the golden columbine, is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. The plant, with a height of between 40 centimetres (16 in) and 120 centimetres (47 in), has yellow flowers. A. chrysantha. as with other members of the Aquilegia coerulea species complex, is evolved for pollination by hawkmoth. It favors moist environments in its mountainous range.

items.name: Eastern red columbine
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn on the soil surface as they need winter cold and light to germinate in UK gardens
Plant in free-draining neutral soil to prevent winter crown rot during wet UK winters
Cut back foliage to the ground in July if columbine leaf miner leaves unsightly white trails
Water weekly during dry spring spells but leave established plants alone once summer rain returns
Sow away from Aquilegia vulgaris to prevent cross-hybridisation and keep the red species true
items.description: Aquilegia canadensis, the Canadian columbine, Canada columbine, eastern red columbine, or wild columbine, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family. It is a perennial plant that is native to the woodlands and rocky areas in eastern North America in both the United States and southern Canada. It readily hybridizes with other plants in the columbine genus and is a common garden plant.

items.name: Campanula persicifolia
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late spring on the surface of damp compost as they need light to germinate in UK sun.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early autumn to maintain vigor and prevent crown rot.
Deadhead individual faded blooms weekly in summer to stimulate a second flush of blue or white flowers.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers in damp UK weather.
Plant in fertile, moist but well-drained soil in partial shade to prevent the foliage from drying out.
items.description: Campanula persicifolia, the peach-leaved bellflower, is a flowering plant species in the family Campanulaceae. It is an herbaceous perennial growing to 1 m. Its flowers are cup-shaped and can be either lilac-blue or white. Its foliage is narrow and glossy with a bright green appearance.

items.name: Dane's blood
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, free-draining chalky or alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and flowering power.
Cut stems back to ground level immediately after the first summer flush to encourage a second bloom.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit or beer traps.
Grow alongside Geranium rozanne or Alchemilla mollis to mask the scruffy post-flowering foliage.
items.description: Campanula glomerata, known by the common names clustered bellflower or Dane's blood, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Campanula, belonging to the family Campanulaceae. It is the county flower of Rutland, England.

items.name: Campanula medium
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in June on the surface of damp compost as they need light to germinate in UK summers.
Prune the central flower spike right back to the base in July to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Protect young autumn rosettes from slugs and snails using organic bait or grit in damp UK weather.
Plant out in autumn into free-draining alkaline soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Stake the tall flower spikes in April before May winds bend the heavy bell-filled stems.
items.description: Campanula medium, common name Canterbury bells, is an annual or biennial flowering plant of the genus Campanula, belonging to the family Campanulaceae. In floriography, it represents gratitude, or faith and constancy. It is the national flower of Monaco

items.name: C. cyanus
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in September for larger, earlier-flowering plants the following spring.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of 5mm into finely raked, weed-free soil in a fully sunny UK spot.
Support taller cultivars like Blue Boy with brushwood twigs inserted when seedlings are 10cm high.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly to prevent self-seeding and prolong the flowering season until autumn.
Grow in poor, well-drained soil as rich borders cause floppy stems and excessive foliage growth.
items.description: Centaurea cyanus, commonly known as cornflower or bachelor's button, is an annual flowering plant in the family Asteraceae native to Europe. In the past, it often grew as a weed in cornfields, hence its name.

items.name: Centaurea montana
items.growersTips:
Cut back to ground level immediately after the first summer flush to trigger a second autumn bloom.
Plant in well-drained soil as wet UK winter clay causes root rot, though it tolerates poor dry soil.
Divide the congested root clump every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and shape.
Watch for powdery mildew in dry UK summers and water at the base of the plant to keep foliage dry.
Grow alongside Nepeta or Geranium Rozanne to hide the scruffy post-flowering Centaurea foliage.
items.description:
Centaurea montana, the perennial cornflower, mountain cornflower, bachelor's button, montane knapweed or mountain bluet, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, endemic to Europe. It is widespread and common in the more southerly mountain ranges of Europe, but is rarer in the north. It escapes from gardens readily, and has thereby become established in the British Isles, Scandinavia and North America. This plant has become an invasive species in British Columbia, Canada.

items.name: Montbretia 'Bicolor'
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8cm deep in well-drained soil during spring, spacing them 10cm apart to prevent crowding.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain the distinct two-tone blooms.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to keep soil moist but never waterlogged to avoid corm rot.
Cut dead foliage back to the ground in late autumn after the first frost to prevent overwintering.
Mulch the crown with 5cm of compost in November to protect shallow corms from severe UK winter frost.
items.description: Crocosmia × crocosmiiflora, or montbretia, is a garden hybrid of C. aurea and C. pottsii, first bred in 1880 in France by Victor Lemoine. The basionym of the hybrid is Montbretia crocosmiiflora Lemoine. In 1932 it was reclassified as C. × crocosmiiflora (Lemoine) N.E.Br., but the common name "montbretia" is still often found in horticultural literature, and is commonly used in the British Isles for orange-flowered cultivars that have naturalised, while "crocosmia" is reserved for less aggressive red-flowered cultivars.

items.name: Falling stars
items.growersTips:
Plant Crocosmia aurea corms 8cm deep in spring in moisture-retentive, humus-rich, well-drained soil.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to prevent the soil from drying out and stalling blooms.
Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering.
Cut dead foliage back to the ground in late autumn and apply a thick mulch to protect from hard frost.
Watch for red spider mite in dry summers, spraying the undersides of leaves with water to deter them.
items.description: Crocosmia aurea, common names falling stars, Valentine flower, or montbretia, is a perennial flowering plant belonging to the family Iridaceae.

items.name: Delphinium grandiflorum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter crown rot in wet UK climates.
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry summer spells, keeping foliage dry to avoid mildew.
Apply organic copper slug pellets or grit barriers early in spring as new shoots emerge.
Cut back faded flower stems to ground level in July to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Grow in full sun in a sheltered spot to protect the naturally short, bushy stems from wind damage.
items.description: Delphinium grandiflorum is a species of Delphinium known by the common names Siberian larkspur and Chinese delphinium. It is native to Russia and China. There are several popular cultivars in several colours which are grown as ornamental plants, including 'Blue Butterfly', 'Summer Morning', 'Blue Mirror', and 'Summer Stars'. Like many other larkspurs, this plant is poisonous. It is much shorter and more compact than the more familiar tall D. elatum, with dispersed flowers, rather than single spikes.

items.name: Echinops ritro
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep in spring using a cold frame to protect from frost.
Water young plants weekly until established, then leave dry as they are highly drought-tolerant.
Cut stems back to ground level in autumn to encourage healthy new crown growth the following spring.
Plant alongside lavender or rudbeckia to create a vibrant, pollinator-friendly UK border display.
items.description: Echinops ritro, the southern globe thistle, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, native to southern and eastern Europe, from Spain east to Turkey, Ukraine, and Belarus, and western and central Asia east to Mongolia. The species is also sparingly naturalised in scattered locations within North America.

items.name: Blue eryngo
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chilling to break dormancy.
Cut back the faded flower stems to ground level in autumn to keep the basal rosette healthy.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Divide established clumps in spring using a sharp spade to avoid damaging the deep taproot.
items.description: Eryngium planum, the blue eryngo or flat sea holly, is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae, native to the area that includes central and southeastern Europe and Central Asia. It is a thistle-like herbaceous perennial growing to 50 cm (20 in) with branched silvery-blue stems, and numerous small blue conical flowerheads surrounded by spiky bracts in summer.

items.name: Gaura lindheimeri
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Cut back hard to ground level in March to stimulate fresh bushy growth and prevent woodiness.
Sow seeds or take softwood cuttings in spring as Gaura is short-lived and needs replacing often.
Avoid rich fertilizers which cause floppy weak stems that collapse in typical British summer rain.
Grow alongside Lavender or Salvia in full sun to create a drought-tolerant cottage garden display.
items.description: Oenothera lindheimeri, commonly known as Lindheimer's beeblossom, white gaura, pink gaura, Lindheimer's clockweed, and Indian feather, is a species of Oenothera. Several of its common names derive from the genus Gaura, in which this species was formerly placed.

items.name: Purple hellebore
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained alkaline soil adding grit to the planting hole to prevent winter rot
Cut back flowered stems to ground level in late spring to encourage vigorous new basal growth
Position in partial shade sheltered from cold drying winds which scorch the architectural foliage
Water deeply during dry summer spells in their first year to help the deep root system establish
Watch for hellebore black spot in damp UK autumns and promptly remove and destroy affected leaves
items.description: Helleborus argutifolius, the holly-leaved hellebore, or Corsican hellebore, syn. H. corsicus, H. lividus subsp. corsicus is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to Corsica and Sardinia. It is an evergreen perennial growing to 120 cm (47 in) tall by 90 cm (3 ft) wide, with large leathery leaves comprising three spiny-toothed leaflets, and green bowl-shaped flowers in late winter and early spring.

items.name: Helleborus ×hybridus
items.growersTips:
Cut back all old leathery leaves to the ground in late winter to prevent black spot and show off blooms.
Plant crowns shallowly with the bud just below the soil surface to prevent rot in damp UK winters.
Apply a generous mulch of well-rotted organic matter in autumn to mimic their woodland habitat.
Watch for hellebore aphid in spring, blasting them off with water before they distort new growth.
Sow fresh seed immediately in summer as they lose viability quickly in the UK climate.

items.name: Iberis sempervirens
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet root rot in damp UK climates.
Cut back by half immediately after flowering in June to maintain a neat mound and prevent leggy stems.
Space plants thirty centimetres apart in raised beds or rockeries to ensure good air circulation.
Water newly planted Iberis weekly during dry spring spells, but leave established plants dry.
Watch for slugs and snails on tender new spring shoots, especially during wet UK April weather.
items.description: Iberis sempervirens, the evergreen candytuft or perennial candytuft, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae, native to southern Europe. The species is often used as an ornamental garden shrub because of its decorative flowers. Iberis is so named because many members of the genus come from the Iberian Peninsula in south west Europe. Sempervirens means "always green", referring to the evergreen foliage.

items.name: Macedonica scabiosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining chalky or sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds shallowly at 3mm deep in spring or autumn, as they need light to trigger germination.
Cut back faded stems to ground level in July to stimulate a second flush of autumn flowers.
Water young plants weekly during dry spells, but leave established clumps entirely self-sufficient.
Divide overcrowded clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent mildew.
items.description: Knautia macedonica, the Macedonian scabious, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caprifoliaceae. It is native to Southeastern Europe: Albania, Bulgaria, Greece, North Macedonia, southeastern Romania and Kırklareli in Turkey. Growing to 75 cm (30 in), this herbaceous perennial produces rich red "pincushion" flowers, similar to those of its close relative scabious (Scabiosa), on slender upright stems throughout summer.

items.name: Red Hot Poker
items.growersTips:
Plant crowns exactly at soil level in spring to prevent rot in wet UK winters.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells but keep soil bone dry throughout the winter.
Tie the leaves together over the crown in November to protect the plant from heavy UK frosts.
Cut faded flower spikes down to the base in August to encourage a second flush of blooms.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring using two forks back-to-back to boost flowering.
items.description: Kniphofia uvaria is a species of flowering plant in the family Asphodelaceae, commonly known as tritomea, torch lily, or red hot poker, due to the shape and color of its inflorescence. The leaves are reminiscent of a lily, and the flowerhead can reach up to 1.5 m (5 ft) in height. There are many varieties of torch lily, and they bloom at different times during the growing season. The flowers are red, orange, and yellow.

items.name: Winter Poker
items.growersTips:
Plant Kniphofia rooperi crowns 7cm deep in free-draining soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Tie the architectural foliage together in November to protect the crown from severe UK frosts.
Cut faded flower spikes down to the base in late autumn to encourage healthy blooms next autumn.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring using two forks to maintain plant vigour.
Plant alongside late-season Aster or Helenium to create a classic UK autumn border display.
items.description: Kniphofia rooperi, Rooper's red-hot poker, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asphodelaceae, native to the Eastern Cape of South Africa. Growing to 1.2 m (3.9 ft) tall, it is a robust evergreen perennial with strap-shaped leaves produced at an angle from the main stem. In autumn the stout central stems bear flattened oval flowerheads consisting of many tubular florets packed closely together. Green in bud, the flowers open to bright red and fade from the base to yellow and brown, thus giving the appearance of a red-hot poker.

items.name: Oxeye daisy
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn at a depth of two millimetres to mimic natural UK self-seeding cycles.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile well-drained soil to prevent excessive floppy vegetative growth.
Cut back faded stems to ground level in late summer to trigger a second flush of autumn flowers.
Divide established clumps every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and flowering.
Plant alongside red campion and yellow rattle in wildflower patches to balance competitive grasses.
items.description: Leucanthemum vulgare, commonly known as the ox-eye daisy, oxeye daisy, dog daisy, marguerite and other common names, is a widespread flowering plant native to Europe and the temperate regions of Asia, and an introduced plant to North America, Australia and New Zealand.

items.name: Leucanthemella serotina
items.growersTips:
Support the tall stems in late spring using hazel twigs before autumn winds cause them to flop.
Plant crowns just below the soil surface in moisture-retentive clay that does not dry out in July.
Propagate by division in March as new growth emerges to maintain vigor and control its spread.
Cut the entire plant down to ground level in late November after the white flowers fade to brown.
Grow alongside late-season Aster amellus or Miscanthus to hide the bare lower stems in late summer.
items.description: Leucanthemella serotina, called the autumn ox-eye, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Leucanthemella, native to Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia, Romania, Bulgaria, and Ukraine, and introduced to Connecticut, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota and New York in the United States, Ontario and Québec in Canada, and France, Germany, Great Britain, and Switzerland. It is a vigorous, erect perennial growing to 1.5 m (5 ft) tall, bearing flowerheads with white ray florets and greenish-yellow centres, throughout autum

items.name: Prairie feather
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 8cm deep in autumn or spring in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter wet rot.
