Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers rather than daily light sprinkles to rot-proof roots.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Cut faded flower spikes down to the basal foliage in autumn to keep the clump tidy and disease-free.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
items.description: Liatris spicata, the dense blazing star, prairie feather, gayfeather or button snakewort, is a herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is native to eastern North America where it grows in moist prairies and meadows.

items.name: Linaria purpurea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in autumn onto well-drained grit to let UK winter cold trigger germination.
Grow in poor, sharply drained soil to prevent floppy stems and encourage self-seeding in gravel.
Cut flower spikes to the base in August to prompt a second flush and control prolific self-seeding.
Plant alongside dry-loving UK partners like Nepeta or Lavender in full sun to prevent root rot.
Watch for rosemary beetle damage in dry summers and hand-pick them off the purple flower spikes.
items.description: Linaria purpurea or purple toadflax is a purple-flowered plant native to Italy, part of the plantain family (Plantaginaceae). It is sometimes planted in gardens and is also an introduced weed in North America and other parts of Europe.

items.name: Lupinus arboreus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining sandy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Prune hard in late summer after flowering to keep this short-lived shrub compact and woody.
Sow seeds in spring after scarifying with sandpaper to break the tough outer dormancy coat.
Watch for giant lupin aphids in May and squash them immediately before they ruin the flower spikes.
Avoid rich soil or heavy feeding as excess nitrogen causes floppy growth and reduces winter survival.
items.description: Lupinus arboreus, the yellow bush lupine (US) or tree lupin (UK), is a species of flowering plant in the legume family Fabaceae.

items.name: Lychnis chalcedonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn or spring at a depth equal to the pot size in moisture-retentive, well-drained soil.
Stake the tall flower stems in May using hazel twigs to prevent collapse during heavy UK summer rain.
Deadhead spent scarlet blooms weekly in July to encourage a second flush of flowers in late summer.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and flower size.
Cut the entire plant back to ground level in autumn after the foliage dies back to prevent rot.
items.description: Silene chalcedonica, the Maltese-cross or scarlet lychnis, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caryophyllaceae, native to Eurasia. Other common names include flower of Bristol, Jerusalem cross and nonesuch.

items.name: Lysimachia clethroides
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam in partial shade to stop the soil drying out in UK summers.
Contain the invasive running rhizomes by planting inside a bottomless bucket sunk into the border.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigorous white flowering spikes.
Cut the spent flower stems back to the ground in late autumn once the foliage turns deep orange.
Watch for slugs and snails attacking the tender emerging shoots during damp British spring weather.
items.description: Lysimachia clethroides, the gooseneck loosestrife, is a species of flowering plant, traditionally classified in the family Primulaceae. It was transferred to the family Myrsinaceae based on a molecular phylogenetic study, but this family was later merged into the Primulaceae.

items.name: Dotted loosestrife
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous spreader in heavy clay or boggy soil to naturally restrict its invasive roots.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp and prevent powdery mildew.
Divide the congested root clumps every three years in autumn to control spread and renew vigour.
Cut the spent flower stems down to the ground in late October to keep the winter border tidy.
Pair with moisture-loving Astilbe or Hostas to create a contrasting texture in damp shade.
items.description: Lysimachia punctata, the dotted loosestrife, large yellow loosestrife, circle flower, or spotted loosestrife, is a flowering plant species in the family Primulaceae.

items.name: Macleaya cordata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun or partial shade, sheltered from strong UK winds.
Control its invasive rhizomes by planting inside a buried, bottomless bucket or deep root barrier.
Cut the hollow stems right back to ground level in late autumn or winter using sharp secateurs.
Wear gloves when pruning to avoid skin irritation from the toxic, staining orange-yellow sap.
Propagate in spring by dividing the root clump or taking root cuttings before new growth starts.
items.description: Macleaya cordata, the five-seeded plume-poppy, is a species of flowering plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae, which is used ornamentally. It is native to China and Japan. It is a large herbaceous perennial growing to 2.5 m (8 ft) tall by 1 m (3 ft) or more wide, with olive green leaves and airy panicles of buff-white flowers in summer.

items.name: Meconopsis betonicifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics a damp, cool Scottish woodland floor.
Water with rainwater to keep soil constantly moist but never waterlogged during dry UK summers.
Protect emerging spring crowns from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Cut back faded flower stems in autumn to prevent self-seeding and encourage strong winter crowns.
Plant alongside shade-loving Hostas or Ferns to shelter the delicate blue blooms from harsh winds.
items.description: Meconopsis betonicifolia, the Himalayan blue poppy, is a species of flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae. It was first formally named for western science in 1912 by the British officer Lt. Col. Frederick Marshman Bailey.

items.name: Bishop's wort
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly outdoors in spring or autumn at a depth of one centimetre to avoid root disturbance.
Water seedlings lightly until established then leave to tolerate dry UK summer soil without rotting.
Thin emerging seedlings to fifteen centimetres apart to prevent mildew in damp British weather.
Leave the decorative balloon-like seed pods on the stem to self-seed naturally for the next spring.
Sow alongside calendula to attract beneficial ladybirds that control aphids in UK cottage gardens.
items.description:
Nigella damascena, love-in-a-mist, or devil in the bush, is an annual garden flowering plant, belonging to the buttercup family Ranunculaceae. 
It is native to southern Europe, north Africa and southwest Asia, where it is found on neglected, damp patches of land.

items.name: Blue Jacob's ladder
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic cool British woodland edges.
Position in partial shade as hot midday UK summer sun will quickly scorch and bleach the foliage.
Deadhead spent flower spikes in July to prevent self-seeding and encourage a second flush of blooms.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp spring weather as they target the tender emerging fern-like leaves.
Propagate by division in autumn or spring every three years to maintain plant vigour and health.
items.description: Polemonium caeruleum, known as Jacob's-ladder or Greek valerian, is a hardy perennial flowering plant. The plant produces cup-shaped, blue or white flowers. It is native to temperate regions of Europe. It is the type species of the phlox family, Polemoniaceae.

items.name: Common Primrose
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root primroses in autumn at crown level so the base of the leaves sits flush with the soil
Water thoroughly during dry summer spells to mimic damp UK woodlands and prevent leaf scorch
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating roots in autumn and apply biological nematode controls in September
Divide congested clumps every three years immediately after spring flowering to maintain plant vigour
Incorporate leaf mould or well-rotted manure into heavy clay soils to ensure moisture-retentive loam
items.description: Primula vulgaris is a species of flowering plant in the family Primulaceae, native to Eurasia. The common name of this plant is primrose, or occasionally common primrose or English primrose to distinguish it from other Primula species referred to as primroses.

items.name: Herb Peter
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in autumn outdoors as they require winter cold stratification to germinate in UK spring.
Plant crowns just at soil level in moisture-retentive, heavy clay or loam with neutral to lime soil.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers to mimic their natural damp meadow habitat.
Divide established clumps every three years in late summer after seed heads have fully dispersed.
Watch for vine weevil larvae eating roots in container-grown plants and treat with nematodes.
items.description: Primula veris, the cowslip, common cowslip, or cowslip primrose, is a herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the primrose family Primulaceae. The species is native throughout most of temperate Europe and western Asia, and although absent from more northerly areas including much of northwest Scotland, it reappears in northernmost Sutherland and Orkney and in Scandinavia. This species frequently hybridizes with other Primulas such as the common primrose Primula vulgaris to form false oxlip which is often confused with true oxlip, a much rarer plant.

items.name: Primula denticulata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that mimics UK damp meadows, avoiding dry sandy spots.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in late summer as they require light and UK winter cold to germinate.
Water consistently during dry UK summer spells to prevent the shallow root system from drying out.
Watch for vine weevil grubs in autumn, which actively destroy the roots of these primulas in pots.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering in late spring to maintain vigor and plant health.
items.description:
Primula denticulata, the drumstick primula, is a species of flowering plant in the family Primulaceae, native to moist alpine regions of China, Afghanistan, Bhutan, India, N Myanmar, Nepal, and Pakistan. It is an herbaceous perennial growing to 45 cm (18 in) tall and wide, with rosettes of oval leaves and sturdy stems bearing spherical umbels of purple flowers in late spring and early summer. Flowers can also be lavender, pink, or white in colour. 
The specific epithet denticulata means "small-toothed", referring to the serrated leaf edges.
The plant's common name, drumstick primula, refers to

items.name: Pulsatilla vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Position in full sun and avoid watering once established, as they hate damp summer conditions.
Sow fresh seed in summer immediately after harvesting, as viability drops rapidly over time.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
Avoid moving or dividing established plants because their deep taproots resent disturbance.
items.description: Pulsatilla vulgaris, the pasqueflower, is a species of flowering plant belonging to the buttercup family (Ranunculaceae), found locally on calcareous grassland in Europe, and widely cultivated in gardens. It was considered part of the genus Anemone, to which it is closely related. Several sources still list Anemone pulsatilla as the accepted name, with Pulsatilla vulgaris as a synonym.

items.name: Salvia × sylvestris
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Cut back faded flower spikes to the base in July to stimulate a second flush of autumn blooms.
Leave dead stems intact over winter to protect the crown from frost, then clear them in March.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.
Water newly planted salvias weekly during dry UK summers until their deep root system establishes.

items.name: Salvia farinacea
items.growersTips:
Grow as a half-hardy annual in the UK, sowing seeds indoors in warm propagators during early March.
Plant out in late May after frosts, spacing 30cm apart in free-draining soil with grit added.
Water weekly during dry summer spells, aiming at the base to prevent powdery mildew on leaves.
Deadhead faded blue flower spikes weekly in July and August to stimulate continuous fresh blooms.
Take stem cuttings in September to overwinter indoors as the UK winter wet and frost will kill them.
items.description: Salvia farinacea, the mealycup sage, or mealy sage, is a herbaceous perennial native to Nuevo León, Mexico and parts of the United States including Texas and Oklahoma. Violet-blue spikes rest on a compact plant of typically narrow salvia-like leaves; however, the shiny leaves are what set this species apart from most other Salvia, which bear velvety-dull leaves.

items.name: Salvia uliginosa
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered, boggy spot or moist border as this species craves more water than other salvias.
Mulch the crown deeply with bark chips in late autumn to protect its roots from wet UK winter frosts.
Cut the tall, hollow stems back to ground level only in spring after the worst winter frosts pass.
Stake the floppy six-foot stems in May using hazel twigs before the sky-blue flowers weigh them down.
Propagate by digging up and dividing the vigorous underground runners in April as new growth starts.
items.description: The plant known as Salvia uliginosa, the bog sage, is a species of flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, native to southern Brazil, Uruguay, and Argentina. It was described and named by botanist George Bentham for its typical habitat "of swamps and marshes", or uliginosa.

items.name: Great Burnet
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loamy soil that mimics UK damp meadows, keeping it neutral to acid.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn as they require winter chilling to germinate successfully.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent the damp-loving foliage from crisping at the edges.
Cut back faded flower stems to the ground in autumn to maintain a tidy clump and prevent self-seeding.
Divide mature congested clumps in early spring to propagate and maintain the plant's vigour.
items.description: Sanguisorba officinalis, commonly known as great burnet, is a plant in the family Rosaceae, subfamily Rosoideae. It is native throughout the cooler regions of the Northern Hemisphere in Europe, northern Asia, and northern North America.

items.name: Scabiosa caucasica
items.growersTips:
Incorporate plenty of grit when planting in heavy UK clay to prevent winter root rot in wet soil.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly down to the next bud to prolong the flowering season from June to October.
Apply garden lime annually in autumn to raise soil pH, as this perennial thrives in alkaline conditions.
Propagate by division in early spring every three years to maintain plant vigour and prevent dieback.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps in damp weather.
items.description: Lomelosia caucasica, the Caucasian pincushion flower, pincushion-flower or Caucasian scabious, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caprifoliaceae, native to the Caucasus, north eastern Turkey, and northern Iran. Growing to 60 cm (24 in) tall and broad, it is a clump-forming perennial with grey-green, divided leaves. Pincushion-shaped buds, borne on erect hairy, stems, open to pale blue or lavender flower heads, 4–8 cm (2–3 in) in diameter, from late summer through to autumn.

items.name: Bacherlor's buttons
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring just covered with grit in free-draining chalky soil to prevent winter wet rot.
Water newly planted scabious weekly until established, then only during severe summer UK droughts.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly from July to October to stimulate a continuous flush of new flowers.
Cut the faded foliage back to the ground in March to encourage fresh healthy spring basal growth.
Divide mature clumps every three years in April to maintain plant vigour and prevent center dieback.
items.description: Scabiosa columbaria, called the small scabious or dwarf pincushion flower, is a widespread species of flowering plant in the genus Scabiosa, native to Europe, Africa, and western Asia, from Sweden to Angola. In the garden it is a short-lived deciduous perennial. In the wild in Europe it prefers to grow in calcareous grasslands.

items.name: Biting stonecrop
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural sand to prevent winter wet root rot.
Water only during extreme summer droughts, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings.
Position in full sun, such as a south-facing rockery, to maintain its compact, golden carpet habit.
Propagate in spring by pressing stem cuttings lightly into the soil surface without burying them deep.
Grow alongside Sempervivum and Thymus serpyllum which thrive in the same dry, nutrient-poor conditions.
items.description: Sedum acre, commonly known as the goldmoss stonecrop, mossy stonecrop, goldmoss sedum, biting stonecrop, and wallpepper, is a perennial flowering plant in the family Crassulaceae. It is native to Europe, northern and western Asia and North Africa, but is also naturalised in North America, southern South America, Japan, and New Zealand.

items.name: Solidago canadensis
items.growersTips:
Plant dwarf cultivars like Goldenmosa in heavy clay to prevent the invasive spreading of wild types.
Cut stems to the ground in late autumn to prevent self-seeding across damp UK lawns and borders.
Divide the root clump every three years in March to maintain flower vigour and control its spread.
Grow alongside Aster novi-belgii in moist, well-drained soil to create a mildew-resistant display.
Watch for powdery mildew in dry Augusts and water at the base rather than wetting the foliage.
items.description: Solidago canadensis, known as Canada goldenrod or Canadian goldenrod, is an herbaceous perennial plant of the family Asteraceae. It forms colonies of upright growing plants, with many small yellow flowers in a branching inflorescence held above the foliage. It is native to northeastern and north-central North America and is an invasive plant in other parts of the continent and several areas worldwide, including Eurasia.

items.name: Stachys macrantha
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn or spring at a depth level with the soil surface in moist, well-drained clay or loam.
Water weekly during dry UK summers until established, then only during prolonged periods of drought.
Cut back faded flower spikes to the base in August to encourage a second flush of fresh foliage.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent center dieback.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to utilize natural winter chilling for spring germination.
items.description: Betonica macrantha, formerly Stachys macrantha, known as big betony, is a species of flowering plant in the mint family Lamiaceae. It is native to the Caucasus, northeastern Turkey, and northwestern Iran. Growing to 60 cm (24 in) tall by 30 cm (12 in) broad, it is an erect herbaceous perennial with scalloped cordate leaves. Spikes of hooded purplish-pink flowers are borne throughout summer.

items.name: Thalictrum delavayi
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edge conditions.
Provide sturdy brushwood support or hazel twigs in spring before the tall, delicate stems emerge.
Mulch annually in autumn with well-rotted leafmould to protect crown roots from wet winter rot.
Cut dead stems back to ground level in early spring just as new basal foliage begins to show.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Thalictrum delavayi, Chinese meadow-rue, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae native to China. Growing to 1.2 m (4 ft) tall by 60 cm (24 in) wide, it is a herbaceous perennial with leaves divided into many small leaflets, and panicles of lilac flowers with green or white stamens in summer.

items.name: French Meadow-rue
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade to mimic cool UK woodland edges.
Apply a thick mulch of leaf mould or compost each spring to keep the shallow root system damp.
Cut back the faded flower stems to ground level in autumn after the purple seed heads turn brown.
Provide brushwood support or ring stakes in windy UK gardens before the tall stems reach one metre.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as the delicate columbine-like foliage starts to emerge.
items.description: Thalictrum aquilegiifolium is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae. It is known by the common names Siberian columbine meadow-rue, columbine meadow-rue, French meadow-rue, and greater meadow-rue. Its native range extends through Europe and temperate Asia, with a naturalized distribution in North America limited to New York and Ontario.

items.name: Verbascum bombyciferum
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in free-draining chalky soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Sow seeds on the soil surface in spring as they require light and UK spring warmth to germinate.
Avoid watering established plants in summer to prevent crown rot in damp British weather.
Cut spent flower spikes to the base in August to encourage a second flush of blooms before autumn.
Watch for mullein moth caterpillars in June and handpick them to protect the silver woolly foliage.
items.description: Verbascum bombyciferum, called the giant silver mullein, Turkish mullein and Broussa mullein, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Verbascum, native to Turkey, and introduced to California, Great Britain and Germany. It is considered a good plant to attract pollinators. With Verbascum chaixii it is a parent of the 'Pink Domino' cultivar, which has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Verbascum chaixii
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Cut faded flower spikes to the base in August to encourage a second flush of autumn blooms.
Space plants 45cm apart in full sun to prevent powdery mildew in humid British summers.
Check the crown regularly in spring for mullein moth caterpillars and handpick them off.
Propagate by taking root cuttings in late autumn when the plant enters winter dormancy.
items.description: Verbascum chaixii, the nettle-leaved mullein, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Verbascum, native to Spain, France, Italy, the former Yugoslavia, and Greece. It is considered a good plant to attract pollinators. With Verbascum bombyciferum it is a parent of the 'Pink Domino' cultivar, which has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Spiked Speedwell
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly in May on free-draining UK soil to ensure winter cold triggers next year's bloom.
Water young plants weekly during dry spells but keep soil dry in winter to prevent root rot.
Cut faded flower spikes to the base in July to encourage a second flush of late summer blooms.
Watch for powdery mildew in humid UK summers by spacing plants thirty centimetres apart for airflow.
Plant alongside English lavender to deter slugs and snails that target tender spring growth.
items.description: Veronica spicata is a species of flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae. It is 1–3 feet (0.30–0.91 m) tall and bears 1 foot long spikes with blue, pink, purple and white flowers.

items.name: Veronica longifolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, fertile soil, adding leaf mould to mimic UK damp meadow conditions.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut back faded flower spikes to the base in July to encourage a second flush of late-summer blooms.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain plant vigour and flower size.
Watch for powdery mildew in humid August weather, ensuring wide spacing for good air circulation.
items.description: Veronica longifolia, known as garden speedwell or longleaf speedwell, is a flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae.

items.name: Wood violet
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn at a depth equal to the root ball in moist, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees.
Water weekly during dry UK spring spells to prolong flowering, keeping soil damp but never soggy.
Clear fallen autumn leaves from crowns to prevent rot and deter slugs from eating young spring buds.
Divide congested clumps every three years in late summer after flowering to maintain plant vigour.
Sow fresh seed in cold frames in autumn, as they require winter chilling to trigger germination.
items.description: Viola odorata is a species of flowering plant in the family Violaceae. The small hardy herbaceous perennial is commonly known as wood violet, sweet violet, English violet, common violet, florist's violet, or garden violet.

items.name: Wild Pansy
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of 1.5mm in late summer for robust spring-flowering plugs.
Grow in gritty, free-draining neutral soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Deadhead spent blooms weekly from May to September to prolong the flowering window.
Water the soil directly at dawn to prevent powdery mildew on the delicate foliage.
Watch for violet gall midge damage and immediately prune out distorted leaves in June.
items.description: Viola tricolor is a common European wild flower, growing as an annual or short-lived perennial. The species is also known as wild pansy, Johnny Jump up, heartsease, heart's ease, heart's delight, tickle-my-fancy, Jack-jump-up-and-kiss-me, come-and-cuddle-me, three faces in a hood, love-in-idleness, and pink of my john.

items.name: Pansy
items.growersTips:
Plant winter-flowering cultivars like Matrix in September for reliable colour through UK frosts.
Deadhead faded flowers weekly by pinching the stem base to prevent seed pods and prolong blooming.
Water at the base in the morning to keep foliage dry and prevent downy mildew in damp UK weather.
Plant plugs 15cm apart with the crown level with the soil to prevent stem rot in wet winter clay.
Check under leaves in mild autumns for aphids and slugs, using organic grit barriers around pots.
items.description: The garden pansy is a type of polychromatic large-flowered hybrid plant cultivated as a garden flower. It is derived by hybridization from several species in the section Melanium of the genus Viola, particularly V. tricolor, a wildflower of Europe and western Asia known as heartsease. It is sometimes known as V. tricolor var. hortensis, but this scientific name is suspect. While V. tricolor var. hortensis Groenland & Rümpler is a synonym of Viola × wittrockiana, V. tricolor var. hortensis DC. refers to a horticultural variety of wild pansy that had been illustrated in Flora Danica in 1777 befo

items.name: Orange eye
items.growersTips:
Prune hard in March down to 30cm from the ground to encourage vigorous new flowering stems.
Plant in poor well-drained soil as rich UK garden soils produce excessive leaf growth over flowers.
Deadhead faded flower spikes in August to prevent prolific self-seeding in nearby paving cracks.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry UK spells but leave established plants entirely alone.
Grow in full sun to attract maximum numbers of native UK tortoiseshell and peacock butterflies.
items.description: Buddleja davidii, also called butterfly-bush, orange eye, or summer lilac, is a species of flowering plant in the family Scrophulariaceae, native to most of China except for the far northeast. It is widely used as an ornamental plant, and many named cultivars are in cultivation. The genus was named Buddleja after the English botanist, Reverend Adam Buddle. The species name, davidii, is after the French missionary and explorer in China, Father Armand David, who was the first European to report the shrub. It was found near Yichang by Dr Augustine Henry about 1887 and sent to St Petersburg. Anoth

items.name: Buddleja globosa
items.growersTips:
Prune immediately after flowering in June by cutting back flowered shoots to strong new growth.
Plant in well-drained soil in a sheltered south or west facing spot to protect from cold UK winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first two years until fully established.
Propagate in July using semi-ripe cuttings taken from non-flowering shoots of the current season.
Watch for capsid bug damage in spring which causes distorted leaves and tiny holes in new growth.
items.description: Buddleja globosa, also known as the orange-ball-tree, orange ball buddleja, and matico, is a species of flowering plant native to Chile and Argentina, where it grows in dry and moist forest, from sea level to 2,000 m. The species was first described and named by Hope in 1782.

items.name: Border forsythia
items.growersTips:
Prune immediately after flowering in May by cutting back one-third of old stems to the ground.
Plant bare-root shrubs between November and March in moist but well-drained soil during mild weather.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry spells in their first UK summer to establish roots.
Propagate in July by taking semi-ripe cuttings of non-flowering shoots to grow on in cold frames.
Mulch annually in late winter with well-rotted manure to retain moisture in sandy or chalky soils.
items.description: Forsythia × intermedia, or border forsythia, is an ornamental deciduous shrub of garden origin.

items.name: Old-fashion weigela
items.growersTips:
Prune immediately after flowering in July by cutting back one in three oldest stems to the base.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam soil enriched with garden compost to prevent summer wilt.
Position in full sun for the best leaf colour on dark cultivars like Alexandra or Variegata.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK spells in June and July while the shrub is establishing.
Mulch annually in March with well-rotted manure to feed the plant and lock in winter moisture.
items.description: Weigela florida, the old-fashioned weigela, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caprifoliaceae. It is native to Inner Mongolia, Manchuria, northern and south-central China, Primorsky Krai in the Russian Far East, the Korean Peninsula, and Kyushu in Japan, and it has been introduced to Bulgaria, Great Britain, Ireland, the United States, and Uzbekistan. A deciduous shrub reaching 2.5 m (8 ft), it is typically found in scrublands and mixed evergreen/deciduous forests, at elevations from 100 to 1,500 m above sea level. Recommended for screens and hedges, and attractive to hummingbirds,

items.name: Japanese Spiraea
items.growersTips:
Prune hard in March down to 15cm to stimulate vigorous new pink-flushed shoots and summer flowers.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay loam enriched with garden compost to prevent midsummer leaf scorch.
Water deeply once a week during dry July spells to stop powdery mildew, a common UK summer issue.
Deadhead faded pink flower clusters in August to encourage a second flush of blooms before autumn.
Grow alongside blue-flowered Geranium Rozanne to contrast beautifully with golden-leaved cultivars.
items.description: Spiraea japonica, the Japanese meadowsweet or Japanese spiraea, is a plant in the family Rosaceae.

items.name: Spiraea ×vanhouttei
items.growersTips:
Prune immediately after June flowering by cutting one-third of old stems to the base to boost blooms.
Plant in moist, well-drained clay or loam, adding garden compost to the planting hole to retain water.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers for the first two years until the roots establish.
Watch for aphids and powdery mildew in damp British springs, pruning congested branches for airflow.
Underplant with spring bulbs like bluebells that bloom before the shrub leafes out in UK gardens.

items.name: Cramp bark
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam, adding leaf mould to mimic UK woodland edge conditions.
Prune in late summer after berries fade, cutting back one-fifth of old stems to ground level.
Water weekly during dry UK summers for the first two years to establish a deep, resilient root system.
Inspect leaves in May for Viburnum beetle larvae, hand-picking them to prevent severe defoliation.
Sow seeds in cold frames in autumn, as they require two winter chills to germinate in UK climates.
items.description: Viburnum opulus, commonly known as the guelder-rose, or guelder rose, is an Old World species of flowering plant in the family Adoxaceae.

items.name: Viburnum tinus
items.growersTips:
Prune in May after flowering to shape the shrub and prevent it from outgrowing its garden space
Plant in well-drained soil enriched with compost to prevent root rot during wet UK winters
Watch for viburnum beetle grubs in spring and pick them off to prevent severe leaf shredding
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish deep roots
Grow the compact cultivar Eve Price in smaller gardens to avoid the need for heavy annual pruning
items.description: Viburnum tinus, the laurustinus or laurustine, is a species of flowering plant in the family Adoxaceae, native to the Mediterranean area of Europe and North Africa.

items.name: Viburnum × bodnantense
items.growersTips:
Prune established stems by cutting one-fifth of the oldest wood to the base in April after flowering
Plant in a spot sheltered from cold UK winds to prevent frost damage to the winter-scented blooms
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to retain moisture in dry southern UK summers
Grow in moist but well-drained soil with a neutral to acidic pH to prevent leaf chlorosis
Choose the cultivar Dawn for the most reliable deep pink flowers during dark British winters
items.description: Viburnum × bodnantense, the Bodnant viburnum, is a Group of hybrid flowering plant cultivars of garden origin. They originate in a cross between V. farreri and V. grandiflorum made by Charles Puddle, head gardener to Lord Aberconway at Bodnant Garden, Wales around 1935.

items.name: Tall Oregon-grape
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, keeping the root flare level with the ground.
Water weekly during the first dry summer, then leave to rely on natural UK rainfall once established.
Prune immediately after spring flowering, cutting back leggy stems to a strong bud to keep it bushy.
Watch for rust and powdery mildew in damp UK autumns, clearing fallen leaves to prevent reinfection.
Underplant with shade-loving UK native wood anemones or winter aconites to mask bare lower stems.
items.description: Berberis aquifolium, the Oregon grape holly-leaved barberry, or Mahonia, is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae. It is an evergreen shrub growing up to 3 metres (10 ft) tall and 1.5 m (5 ft) wide. It has pinnate leaves consisting of spiny leaflets, exhibiting dense clusters of yellow flowers in early spring, followed by dark bluish-black berries.

items.name: Mahonia ×media
items.growersTips:
Prune immediately after flowering in spring by cutting leggy stems back to a strong lower bud.
Plant in fertile moisture-retentive soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish a deep resilient root system.
Watch for rust disease on leaves in damp UK autumns and prune out affected foliage to prevent spread.
Underplant with shade-loving dry-soil tolerant cyclamen or hellebores to cover the bare woody base.
items.description: Berberis × hortensis is an interspecific hybrid shrub. Its parents are Berberis oiwakensis and Berberis japonica. It was raised in gardens during the 20th century, and has become an important garden and landscape plant.

items.name: Black elder
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam, adding leaf mould to mimic its native UK woodland edge.
Prune hard in late winter to encourage the most vibrant foliage on dark cultivars like Black Lace.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish a deep, resilient root system.
Watch for black bean aphid infestations on tender new spring shoots and blast them off with water.
Propagate easily by taking hardwood cuttings in late autumn and inserting them directly into soil.
items.description: Sambucus nigra is a species complex of flowering plants in the family Viburnaceae native to most of Europe. Common names include elder, elderberry, black elder, European elder,  European elderberry, and European black elderberry. It grows in a variety of conditions including both wet and dry fertile soils, primarily in sunny locations. The plant is widely grown as an ornamental shrub or small tree.

items.name: Cotoneaster horizontalis
items.growersTips:
Plant against a south or west wall using rawlplugs and wire to train the herringbone branches flat.
Prune in late winter to remove dead wood and keep the flat shape before new spring growth starts.
Watch for cotoneaster webworm caterpillars in summer and cut out silk-webbed branches immediately.
Grow in well-drained UK soil as wet winter clay causes root rot; add grit to the planting hole.
Do not plant near pear orchards due to fireblight risk, a serious bacterial disease in the UK.
items.description: Cotoneaster horizontalis is a species of flowering plant in the genus Cotoneaster of the family Rosaceae.

items.name: Darwin's barberry
items.growersTips:
Prune immediately after flowering in late summer to avoid cutting off next springs orange blooms
Plant in well-drained soil with a handful of grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot
Watch for berberis sawfly larvae defoliating leaves from May to October and handpick them off
Grow alongside Choisya ternata for contrasting foliage textures and overlapping UK flowering times
Mulch annually in spring with compost to maintain the acidic to neutral soil this shrub prefers
items.description: Berberis darwinii, Darwin's barberry, is a species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae. It is native to southern Chile and Argentina and naturalized elsewhere. Regional vernacular names include michay, calafate, and quelung. Growing to 3–4 m (9.8–13.1 ft) tall, it is an evergreen thorny shrub.

items.name: Red barberry
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun to maximise the intense red foliage colour, as partial shade turns leaves green.
Prune in late winter or early spring by removing one-fifth of old stems to keep the shrub compact.
Water weekly during the first dry UK summer, then leave to rely solely on natural British rainfall.
Watch for berberis sawfly larvae in May and hand-pick them to prevent rapid defoliation of leaves.
Grow in well-drained soil, adding grit to heavy UK clay to prevent root rot during wet winters.
items.description: Berberis thunbergii, the Japanese barberry, Thunberg's barberry, or red barberry, is a species of flowering plant in the barberry family Berberidaceae, native to Japan and eastern Asia, though widely naturalized in China and North America, where it has become a problematic invasive in many places, leading to declines in species diversity, increased tick habitat, and soil changes. Growing to 1 m tall by 2.5 m broad, it is a small deciduous shrub with green leaves turning red in the autumn, brilliant red fruits in autumn and pale yellow flowers in spring.

items.name: Hamamelis x intermedia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to prevent summer leaf scorch.
Prune in spring immediately after flowering by cutting back weak shoots to a strong outward bud.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to ensure next winters flower buds develop successfully.
Underplant with early bulbs like Galanthus nivalis to complement the bare winter flowering stems.
Choose cultivar Pallida for reliable strong scent or Jelena for striking copper autumn foliage.
items.description: Hamamelis × intermedia, the hybrid witch hazel, is a flowering plant in the family Hamamelidaceae. It is a hybrid of garden origin between H. japonica and H. mollis. Its Latin name refers to its intermediate appearance between those two species.

items.name: Hamamelis mollis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil, adding plenty of composted bark to the pit.
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer spells to ensure next winter's flower buds develop.
Prune only in spring immediately after flowering, removing dead wood and crossing branches gently.
Watch for vine weevil larvae eating the roots of young plants and treat with autumn nematodes.
Underplant with Galanthus nivalis to create a striking winter display beneath the bare branches.
items.description: Hamamelis mollis, also known as Chinese witch hazel, is a species of flowering plant in the witch hazel family Hamamelidaceae, native to central and eastern China, in Anhui, Guangxi, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Sichuan, and Zhejiang.

items.name: White dogwood
items.growersTips:
Prune hard to the ground in late March to stimulate the brightest red winter stems on new growth.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay soil in full sun to maximise the vibrant winter stem colour.
Mulch annually in autumn with well-rotted manure to keep the shallow root system damp and cool.
Watch for horse chestnut scale insects on the stems and treat with organic fatty acid sprays.
Propagate easily in November using hardwood cuttings inserted directly into outdoor soil trenches.
items.description: Cornus alba, the red-barked, white or Siberian dogwood, is a species of flowering plant in the family Cornaceae, native to Siberia, northern China and Korea. It is a large deciduous surculose (suckering) shrub that can be grown as a small tree. As a popular ornamental used in landscaping its notable features include the red stems in fall (autumn) through late winter, bright winter bark; and the variegated foliage in some cultivars, such as C. alba 'Elegantissima'. C. alba can grow to 3 m (10 ft) high, but variegated forms are less vigorous. For the brightest winter bark, young shoots are encou

items.name: Red osier
items.growersTips:
Prune stems to the ground in late March to encourage the brightest red winter colour on new growth.
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or boggy soil near ponds to mimic its natural wet UK habitat.
Mulch annually in April with well-rotted manure to boost the vigorous growth needed for red stems.
Propagate easily in November using hardwood cuttings inserted directly into outdoor soil trenches.
Watch for horse chestnut scale insects on older wood and treat with organic plant oil sprays.
items.description: Cornus sericea, the red osier or red-osier dogwood, is a species of flowering plant in the family Cornaceae, native to much of North America. It has sometimes been considered a synonym of the Asian species Cornus alba. Other names include red brush, red willow, redstem dogwood, redtwig dogwood, red-rood, American dogwood, creek dogwood, and western dogwood.

items.name: Flowering dogwood
items.growersTips:
Plant in acidic to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic their native woodland floor.
Water deeply weekly during dry UK summers to prevent shallow root scorch and leaf margin browning.
Prune only in late winter to remove dead wood as they dislike hard pruning and bloom on old wood.
Watch for powdery mildew in humid UK summers by spacing plants well to ensure good air circulation.
Mulch annually in spring with composted pine needles to maintain the low soil pH they require.
items.description: Cornus florida, the flowering dogwood or American dogwood, is a species of flowering tree in the family Cornaceae native to eastern North America and northern Mexico. An endemic population once spanned from southernmost coastal Maine south to northern Florida and west to the Mississippi River. The tree is commonly planted as an ornamental in residential and public areas because of its showy bracts and interesting bark structure.

items.name: Kousa dogwood
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn to avoid UK summer drought stress, keeping the root flare level with the soil surface.
Incorporate acidic leaf mould or peat-free compost into sandy or chalky UK soils to prevent chlorosis.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK spells for the first three years to establish fibrous roots.
Prune only in late winter to remove crossing branches, as spring pruning causes sap bleeding.
Watch for horse chestnut scale insects on stems and treat with organic winter wash in December.
items.description: Cornus kousa is a small deciduous tree 8–12 m (26–39 ft) tall, in the flowering plant family Cornaceae. Common names include kousa, kousa dogwood, Chinese dogwood, Korean dogwood, and Japanese dogwood. Synonyms are Benthamia kousa and Cynoxylon kousa. It is a plant native to East Asia including Korea, China and Japan. Widely cultivated as an ornamental, it is naturalized in the state of New York.

items.name: Magnolia stellata
items.growersTips:
Plant in neutral to acidic soil enriched with compost to prevent chlorosis in chalky UK gardens.
Position in a sheltered, west-facing spot to protect early spring buds from late UK frosts.
Prune lightly in midsummer after flowering to maintain shape and avoid bleeding sap.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or bark to retain moisture in sandy or clay soils.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to ensure next year's flower buds develop successfully.
items.description: Magnolia stellata, the star magnolia, is a slow-growing deciduous shrub or small tree native to Japan. It bears large, showy white or pink flowers in early spring, before its leaves open. This species is closely related to the Kobushi magnolia, Magnolia stellata was accepted as a distinct species in the 1998 monograph by Hunt.

items.name: Tulip magnolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered spot facing south or west to protect early spring buds from late UK frosts.
Incorporate acidic peat-free compost or leaf mould into neutral to acid soil to prevent chlorosis.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first three years to establish a strong root system.
Prune only in midsummer after flowering to prevent bleeding sap and allow wounds to heal quickly.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted bark to retain moisture and protect shallow roots.
items.description: Magnolia × soulangeana, the saucer magnolia or sometimes the tulip tree, is a hybrid flowering plant in the genus Magnolia and family Magnoliaceae. It is a deciduous tree with large, early-blooming flowers in various shades of white, pink, and purple. It is one of the most commonly used magnolias in horticulture, being widely planted in the British Isles, especially in the south of England; and in the United States, especially the east and west coasts.

items.name: Bull bay
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring in a south-facing, sheltered spot to protect buds from harsh UK winter winds.
Incorporate acidic peat-free compost and leaf mould deeply into the planting hole to lower soil pH.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells for the first three years until fully established.
Prune lightly in spring only to shape or remove frost damage, as heavy pruning ruins the form.
Watch for scale insects on the undersides of the glossy leaves and treat with organic insecticidal soap.
items.description: Magnolia grandiflora, commonly known as the southern magnolia or bull bay, is a tree of the family Magnoliaceae native to the Southeastern United States, from Virginia to central Florida, and west to East Texas. Reaching 27.5 m (90 ft) in height, it is a large, striking evergreen tree, with large, dark-green leaves up to 20 cm long and 12 cm wide, and large, white, fragrant flowers up to 30 cm (12 in) in diameter.

items.name: Acer palmatum
items.growersTips:
Plant in a site sheltered from cold easterly winds to prevent spring frost damage to emerging leaves.
Incorporate ericaceous compost and grit to ensure a slightly acidic, moist yet free-draining soil.
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer spells to prevent leaf scorch on delicate foliage.
Prune only during mid-winter dormancy to avoid sap bleeding which weakens the tree and invites rot.
Position red-leaved cultivars in dappled sunlight to prevent leaf scorch while maintaining color.
items.description: Acer palmatum, commonly known as Japanese maple, palmate maple, or smooth Japanese maple, is a species of woody plant native to Korea, Japan, China, eastern Mongolia, and southeast Russia. Many different cultivars of this maple have been selected and they are grown worldwide for their large variety of attractive forms, leaf shapes, and spectacular colors.

items.name: Acer japonicum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acidic to neutral soil enriched with composted pine bark or leaf mould.
Position in dappled shade sheltered from cold easterly winds to prevent leaf scorch in dry springs.
Water deeply weekly during dry summer spells using stored rainwater rather than alkaline tap water.
Prune only in late autumn or midwinter to prevent sap bleeding and reduce the risk of coral spot.
Mulch annually in spring with composted bark keeping the mulch clear of the main woody stem.
items.description: Acer japonicum, fullmoon maple, or downy Japanese-maple, is a species of maple native to Japan, on Honshū, Hokkaidō, Kyūshū, and also southern Korea.

items.name: Paperbark maple
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained loam enriched with leaf mould to mimic UK woodland soil conditions.
Water deeply during dry summer spells for the first three years to establish its shallow root system.
Prune only in late autumn or winter to prevent the sap bleeding that weakens the tree in spring.
Position in full sun or dappled shade to maximise the dramatic orange-red autumn foliage display.
Plant away from harsh drying winds to protect the delicate peeling bark from premature weathering.
items.description: Acer griseum, the paperbark maple or blood-bark maple, is a species of flowering plant in the family Sapindaceae, native to central China. Acer griseum is found in the Chinese provinces of Gansu, Henan, Hubei, Hunan, Shaanxi, Shanxi and Sichuan, at altitudes of 1,500–2,000 m (4,921–6,562 ft).

items.name: Skimmia japonica
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial to full shade as strong UK summer sun will bleach and scorch the evergreen leaves.
Incorporate ericaceous compost into the planting hole to keep the soil acidic and prevent yellowing.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water to maintain the low soil pH that these shrubs require.
Plant a male cultivar like Rubella near female Rubella clones to ensure a display of red berries.
Prune lightly in mid-spring after flowering only to shape the shrub or restrict its spread.
items.description: Skimmia japonica, the Japanese skimmia, is a species of flowering plant in the family Rutaceae. Native to Japan, Taiwan, China, Vietnam, Philippines, and the Russian Far East, it is commonly grown in parks and gardens for its evergreen leaves, fragrant flowers, and attractive fruit. It is a highly variable species, with its varieties differing in height, spread, and chromosome count, among other things.

items.name: Mexican mock orange
items.growersTips:
Prune immediately after the spring flowering in June to encourage a second flush of blooms in autumn.
Plant in a sheltered south or west-facing spot to protect glossy foliage from cold drying UK winds.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells for the first two years until fully established.
Apply a thick mulch of compost in spring, keeping it clear of the stem to prevent collar rot.
Grow the yellow-leaved Sundance cultivar in partial shade to prevent the bright foliage from scorching.
items.description: Choisya ternata is a species of flowering plant in the family Rutaceae, known as Mexican orange blossom or Mexican orange.

items.name: Winter daphne
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sheltered spot with free-draining, neutral to acidic soil to prevent fatal root rot.
Position near a pathway or doorway to enjoy the intense winter fragrance in cold UK months.
Prune only lightly in spring after flowering to remove damaged stems, as they dislike hard cutting.
Water sparingly during dry summer spells once established to avoid waterlogging the delicate roots.
Grow the cultivar Aureomarginata for improved hardiness against severe British winter frosts.
items.description: Daphne odora, winter daphne, is a species of flowering plant in the family Thymelaeaceae, native to China, later spread to Japan and Korea. It is an evergreen shrub, grown for its very fragrant, fleshy, pale-pink, tubular flowers, each with four spreading lobes, and for its glossy foliage. It rarely fruits, producing red berries after flowering.

items.name: Daphne mezereum
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, alkaline to neutral soil, incorporating well-rotted organic matter.
Position in partial shade to mimic its native woodland edge, avoiding hot, dry south-facing spots.
Apply a thick annual mulch of leaf mould in spring to keep the shallow root system cool and damp.
Avoid pruning entirely as this species is highly susceptible to dieback and fungal decay from cuts.
Wear gloves when handling as all parts, especially the bright red summer berries, are highly toxic.
items.description: Daphne mezereum, the mezereon, is a species of Daphne in the flowering plant family Thymelaeaceae, native to most of Europe and Western Asia, north to northern Scandinavia and Russia. In southern Europe it is confined to medium to higher elevations in the subalpine vegetation zone, but descends to sea level in northern Europe. It is generally confined to soils derived from limestone. In the United Kingdom, the native population became a protected species in 1975 under the Conservation of Wild Creatures and Wild Plants Act.

items.name: Blue blossom ceanothus
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining soil against a south or west-facing wall to shelter from cold UK winds.
Prune immediately after flowering in June by cutting back spent shoots by half to keep it bushy.
Water newly planted shrubs weekly during dry UK summers but avoid waterlogging in heavy clay soils.
Choose the cultivar Repens for a low-growing groundcover that tolerates exposed coastal gardens.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted grit and compost to improve drainage and feed the roots.
items.description: Ceanothus thyrsiflorus, known as blueblossom or blue blossom ceanothus, is an evergreen shrub in the buckthorn family Rhamnaceae that is endemic to Oregon and California in the US. The term 'Californian lilac' and ‘Mountain lilac’ is also applied to this and other varieties of ceanothus, though it is not closely related to Syringa, the true lilac.

items.name: Rose of Sharon
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun in a south-facing, sheltered spot to ensure the wood ripens for late-summer blooms.
Prune hard in March to encourage strong new growth, as flowers only form on the current season wood.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent bud drop in the typical UK dry periods.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to retain moisture in light, sandy British soils.
Watch for aphids on young spring shoots and blast them off with a garden hose to prevent damage.
items.description:
Hibiscus syriacus is a species of flowering plant in the mallow family, Malvaceae. 
It is native to areas of east Asia, but widely introduced elsewhere, including much of Europe and North America. It was given the epithet syriacus because it had been collected from gardens in Syria.
Common names include the rose of Sharon, Syrian ketmia,
shrub althea
(or simply althea), Korean rose and rose mallow. It is the national flower of South Korea and is mentioned in the South Korean national anthem.

items.name: Common honeysuckle
items.growersTips:
Plant the roots in shade but let the vines climb into sun to mimic its natural UK woodland edge.
Prune immediately after flowering in late summer by cutting back one-third of the oldest stems.
Watch for honeysuckle aphids in spring and spray them off with a sharp blast of water from a hose.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into clay soil before planting to ensure moist but free-draining soil.
Grow alongside clematis to provide support and create a dense screen of complementary blooms.
items.description: Lonicera periclymenum, common names honeysuckle, common honeysuckle, European honeysuckle, or woodbine, is a species of flowering plant in the family Caprifoliaceae native to much of Europe, North Africa, Turkey and the Caucasus. It is found as far north as southern Norway, Sweden and Finland.

items.name: Lonicera nitida
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn to establish roots in moist UK soil before spring growth begins.
Trim three times between May and September to maintain a neat formal hedge shape.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first year after planting.
Grow in well-drained soil with added grit to prevent root rot in wet UK winters.
Watch for aphids in late spring and wash them off with a sharp blast from the hose.
items.description: Lonicera nitida is a species of flowering plant in the honeysuckle family. In English, it is sometimes given the common names box honeysuckle or Wilson's honeysuckle. It is widely used as a low hedging plant, and for topiary. It is also a popular low-maintenance ground cover plant for urban landscaping.

items.name: Common jasmine
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained soil against a warm, south or west-facing wall to maximize UK summer sun.
Prune immediately after flowering in late summer by cutting back flowed shoots to a strong bud.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells, focusing on the root base rather than wetting foliage.
Apply a five-centimeter mulch of compost in spring to retain moisture and protect roots from frost.
Tie young stems securely to a sturdy trellis or wire support to guide its vigorous climbing habit.
items.description: Jasminum officinale, known as the common jasmine or simply jasmine, is a species of flowering plant in the olive family Oleaceae. It is native to the Caucasus and parts of Asia, also widely naturalized.

items.name: Jasminum nudiflorum
items.growersTips:
Prune hard immediately after flowering in March by cutting back flowered shoots to strong buds.
Train stems to a sturdy UK wall trellis as this shrub lacks self-clinging tendrils or aerial roots.
Plant in well-drained soil enriched with grit to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Mulch the base annually in autumn with well-rotted manure to boost winter blooms on new wood.
Propagate easily in summer by pegging a low-growing stem into the soil until it roots.
items.description: Jasminum nudiflorum, the winter jasmine, is a slender, deciduous shrub native to China. The flower's blossoming peaks right after winter, which is why it is also named Yingchun (迎春) in Chinese, which means "the flower that welcomes Spring". It is widely cultivated as an ornamental and is reportedly naturalized in France and in scattered locations in the United States.

items.name: Mock orange
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining soil with grit added to the planting hole to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Protect young plants from freezing winds with fleece during severe UK winter frosts below minus five.
Prune immediately after flowering in late spring to shape the shrub without cutting off next blooms.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent shallow sprinkles.
Watch for sticky honeydew on leaves in spring which indicates a sap-sucking Pittosporum sucker attack.
items.description: Pittosporum tobira is a species of sweet-smelling flowering plant in the pittosporum family Pittosporaceae known by several common names, including Australian laurel, Japanese pittosporum, mock orange and Japanese cheesewood. It is native to Japan, China, Taiwan, and Korea, but it is used throughout the world as an ornamental plant in landscaping and as cut foliage.

items.name: New Zealand flax
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at the same depth as the pot in free-draining soil to prevent winter crown rot.
Water young plants weekly in dry summer spells but leave established clumps to survive on rainfall.
Tie leaves together in late autumn to protect the crown from severe UK frosts and heavy snow loads.
Prune tattered outer leaves in April by cutting them cleanly at the very base with sharp secateurs.
Divide congested clumps in May using two garden forks back-to-back to lift and split the tough roots.
items.description: Phormium tenax is an evergreen perennial plant native to New Zealand and Norfolk Island that is an important fibre plant and a popular ornamental plant. The plant grows as a clump of long, straplike leaves, up to two metres long, from which arises a much taller flowering shoot, with dramatic yellow or red flowers.

items.name: Needle palm
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-heavy soil to prevent root rot during wet British winters.
Position in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to maximize summer heat and trigger blooms.
Cut faded flower spikes down to the base in late autumn using sharp shears to keep the crown tidy.
Water young plants fortnightly in dry summer spells but keep established shrubs completely dry.
Protect the crown from heavy winter snow by tying the sword-like leaves together with soft twine.
items.description: Yucca filamentosa, Adam's needle and thread, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae native to the southeastern United States. Growing to 3 metres tall, it is an evergreen shrub valued in horticulture.

items.name: Sarcococca confusa
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained humus-rich soil in full or partial shade to prevent leaf bleaching.
Water weekly during the first dry UK summer after planting to establish a deep, resilient root system.
Prune lightly in late spring after flowering to maintain shape and encourage new winter-blooming wood.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould or composted bark to retain moisture and mimic forest soil.
Plant near a frequently used path or doorway to enjoy the intense winter fragrance from Jan to Feb.
items.description: Sarcococca confusa, the sweet box, is a species of flowering plant in the family Buxaceae, probably native to western China. It is an evergreen shrub growing to 2 m (7 ft) tall by 1 m (3 ft) broad, with glossy green ovate leaves and honey-scented white flowers in winter, followed by glossy black spherical fruits, 5 mm in diameter.

items.name: Spotted laurel
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade to prevent the variegated leaves from scorching in intense midday UK sun.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells until established to prevent root rot in clay.
Prune with secateurs in April to avoid cutting leaves in half, which causes unsightly brown edges.
Feed with a balanced organic fertiliser in spring to boost foliage colour in nutrient-poor soils.
Watch for scale insects on the undersides of leaves and treat with horticultural oil in summer.
items.description: Aucuba japonica, commonly called spotted laurel, Japanese laurel, Japanese aucuba or gold dust plant (U.S.), is a shrub native to rich forest soils of moist valleys, thickets, by streams and near shaded moist rocks in China, Korea, and Japan. This is the species of Aucuba commonly seen in gardens - often in variegated form. The leaves are opposite, broad lanceolate, 5–8 cm (2.0–3.1 in) long and 2–5 cm (0.79–1.97 in) wide. Aucuba japonica are dioecious. The flowers are small, 4–8 mm (0.16–0.31 in) diameter, each with four purplish-brown petals; they are produced in clusters of 10-30 in a loose

items.name: Photinia × fraseri
items.growersTips:
Prune in late spring after the first flush of red leaves to encourage a second vibrant red display.
Water deeply during dry summer spells to prevent leaf drop and protect against powdery mildew.
Plant in a site sheltered from cold, drying winds to prevent frost damage to tender new red shoots.
Watch for purple-rimmed spots of Photinia leaf spot fungus and prune out affected twigs in spring.
Enrich heavy UK clay soils with organic matter and grit to ensure the free-draining conditions needed.
items.description: Photinia × fraseri, known as red tip photinia and Christmas berry, is a nothospecies in the rose family, Rosaceae. It is a hybrid between Photinia glabra and Photinia serratifolia.

items.name: Escallonia rubra
items.growersTips:
Plant in a sunny, sheltered south or west-facing spot to protect it from cold, drying winter winds.
Prune immediately after flowering in late summer by cutting back flowed shoots to strong buds.
Watch for Escallonia leaf spot disease and destroy affected fallen leaves to prevent reinfection.
Grow in well-drained soil as it dislikes waterlogging, especially during wet UK winters.
Plant alongside Griselinia or Fuchsia magellanica for a resilient, salt-tolerant coastal hedge.
items.description: Escallonia rubra, called redclaws and red escallonia, is a species of flowering plant in the family Escalloniaceae. It is native to southern Chile and neighboring areas of Argentina.

items.name: Garrya elliptica
items.growersTips:
Plant James Roof for much longer winter catkins than the standard species in UK gardens.
Prune lightly in mid spring immediately after catkins fade to avoid cutting off next winters buds.
Plant against a south or west facing wall to shelter catkins from freezing UK winter winds.
Grow in free draining soil as wet winter clay causes root rot and leaf spot in British climates.
Propagate by taking semi ripe cuttings with a heel in late summer using a cold frame.
items.description: Garrya elliptica, the coast silk-tassel, silk tassel bush or wavyleaf silktassel, is a species of flowering plant in the family Garryaceae, native to the coastal ranges of California and southern Oregon. It is an erect, bushy, evergreen shrub reaching a height of 2–5 m (7–16 ft).

items.name: Clematis armandii var. hefengensis
items.growersTips:
Plant the crown 5cm deep in moist, alkaline to neutral soil against a warm south or west facing wall
Prune immediately after spring flowering by cutting back overlong stems to a strong pair of buds
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to establish the vigorous evergreen root system
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers around the base
Mulch the root zone annually in late winter with well-rotted manure to keep the shallow roots cool
items.description: Clematis armandii is a flowering climbing plant of the genus Clematis. Like many members of that genus, it is prized by gardeners for its showy flowers. It is native to much of China and northern Burma. The plant is a woody perennial. It attracts bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds.

items.name: Clematis tangutica
items.growersTips:
Plant the root ball 5cm deeper than the pot soil level to encourage strong shoots from the base.
Prune hard to 30cm from the ground in late February to promote vigorous new flowering stems.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells rather than giving daily light sprinkles.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to easily propagate this specific species for free.
Grow through a sturdy dark evergreen shrub to showcase the bright yellow bell-shaped flowers.
items.description: Clematis tangutica, the golden clematis, is a species of flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae. It is found from Central Asia through to most of China, and it has been introduced to western Canada, Czechia, Slovakia, Switzerland, and the South Island of New Zealand. Its cultivars 'Bill MacKenzie' and 'Lambton Park', both members of the Tangutica Group, have gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Clematis alpina
items.growersTips:
Plant the crown 5cm deep in fertile, moist, well-drained soil to protect against clematis wilt.
Position in a north or east-facing spot as it thrives in cool UK shade unlike most other clematis.
Prune immediately after spring flowering in May by only cutting back dead or overgrown stems.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to keep the shallow root run cool and damp.
Protect early spring buds from slugs and snails using organic pellets or beer traps in March.
items.description: Clematis alpina, the Alpine clematis, is a flowering deciduous vine of the genus Clematis. Like many members of that genus, it is prized by gardeners for its showy flowers. It bears 1 to 3-inch spring flowers on long stalks in a wide variety of colors. C. alpina is native to Europe; in the United States it grows best in American Horticultural Society zones 9 to 6, which are generally found in the southern USA.

items.name: Clematis × jackmanii
items.growersTips:
Plant the root ball 10cm deeper than the pot soil level to encourage shoots and survive wilt.
Prune hard annually in late February down to 30cm above ground level just above a strong bud pair.
Keep the roots cool and shaded using slate pieces or low-growing companion plants like geraniums.
Water deeply once a week at the base during dry UK summer spells to prevent clematis wilt disease.
Feed in March with a high-potassium tomato fertiliser to boost the midsummer purple flower flush.
items.description: Clematis 'Jackmanii' is a Clematis cultivar which, when it was introduced in 1862, was the first of the modern large-flowered hybrid clematises of gardens. It is a climber with large violet-purple blooms, still among the most familiar climbers seen in gardens. It was produced from crosses made by the prominent nurseryman George Jackman (1837–1887), of Jackman & Sons, Woking, Surrey.

items.name: Common Ivy
items.growersTips:
Plant goldheart ivy in partial shade to keep its bright yellow variegation from scorching in UK sun.
Prune established ivy hard in late winter before nesting birds occupy the foliage from March onwards.
Water newly planted ivy weekly during dry summer spells until its deep root system is established.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into heavy UK clay soils to improve drainage before planting ivy.
Pair ivy with hardy cyclamen coum to provide winter color beneath the dense evergreen canopy.
items.description: Hedera helix, simply ivy, or common ivy, English ivy, European ivy, King's choice ivy, is a species of flowering plant in the family Araliaceae. It is native to most of Europe and parts of western Asia. Ivy is a clinging evergreen vine that grows on tree trunks, walls, and fences in gardens, waste spaces, and wild habitats. Ivy is popular as an ornamental plant, but escaped plants have become naturalised outside its native range. Ivy has considerable cultural significance and symbolism.

items.name: Hedera colchica
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, alkaline to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Prune hard in late spring after frosts to control spread and encourage fresh, large-leaved growth.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first two years until the root system is established.
Watch for scale insects and aphids on young shoots, treating with organic insecticidal soap.
Grow alongside shade-loving ferns or hostas to create a contrasting texture in damp UK borders.
items.description: Hedera colchica is a species of flowering plant in the family Araliaceae . It is native to the Middle East and commonly called Persian ivy or colchis ivy. It is an evergreen climbing plant, growing to 30 m high where suitable surfaces are available, and also growing as ground cover where there are no vertical surfaces. It climbs by means of aerial rootlets which cling to the substrate. In warm climates, it grows more rapidly and becomes established faster than other Hedera species.

items.name: Chocolate vine
items.growersTips:
Plant two different cultivars like Cream Form and Silver Bells to ensure successful cross-pollination.
Prune immediately after spring flowering by cutting back lateral shoots to two buds from the main stem.
Provide a strong trellis against a south or west wall to shelter early blooms from late UK frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent the root system from drying out.
Grow in well-drained loamy soil enriched with garden compost to mimic its native woodland floor.
items.description: Akebia quinata –commonly known as akebi (木通), chocolate vine, five-leaf chocolate vine, or five-leaf akebia– is a vine that is native to Japan, China and Korea, commonly used as an ornamental or edible plant in the United States and Europe. In its native habitat, it is often found on hills, in hedges, on trees, along forest edges and streams, and on mountainous slopes.

items.name: Blue Passionflower
items.growersTips:
Plant in a south or west-facing position against a warm wall to survive wet UK winter frosts.
Prune hard in early spring by cutting back flowered shoots to two buds to promote new summer blooms.
Grow in free-draining, gritty soil to prevent root rot during cold, waterlogged British winters.
Apply a thick organic mulch over the root zone in late autumn to protect the crown from hard frosts.
Restrict roots in a container or use buried paving slabs to limit rampant growth and boost flowers.
items.description: Passiflora caerulea, the blue passionflower, bluecrown passionflower or common passion flower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Passifloraceae. It is native to South America and has been introduced elsewhere.

items.name: Trachelospermum jasminoides
items.growersTips:
Plant in a south or west-facing sheltered spot to protect from cold, drying UK winter winds.
In spring, prune back any frost-damaged stems to a healthy bud and tie in new shoots to supports.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first two years until the root system is established.
In cold UK regions, apply a thick organic mulch around the base in autumn to protect roots from frost.
Grow in well-drained soil, adding grit to heavy clay to prevent winter waterlogging and root rot.
items.description: Trachelospermum jasminoides is a species of flowering plant in the family Apocynaceae, native to eastern and southeastern Asia. Common names include Confederate jasmine, star jasmine, Confederate jessamine, and Chinese star jessamine.

items.name: Solanum crispum
items.growersTips:
Plant Glasnevin in free-draining soil against a south wall to protect it from cold UK winter winds.
Prune hard in early spring by cutting back the previous year's shoots to a strong bud near the base.
Tie the lax stems to a sturdy trellis or wire support system as this shrub cannot climb on its own.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to prevent leaf drop and support continuous blooms.
Watch for aphids and potato blight in humid UK summers, removing affected foliage immediately.
items.description: Solanum crispum is a species of flowering plant in the family Solanaceae. It is native to Chile and Peru. Common names include Chilean potato vine, Chilean nightshade, Chilean potato tree and potato vine. Growing to 6 m (20 ft) tall, it is a semi-evergreen, woody-stemmed climbing plant. The small blue fragrant flowers, 2.5 cm in diameter, with prominent yellow ovaries, appear in clusters in summer. They resemble those of the closely related potato. Very small poisonous berries are produced in autumn. The berries start out green, then yellow-orange, and finally purple. The leaves are oval.

items.name: Japanese Creeper
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained soil against a north or east-facing wall to maximise autumn leaf colour.
Prune hard in early winter to keep vines clear of gutters, roof tiles, window frames, and fascia.
Water newly planted climbers deeply once a week during dry UK summer spells until fully established.
Apply a five-centimetre mulch of well-rotted garden compost around the base in spring to boost growth.
Choose the cultivar Veitchii for its superior self-clinging ability on damp British brickwork.
items.description: Parthenocissus tricuspidata is a species of flowering plant in the grape family (Vitaceae) native to eastern Asia, where it thrives in floodplain bushes, riverside woodland and moist mountain mixed forests. Although unrelated to true ivy, it is commonly known as Boston ivy, grape ivy, Japanese ivy, and also as Japanese creeper, and by the name woodbine.

items.name: Parthenocissus quinquefolia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, well-drained soil, adding leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Prune hard in midwinter to control size and keep tendrils away from roof tiles and gutters.
Water newly planted climbers weekly during dry UK summer spells until their root system establishes.
Position in full sun or partial shade, but choose a south-facing wall for the best autumn colour.
Check mortar joints annually on older brickwork to ensure self-clinging pads do not cause damage.
items.description: Parthenocissus quinquefolia, commonly known as Virginia creeper, woodbine, five-leaved ivy, or five-finger, is a species of flowering vine in the grape family Vitaceae.

items.name: Common Grape Vine
items.growersTips:
Prune in midwinter to prevent bleeding sap and thin the summer canopy to expose grapes to UK sun.
Plant against a south-facing wall in well-drained soil with the graft union 10cm above ground level.
Water deeply at the base every ten days during dry summer spells, avoiding the foliage entirely.
Watch for powdery mildew in damp UK summers and space branches widely to maximise air circulation.
Select cold-hardy cultivars like Brandts or Boskoop Glory that reliably ripen in cooler UK climates.
items.description: Vitis vinifera, the common grape vine, is a species of flowering plant, native to the Mediterranean region, Central Europe, and southwestern Asia, from Morocco and Portugal north to southern Germany and east to northern Iran. As of 2012, there were between 5,000 and 10,000 varieties of Vitis vinifera grapes though only a few are of commercial significance for wine and table grape production.

items.name: Vitis coignetiae
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun or partial shade to boost autumn color.
Prune in midwinter when fully dormant to prevent the vine from bleeding sap, which weakens growth.
Provide a sturdy pergola or mature tree support to handle the immense weight of this vigorous climber.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure to retain moisture during dry UK summer spells.
Grow in shelter from strong winds to prevent the large, ornamental leaves from shredding in autumn.
items.description: Vitis coignetiae, commonly called crimson glory vine, is a species of grapevine belonging to the family Vitaceae. Is native to the temperate climes of Asia and can be found in the Russian Far East (Sakhalin), Korea, and Japan. It was described botanically in 1883. It is called meoru (머루) in Korean and yama-budo (ヤマブドウ) in Japanese.

items.name: Common hop
items.growersTips:
