Plant rhizomes in early spring at a depth of ten centimetres in rich well-drained soil.
Train bines clockwise around support structures as they will not self-cling to walls.
Cut all bines back to ground level in late autumn after the first hard UK frost.
Watch for downy mildew in damp UK summers by removing lower leaves to improve airflow.
Limit spread in small gardens by planting hops in large bottomless buckets sunk into the ground.
items.description: Humulus lupulus, the common hop or hops, is a species of flowering plant in the hemp family, Cannabaceae. It is a perennial, herbaceous climbing plant which sends up new shoots in early spring and dies back to a cold-hardy rhizome in autumn. It is dioecious and native to West Asia, Europe and North America.

items.name: Eccremocarpus scaber
items.growersTips:
Plant in spring at the same depth as the pot in free-draining soil against a warm south-facing wall.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells to keep the vigorous root system hydrated.
Prune hard to 30cm from the ground in early spring to stimulate fresh flowering growth from the base.
Protect the root crown with a 10cm layer of dry autumn leaf mulch to survive wet UK winter frosts.
Sow seeds indoors in March on a warm windowsill without covering them as they need light to germinate.
items.description: Eccremocarpus scaber, the Chilean glory-flower or Chilean glory creeper, is a species of perennial plant in the family Bignoniaceae. It is found in Chile.

items.name: Tulipa kaufmanniana
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in November at a depth of 10 to 12cm in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rot.
Position in full sun to ensure the waterlily-like flowers open fully during early spring days.
Leave bulbs in the ground year-round as this species reliably naturalises in dry UK summer borders.
Grow in shallow terracotta pans with alpine grit to protect the dwarf stems from heavy rain splash.
Deadhead immediately after flowering in April but let the foliage die back naturally for six weeks.
items.description: Tulipa kaufmanniana, the water lily tulip, is a species of tulip native to Central Asia.

items.name: Tulipa greigii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in November at a depth of 15cm in gritty, free-draining soil to prevent winter rotting.
Position in the sunniest south-facing border to mimic their native dry, baked summer habitat.
Leave the distinctive purple-mottled foliage to die back naturally to feed next year's bloom.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or organic wool pellets.
Lift and store bulbs in a dry shed over wet UK summers if your garden soil is heavy clay.
items.description: Tulipa greigii, is a species of tulip native to Central Asia and Iran.

items.name: Narcissus tazetta
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimeters in a warm sheltered south-facing border.
Protect early winter buds from hard UK frosts using a temporary layer of horticultural fleece.
Water thoroughly during active spring growth but keep soil dry during summer dormancy to prevent rot.
Let foliage die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before cutting it to the ground.
Grow in gritty free-draining soil or raised beds to survive wet British winters without rotting.
items.description: Narcissus tazetta is a perennial ornamental plant that grows from a bulb. Cultivars of N. tazetta include 'Caniculatus', 'Grand Soleil d'Or' and 'Ziva', which are popularly used for forcing indoors, as is the form of N. tazetta known as Chinese Sacred Lily.

items.name: Narcissus jonquilla
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in early autumn at a depth of ten to fifteen centimetres in well-drained, gritty soil.
Position in full sun to mimic their native Mediterranean habitat and ensure reliable UK flowering.
Allow the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before cutting it down.
Water during dry spring spells but keep the soil relatively dry during their summer dormant phase.
Divide congested clumps every few years in late summer to maintain vigour and prevent blind bulbs.
items.description: Narcissus jonquilla, commonly known as jonquil or rush daffodil, is a bulbous flowering plant, a species of the genus Narcissus (daffodil) that is native to Spain and Portugal but has now become naturalised in many other regions: France, Italy, Turkey, the former Yugoslavia, Madeira, British Columbia in Canada, Utah, Illinois, Minnesota, Ohio, and the southeastern United States from Texas to Maryland.

items.name: Cyclamen hederifolium
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers shallowly in late summer with the smooth side down and the knobby crown facing up.
Water only during their autumn-to-spring active growth and keep them completely dry during summer.
Plant under deciduous trees or shrubs to mimic their native woodland shade and leaf litter soil.
Scatter grit around the base in winter to protect the emerging delicate stems from slug damage.
Propagate by collecting the naturally coiled seed heads in summer to sow immediately in cold frames.
items.description: Cyclamen hederifolium, the ivy-leaved cyclamen or sowbread, is a species of flowering plant in the family Primulaceae. This widespread cyclamen species is widely cultivated and among the most hardy and vigorous in oceanic climates. It is native to woodland, shrubland, and rocky areas in the Mediterranean region from southern France to western Turkey and on Mediterranean islands, and naturalized farther north in Europe and in the Pacific Northwest.

items.name: Eastern sowbread
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers shallowly in late summer with the smooth rounded side down and the top just below soil.
Grow under deciduous shrubs to ensure summer dry dormancy and winter moisture in UK clay or loam.
Mix grit and leafmould into planting holes to prevent tuber rot during wet British winters.
Leave fallen autumn leaves around them to mimic woodland mulch and protect emerging winter blooms.
Plant alongside snowdrops and winter aconites for a synchronized early spring shade display.
items.description: Cyclamen coum, the eastern sowbread, is a species of flowering plant in the family Primulaceae. It is a tuberous herbaceous perennial, growing to 5–8 cm (2–3 in), with rounded heart-shaped leaves and pink shell-shaped flowers with darker coloration at the base. It is valued in horticulture as groundcover, and for the flowers which bloom in winter and early spring.

items.name: Naked ladies
items.growersTips:
Plant Colchicum corms 10cm deep in July or August to ensure they establish before autumn flowering.
Grow them in well-drained soil in full sun to prevent the large dormant corms from rotting in winter.
Plant among low ground cover like thyme to support the top-heavy, leafless autumn blooms from flopping.
Leave the large, unsightly spring foliage to die down naturally in June to feed next year's blooms.
Watch for slugs and snails in September as they quickly ruin the emerging delicate flower buds.
items.description: Colchicum autumnale, commonly known as autumn crocus, meadow saffron, naked boys or naked ladies, is a toxic autumn-blooming flowering plant that resembles the true crocuses, but is a member of the plant family Colchicaceae, unlike the true crocuses, which belong to the family Iridaceae. It is called "naked boys/ladies" because the flowers emerge from the ground long before the leaves appear. Despite the vernacular name of "meadow saffron", this plant is not the source of saffron, which is obtained from the saffron crocus, Crocus sativus – and that plant, too, is sometimes called "autumn crocu

items.name: Allium christophii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in sharply draining soil to prevent rot.
Sow in the sunniest spot available to ensure the heavy flower heads do not flop towards the light.
Leave the fading foliage to die back naturally in summer to feed the bulb for next year's display.
Plant among low-growing hardy geraniums to hide the unsightly withered leaves during flowering.
Leave the dried seed heads intact over winter to provide structural interest in frosty UK gardens.
items.description: Allium cristophii, the Persian onion or star of Persia, is a species of flowering plant in the family Amaryllidaceae, native to Iran, Turkey, and Turkmenistan, though grown as an ornamental bulbous plant in many parts of the world. It may be sold under the synonym of Allium albopilosum.

items.name: Chives
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March or plant clumps 15cm deep in moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in April
Water potted chives consistently from beneath to prevent the bulbs rotting in damp UK winter soil
Cut the entire clump down to 5cm after flowering in July to stimulate a fresh flush of edible leaves
Divide congested clumps every three years in autumn to maintain plant vigour and prevent congestion
Plant near carrots to deter carrot rust fly or near roses to help prevent black spot fungal disease
items.description: Chives, scientific name Allium schoenoprasum, is a species of flowering plant in the family Amaryllidaceae.

items.name: Camassia leichtlinii
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of fifteen centimetres in moisture-retentive, clay-friendly soil.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to prevent the flower spikes from aborting before they bloom.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally until July to feed the bulb for next year's spring display.
Plant alongside late-flowering perennials like hardy geraniums to hide the yellowing summer foliage.
Protect emerging spring shoots from slugs and snails using organic grit barriers or beer traps.
items.description: Camassia leichtlinii, the great camas or large camas, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. This herbaceous perennial is native to western North America in British Columbia, Canada and California, Nevada, Oregon and Washington, in the United States.

items.name: Helleborus hyemalis L.
items.growersTips:
Plant tubers in late summer at a depth of five centimetres and space them ten centimetres apart.
Soak the shrivelled tubers in water for twenty-four hours before planting to trigger active growth.
Grow in moist well-drained alkaline soil enriched with leafmould under deciduous trees or shrubs.
Associate with Galanthus nivalis and Cyclamen coum for a synchronized late winter colour display.
Propagate by lifting and dividing the congested clumps in green immediately after flowering in spring.
items.description: Eranthis hyemalis, the winter aconite, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to calcareous woodland habitats in France, Italy and the Balkans, and widely naturalized elsewhere in Europe.

items.name: Summer Snowflake
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in moist soil that mimics their native UK damp meadow habitat
Grow the robust Gravetye Giant cultivar for larger flowers that cope better with heavy UK rainfall
Keep soil consistently moist during dry spring spells to ensure lush foliage and reliable summer blooms
Cut back yellowed foliage only in midsummer after it has completely died down to feed next years bulb
Watch for the destructive wild leek rust fungus and destroy infected leaves to prevent it spreading
items.description: Leucojum aestivum, commonly called the summer snowflake, giant snowflake, Loddon lily and rarely snowbell and dewdrop among others, is a plant species widely cultivated as an ornamental. It is native to most of Europe from Spain and Ireland to Ukraine, with the exception of Scandinavia, Russia, Belarus and the Baltic countries. It is also considered native to Turkey, Iran and the Caucasus. It is naturalized in Denmark, South Australia, New South Wales, Nova Scotia and much of the eastern United States.

items.name: Spring Snowflake
items.growersTips:
Plant dry bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in moist soil that does not dry out in summer.
Plant them under deciduous shrubs to provide the dappled spring shade and damp soil they require.
Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering while the leaves are still green and active.
Watch for the wild daffodil companion plant to bloom alongside them in damp UK woodland gardens.
Avoid cutting back yellowing foliage after flowering to allow energy to return to the bulb.
items.description: Leucojum vernum, commonly called the spring snowflake, St. Agnes' flower, and rarely snowbell among others, is a species of flowering plant in the family Amaryllidaceae. It is native to central and southern Europe from Belgium to Ukraine. It is considered naturalized in north-western Europe, including Great Britain and parts of Scandinavia, and in the US states of Georgia and Florida. This spring flowering bulbous herbaceous perennial is cultivated as an ornamental for a sunny position. The plant multiplies in favourable conditions to form clumps. Each plant bears a single white flower with gr

items.name: Muscari armeniacum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 10cm in well-drained soil to prevent winter rot in wet UK clay.
Plant alongside early daffodils or red tulips to mask the messy Muscari foliage as it dies back.
Mow or shear the untidy, grass-like leaves to the ground only after they have turned fully yellow.
Divide congested clumps in late summer during their dormant phase to maintain vigorous flowering.
Grow in containers of grit-amended compost to prevent invasive self-seeding in small UK borders.
items.description:
Muscari armeniacum is a species of flowering plant in the squill subfamily Scilloideae of the asparagus family Asparagaceae. It is a bulbous perennial with basal, simple leaves and short flowering stems. It is one of a number of species and genera known as grape hyacinth, in this case Armenian grape hyacinth or garden grape-hyacinth. The flowers are purple, blue, white or pale pink and the plants are usually 15 centimetres (6 in) tall. M. armeniacum blooms in mid-Spring for 3–4 weeks. Some selections are fragrant. Established bulbs leaf in the autumn. 
M. armeniacum is widespread in the woods

items.name: Grass lily
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of ten centimetres in well-drained soil to survive wet UK winters.
Grow in containers or sink pots to restrict the highly invasive bulbils from overtaking lawns.
Withhold summer watering once foliage dies back to allow bulbs a dry dormant period in clay soil.
Cut back spent flower stems in June before seed heads mature to prevent aggressive self-seeding.
Wear gloves when handling bulbs to avoid skin irritation caused by toxic calcium oxalate crystals.
items.description: Ornithogalum umbellatum, the garden star-of-Bethlehem, grass lily, nap-at-noon, or eleven-o'clock lady, is a perennial bulbous flowering plant in the asparagus family (Asparagaceae). O. umbellatum is a relatively short plant, occurring in tufts of basal linear leaves, producing conspicuous white flowers, in a stellate pattern, in mid to late spring. The flowers open late in the day, but when closed have a green stripe on the outside. It is native throughout southern and central Europe, and north-western Africa. O. umbellatum is often grown as a garden ornamental, but in North America and other

items.name: Siberian squill
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in autumn at a depth of 8cm to 10cm to protect them from UK winter frosts and squirrels.
Grow in moist but well-drained soil, keeping it damp during spring growth but dry during dormancy.
Plant under deciduous shrubs like hazel or cornus so they get spring sun before the canopy closes.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally for six weeks after flowering to feed next year's bulbs.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they can quickly destroy the emerging flower buds.
items.description: Scilla siberica, the Siberian squill or wood squill, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to southwestern Russia, the Caucasus, and Turkey. Despite its name, it is not native to Siberia.

items.name: Autumn crocus
items.growersTips:
Plant corms in August at a depth of 10cm to 15cm in gritty, well-drained soil to prevent winter rot.
Position in the sunniest spot possible to mimic Mediterranean heat for reliable autumn flowering.
Protect emerging purple blooms from slugs and snails using organic bait or beer traps in September.
Harvest the three red saffron stigmas using tweezers on a dry morning just as the flowers open.
Leave the grassy foliage to die back naturally in spring to feed the corms for the next season.
items.description: Crocus sativus, commonly known as saffron crocus or autumn crocus, is a species of flowering plant in the iris family Iridaceae. A cormous autumn-flowering cultivated perennial, unknown in the wild, it is best known for the culinary use of its floral stigmas as the spice saffron. Human cultivation of saffron crocus and the trade and use of saffron have endured for more than 3,500 years and span different cultures, continents, and civilizations.

items.name: Crocus chrysanthus
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs in September at a depth of 8cm to protect them from winter frost and hungry mice.
Incorporate grit into heavy clay soil to ensure the sharp drainage needed to prevent winter rot.
Plant under deciduous shrubs so they get full winter sun before the canopy blocks the light in spring.
Let foliage die back naturally for six weeks after flowering before mowing lawns or clearing borders.
Protect emerging February buds from birds by placing wire netting or black thread just above them.
items.description: Crocus chrysanthus, the snow crocus or golden crocus, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae.

items.name: Gladiolus communis
items.growersTips:
Plant corms 10cm deep in autumn in well-drained soil to protect them from wet UK winter rot.
Grow them in full sun alongside lavender or salvia to support their tall, slender flowering stems.
Avoid heavy clay by mixing grit into the planting hole to ensure the corms do not sit in water.
Leave the foliage to die back naturally in autumn so the corm stores energy for next spring.
Watch for gladiolus thrips in dry UK summers and spray the foliage with water to deter them.
items.description: Gladiolus communis, the eastern gladiolus, or common corn-flag, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae, native to temperate northern Africa, western Asia and southern Europe, from the Mediterranean to the Caucasus, and widely naturalised in frost-free locations elsewhere – such as coastal parts of the southwestern British Isles.

items.name: Iris pumila
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer with the tops exposed to the UK sun to ensure next springs bloom
Grow in sharply draining gritty soil to prevent rhizome rot during wet British winters and springs
Place in full south-facing sun to mimic their native dry hillsides and prevent shade-induced failure
Divide congested clumps every three years in July after flowering to maintain vigor and flower yield
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs as they quickly destroy the low-growing early buds
items.description: Iris pumila, sometimes known as pygmy iris or dwarf iris, probably originated as a natural hybrid between Iris pseudopumila Boissier & Heldreich and I. attica Tineo. It ranges from Austria through eastern Europe and the Balkans, in Eurasian steppe in Ukraine, southern Russia into southern Siberia and northern Kazakhstan, and the Caucasus into Turkey.

items.name: Water flag
items.growersTips:
Plant rhizomes shallowly with the tops exposed to the sun in heavy, moisture-retentive clay soil.
Position at the margins of a garden pond up to twenty centimeters deep to control its vigorous spread.
Cut the foliage back to the ground in autumn to prevent rotting leaves from polluting pond water.
Divide congested clumps in late summer using a sharp spade to maintain vigor and control size.
Wear thick gloves when handling to avoid skin irritation from the toxic sap of this native plant.
items.description: Iris pseudacorus, the yellow flag, yellow iris, or water flag, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae. It is native to Europe, western Asia and northwest Africa. Its specific epithet pseudacorus means "false acorus", referring to the similarity of its leaves to those of Acorus calamus, as they have a prominently veined mid-rib and sword-like shape. However, the two plants are not closely related.

items.name: White lily
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs shallowly in late summer with only two centimeters of soil covering the bulb top.
Grow in well-drained alkaline soil with added grit to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Position in full sun but keep the base shaded by planting low-growing violas or hardy geraniums.
Watch for scarlet lily beetles from spring onwards and hand-pick them immediately to save foliage.
Do not cut back the green basal winter rosette of leaves as it feeds the bulb for next summer.
items.description: Lilium candidum, the Madonna lily or white lily, is a plant in the true lily family. It is native to the Balkans and Middle East, and naturalized in other parts of Europe, including France, Italy, and Ukraine, and in North Africa, the Canary Islands, Mexico, and other regions. It has been cultivated since antiquity, for at least 3,000 years, and has great symbolic value since then for many cultures. It is susceptible to several virus diseases common to lilies, and especially to Botrytis fungus. One technique to avoid problems with viruses is to grow plants from seed instead of bulblets.

items.name: Lilium speciosum
items.growersTips:
Plant bulbs 15-20cm deep in late autumn to allow stem roots to develop and anchor the tall stems.
Grow in ericaceous compost or acidic soil as this species cannot tolerate lime or alkaline conditions.
Position in partial shade with the base shaded by low shrubs to mimic its native woodland edge.
Watch for red lily beetles from spring onwards and hand-pick them immediately to prevent defoliation.
Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged during the active summer growing season.
items.description: Lilium speciosum is an East Asian species of plants in the lily family. It is native to southern Japan and southern China, where it can be found at elevations of 600–900 metres (2,000–3,000 ft). It is sometimes called the Japanese lily though there are other species with this common name.

items.name: Stipa tenuissima
items.growersTips:
Comb out dead winter thatch in spring using gloved hands rather than cutting the clump to the ground.
Plant in free-draining gravelly soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Position in full sun to maintain the characteristic golden wispy plumes throughout the autumn.
Divide congested clumps in mid-spring once new green growth begins to emerge at the base.
Pair with purple Salvia caradonna in dry borders for a classic drought-tolerant UK contrast.
items.description: Nassella tenuissima is a species of grass known by the common names Mexican feathergrass, finestem needlegrass, fineleaved nassella, and Argentine needle-grass. It is native to the south-western United States, northern Mexico and Argentina. It is well-matched to climate in Australia and can be harmful to the Australian environment.

items.name: Golden oats
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil in full sun to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Comb out dead thatch with gloved hands in early spring rather than cutting the evergreen base back.
Position in an open, breezy spot so the tall flower spikes can sway without snapping in UK winds.
Divide congested clumps in mid-spring once new growth starts, never in autumn due to winter wet.
Partner with late-flowering purple Verbena bonariensis for a classic UK autumn border contrast.
items.description: Celtica gigantea, commonly called giant feather grass, giant needle grass or golden-oats, is a species of flowering plant in the grass family, Poaceae, native to the Iberian Peninsula and Morocco. Despite being renamed and placed within the genus Celtica, it is still widely referred to—both in horticultural literature and amongst gardeners—by its synonym, Stipa gigantea.

items.name: Maiden silvergrass
items.growersTips:
Cut stems back to ground level in late February before new green shoots emerge to avoid damaging them
Divide congested clumps in mid-spring using two garden forks back-to-back to maintain plant vigour
Plant in full sun and well-drained soil to prevent floppy winter stems in wet UK winters
Water newly planted divisions weekly during their first UK summer to establish deep drought-proof roots
Leave faded flower plumes intact over winter to provide structural interest and shelter for UK wildlife
items.description: Miscanthus sinensis, also called eulalia grass, Chinese silver grass, or elephant grass, is a species of flowering plant in the grass family Poaceae, native to most of East Asia and Southeast Asia.

items.name: Pennisetum alopecuroides
items.growersTips:
Cut back the dead foliage hard to ground level in late March before new green shoots begin to emerge
Plant in full sun and free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay and cold winters
Water newly planted grasses weekly during their first dry UK summer to establish deep root systems
Divide overcrowded clumps in mid-spring using a sharp spade to maintain vigour and propagate plants
Choose the compact cultivar Hameln for reliable flowering in cooler northern UK summer climates
items.description: Cenchrus alopecuroides, previously Pennisetum alopecuroides, commonly known as the Chinese pennisetum, Chinese fountaingrass, dwarf fountain grass, foxtail fountain grass, or swamp foxtail grass, is a species of perennial grass native to Asia and Australia. The culms are erect, and 60–100 cm long. The leaf-blades are erect or drooping; flat, or conduplicate or involute (spiral); and from 10 to 45 cm long by 3–6 mm wide.

items.name: Festuca glauca
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-amended soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK climates.
Comb out dead thatch by hand using rubber gloves in spring rather than cutting the foliage back.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early spring to maintain the intense blue colour.
Position in full south-facing sun as UK shade turns the blue foliage a dull green.
Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers which cause floppy growth and ruin the neat dome shape.
items.description: Festuca glauca, commonly known as blue fescue, is a species of flowering plant in the grass family, Poaceae. It is a commonly cultivated evergreen or semi-evergreen herbaceous perennial.

items.name: Feather reed-grass
items.growersTips:
Cut back the dead stems to ground level in late February before the new green shoots begin to emerge
Divide congested clumps in mid-spring using two garden forks back-to-back to maintain plant vigour
Plant in moisture-retentive clay or loam soils as this grass struggles in dry UK summer borders
Select Karl Foerster for early upright wheat-coloured plumes or Overdam for variegated foliage
Sow companion plants like purple Echinacea or Verbena bonariensis to contrast with the golden stems
items.description: Calamagrostis × acutiflora, called feather reed-grass, is a naturally occurring hybrid species of grass in the genus Calamagrostis, occasionally found in Europe and Asia. Its cultivar 'Karl Foerster' has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

items.name: Carex oshimensis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained soil with the crown level with the soil surface to prevent crown rot.
Comb through the foliage with gloved hands in late winter to remove dead brown leaves without cutting.
Water weekly during dry UK summer spells to maintain the soil moisture this evergreen sedge needs.
Divide congested clumps in mid-spring once the soil warms up to propagate and restore plant vigour.
Plant alongside hostas and astilbes in partial shade to create a contrasting damp-loving display.
items.description: Carex oshimensis, the Japanese sedge, is a species of flowering plant in the genus Carex, native to Japan. With its striped foliage, it is widely used as a non‑spreading ground cover. Its cultivar 'Evergold' has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Growing to 50 cm (20 in) tall and broad, it has a broad yellow stripe down the centre of each leaf. It is an easy subject for moist soils in sun or partial shade.

items.name: Carex pendula
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in heavy clay or boggy soil near UK ponds, keeping the crown at soil level.
Water deeply during dry UK summers to maintain the damp soil conditions this sedge needs to thrive.
Cut back the tattered evergreen foliage and old flower spikes to the ground in early UK spring.
Remove the drooping brown seed heads in late summer to stop aggressive self-seeding across lawns.
Divide large congested clumps in mid-spring using two forks back-to-back to propagate new plants.
items.description: Carex pendula is a large sedge of the genus Carex. It occurs in woodland, scrubland, hedges and beside streams, preferring damp, heavy clay soils. It is sometimes grown as a garden plant because of its distinctive appearance.

items.name: Hakonechloa macra
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained humus-rich acid to neutral soil in partial shade to prevent leaf scorch.
Water deeply weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently damp but never waterlogged.
Cut the dead foliage back to ground level in late winter or early spring before new shoots emerge.
Divide congested clumps in mid-spring using a sharp spade when the soil begins to warm up.
Mulch annually in autumn with leaf mould or well-rotted compost to protect shallow roots from frost.
items.description: Hakonechloa is a genus of bunchgrass in the tribe Molinieae of the grass family, Poaceae, native to eastern Asia.

items.name: Dryopteris felix-mas
items.growersTips:
Plant crowns level with the soil surface in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade.
Water deeply during dry spring spells to help newly planted ferns establish in typical UK soils.
Cut back old, tattered fronds to the ground in late February before new fiddleheads emerge.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating the roots of container-grown specimens in damp autumn weather.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring using a sharp spade to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Dryopteris filix-mas, the male fern, is a common fern of the temperate Northern Hemisphere, native to much of Europe, Asia, and North America. It favours damp shaded areas in the understory of woodlands, but also shady places on hedge-banks, and rocks, and screes. Near the northern limit of its distribution it prefers sunny, well-drained sites. It is much less abundant in North America than in Europe.

items.name: Lady fern
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral soil enriched with leafmould to mimic UK woodlands.
Water deeply at the base during dry summer spells to keep the shallow rhizomes from drying out.
Cut back dead fronds to ground level in late winter before the new fiddleheads emerge in spring.
Plant alongside shade-loving hostas and astilbes to create a contrasting damp-shade border.
Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth begins to maintain plant vigour.
items.description: Athyrium filix-femina, the lady fern or common lady-fern, is a large, feathery species of fern native to temperate Asia, Europe, North America, and North Africa. It is often abundant in damp, shady woodland environments and is often grown for decoration.

items.name: Soft shield fern
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil with the crown level with the soil surface to prevent rot.
Water deeply at the base during dry UK summer spells, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Cut back dead or tattered fronds in late winter to make way for the new unfurling croziers in spring.
Plant alongside shade-loving UK companions like Hostas, Heucheras, and spring-flowering Wood Anemones.
Apply a generous mulch of leaf mould or well-rotted bark annually in autumn to mimic forest soils.
items.description: Polystichum setiferum, or the soft shield fern, is an evergreen or semi-evergreen fern native to southern and western Europe. The stalks and most midribs are coated with cinnamon-brown scales. The Latin specific epithet setiferum means "with bristles".

items.name: Hart's tongue fern
items.growersTips:
Plant in alkaline to neutral soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic their native UK limestone woods.
Water consistently at the base during dry summer spells to keep the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Cut back tattered old fronds flat to the ground in late winter before the new fiddleheads emerge.
Position in full or dappled shade under deciduous trees to prevent the fronds from scorching.
Watch for vine weevil grubs eating the roots and protect young fronds from slugs in damp springs.
items.description: Asplenium scolopendrium, commonly known as the hart's-tongue fern, is an evergreen fern in the family Aspleniaceae native to the Northern Hemisphere.

items.name: Aubrieta deltoidea
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with a handful of horticultural grit to prevent winter wet rot.
Cut back hard by half immediately after flowering in late spring to maintain a tight, bushy mound.
Position in full sun on a south-facing rockery or wall face to mimic its native alpine habitat.
Water newly planted plugs weekly until established, then leave to rely solely on UK rainfall.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring growth, using beer traps or organic pellets to protect.
items.description: Aubrieta deltoidea is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family. Common names include lilacbush, purple rock cress and rainbow rock cress. It should be grown in zones 4a to 9b.

items.name: Saxifraga ×urbium
items.growersTips:
Plant in partial shade in moist well-drained soil to prevent summer leaf scorch in UK gardens.
Divide congested clumps every three years in late spring after flowering to maintain plant vigour.
Water regularly during dry UK summer spells but ensure sharp drainage to prevent winter root rot.
Clear fallen autumn leaves promptly from the rosettes to prevent damp rot in wet winter months.
Combine with hostas or ferns in a woodland border to provide attractive year-round ground cover.
items.description: Saxifraga × urbium, London pride, is an evergreen perennial garden flowering plant. Alternative names for it include St. Patrick's cabbage, whimsey, prattling Parnell, and look up and kiss me. Before 1700 the “London pride” appellation was given to the Sweet William.

items.name: Arabis caucasica
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in full sun to prevent winter wet rot in damp UK climates.
Cut back hard by half immediately after spring flowering to maintain a neat, tight cushion habit.
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of two millimetres in cold frames during autumn for spring planting.
Watch for downy mildew and cabbage root fly, as this plant is in the brassica family.
Divide established clumps every three years in late summer to rejuvenate woody, bare centres.
items.description: Arabis caucasica is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family (Brassicaceae) known by the common names garden arabis, mountain rock cress or Caucasian rockcress.

items.name: Common Rock-rose
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, free-draining soil with added horticultural grit to survive wet UK winters.
Cut back by half immediately after flowering in July to keep the habit tight and prevent legginess.
Water newly planted rock-roses weekly during their first dry summer, then leave to rely on rainfall.
Sow seeds in cold frames during autumn to allow natural UK winter stratification for spring growth.
Associate with wild thyme and English lavender in a south-facing raised bed to mimic chalk downs.
items.description: Helianthemum nummularium is a species of rock-rose (Cistaceae), native to most of Europe.

items.name: Sea pink
items.growersTips:
Plant in sharply draining grit-enriched soil to prevent winter crown rot in wet UK climates.
Position in full sun and do not water once established as they thrive on neglect and drought.
Deadhead faded flower drums weekly in summer to encourage a second flush of pink blooms.
Divide congested clumps every three years in autumn to maintain tight mound-forming foliage.
Avoid high-nitrogen fertilisers which cause lush but floppy growth and reduce flowering.
items.description: Armeria maritima, the thrift, sea thrift or sea pink, is a species of flowering plant in the family Plumbaginaceae. It is a compact evergreen perennial which grows in low clumps and sends up long stems that support globes of bright pink flowers. In some cases purple, white or red flowers also occur. It is a popular garden flower and has been distributed worldwide as a garden and cut flower. It does well in gardens designed as xeriscapes or rock gardens. The Latin specific epithet maritima means pertaining to the sea or coastal.

items.name: Pulmonaria saccharata
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive humus-rich soil in partial to full shade to prevent summer leaf scorch.
Water deeply during dry UK summer spells to prevent powdery mildew which commonly attacks dry roots.
Cut back all tattered foliage to ground level in May after flowering to trigger fresh spotted leaves.
Divide congested clumps every three years in autumn to maintain vigor and prevent center dieback.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots by using organic wool pellets around the crown.
items.description: Pulmonaria saccharata, the Bethlehem lungwort or Bethlehem sage, is a species of flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae, native to France and Italy. It is a rhizomatous herbaceous perennial which is closely related to the common lungwort. Growing to 10 cm (4 in) tall by 60 cm (24 in) wide, it has lance-shaped leaves with white confluent spots, and pink or white flowers in spring.

items.name: Creeping myrtle
items.growersTips:
Plant Vinca minor in autumn at the same depth as its nursery pot to establish before UK winter frosts.
Prune hard in early spring with shears to control spread and encourage fresh variegated foliage.
Water newly planted creeping myrtle weekly during dry UK summers until its root system is mature.
Watch for stem blight in damp UK weather and prune out black wilted stems immediately to ground level.
Underplant beneath deciduous trees in acidic to neutral clay loam to suppress weeds in deep shade.
items.description: Vinca minor is a species of flowering plant in the dogbane family, native to central and southern Europe. Other vernacular names used in cultivation include small periwinkle, common periwinkle, and sometimes in the United States, myrtle or creeping myrtle.

items.name: Greater Periwinkle
items.growersTips:
Cut back hard to ground level in late winter to encourage fresh variegated foliage and more spring flowers.
Plant in dry shade under mature trees where other ground cover fails, watering only during first summer.
Control the invasive runners by digging out rooting tips in autumn before they colonise lawn edges.
Grow with robust companions like dryopteris ferns and wood anemones that can withstand its vigorous spread.
Watch for rust fungus pustules on leaf undersides in damp UK summers and prune out affected stems.
items.description: Vinca major, with the common names bigleaf periwinkle, large periwinkle, greater periwinkle and blue periwinkle, is a species of flowering plant in the family Apocynaceae, native to the western Mediterranean. Growing to 25 cm (10 in) tall and spreading indefinitely, it is an evergreen perennial, frequently used in cultivation as a groundcover.

items.name: Bugle weed
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn or spring at the same depth as the pot in moist, well-drained soil to avoid crown rot.
Water weekly during dry UK summers until established, keeping the soil damp but never waterlogged.
Divide congested clumps every three years in autumn to maintain vigor and prevent powdery mildew.
Plant alongside yellow-flowered Primula vulgaris to create a striking spring colour contrast.
Grow the cultivar Burgundy Glow in partial shade to prevent the variegated leaves from scorching.
items.description: Ajuga reptans is commonly known as bugle, blue bugle, bugleherb, bugleweed, carpetweed, carpet bugleweed, and common bugle, and traditionally as St. Lawrence plant. It is an herbaceous flowering plant in the mint family Lamiaceae, native to Europe. It is also a component of purple moor grass and rush pastures, a Biodiversity Action Plan habitat in the United Kingdom.

items.name: Spotted Dead-nettle
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in moist, well-drained soil enriched with leaf mould to mimic UK woodland floors.
Water weekly during dry summer spells until established, then only during prolonged UK droughts.
Shear back hard to ground level after the first summer flush to stimulate fresh, mildew-free leaves.
Watch for slugs and snails in damp UK springs, using beer traps or organic pellets around new shoots.
Divide congested clumps in early spring or autumn using a spade to propagate and maintain vigour.
items.description: Lamium maculatum is a species of flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, native throughout Europe and temperate Asia.

items.name: Cerastium tomentosum
items.growersTips:
Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil to prevent winter root rot during wet UK winters.
Shear the foliage back by half immediately after flowering in July to keep the mat tight and neat.
Water only during prolonged summer droughts as this plant thrives on neglect and dry conditions.
Divide congested clumps every three years in early autumn to maintain vigour and prevent bald spots.
Plant alongside purple aubrieta or creeping phlox for a classic, contrasting dry stone wall display.
items.description: Cerastium tomentosum (snow-in-summer) is an herbaceous flowering plant and a member of the family Caryophyllaceae. It is generally distinguished from other species of its genus by "tomentose" or felty foliage. It is a low, spreading perennial native to the alpine regions of central and southern Italy. The stems and leaves are silvery-grey, whilst the flowers are star-like, white and about 15 mm (0.59 in) across.

items.name: Phlox stolonifera
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich acid to neutral soil in partial shade to mimic woodland.
Water weekly during dry UK summers to keep the shallow, creeping stolons from drying out and dying.
Prune lightly after spring flowering by shearing spent stems to encourage dense evergreen carpet.
Watch for slugs and snails on young spring shoots, especially in damp British garden borders.
Divide congested clumps in autumn or early spring to propagate and maintain vigour of the groundcover.
items.description: Phlox stolonifera is a species of flowering plant in the family Polemoniaceae. It is a perennial herbaceous plant that is native to the eastern United States. It occurs in woodlands and stream banks in the vicinity of the Appalachian Mountains from Pennsylvania south to northern Georgia. Naturalized populations occur as far north as Québec, Canada.

items.name: Hill cherry
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root Hill cherry in moist, well-drained loam from November to March during dormancy.
Water deeply once a week in dry UK summers during the first two years to establish the root system.
Prune only in mid-summer to prevent silver leaf disease and bacterial canker entering cuts.
Check leaves in spring for cherry blackfly and prune out aphid-infested shoot tips immediately.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure, keeping it clear of the main woody stem.
items.description: Prunus serrulata or Japanese cherry is a species of cherry tree that grows wild in Japan, China, Korea and Vietnam. The term also refers to a cultivar produced from Prunus speciosa, a cherry tree endemic in Japan. Historically, the Japanese have developed many cultivars by selective breeding of cherry trees, which are produced by the complicated crossing of several wild species, and they are used for ornamental purposes all over the world. Of these, the cultivars produced by complex interspecific hybrids based on the Oshima cherry are also known as the Cerasus Sato-zakura Group.

items.name: Prunus itosakura
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn to let roots establish in wet UK winters before the spring blossom energy burst.
In dry UK summers, water deeply once a week at the base rather than frequent light surface sprinkles.
Prune only in midsummer to prevent silver leaf disease, focusing on removing crossing branches.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into heavy UK clay soils to improve drainage and prevent root rot.
Watch for bullfinches in early spring as they strip the flower buds of this specific cherry species.
items.description: Prunus × subhirtella, the winter-flowering cherry, spring cherry, or rosebud cherry, is the scientific name for the hybrid between Prunus itosakura (edohigan) and Prunus incisa (Mamezakura). It is a small deciduous flowering tree originating in Japan, but unknown in the wild.

items.name: Sargent's cherry
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, fertile, well-draining soil, keeping the graft union just above the ground level.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers for the first two years to establish roots.
Prune only in midsummer to prevent silver leaf disease, focusing on dead or crossing branches.
Watch for cherry blackfly in spring, spraying soapy water on young leaves to protect new growth.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in late winter, keeping it clear of the main stem.
items.description: Prunus sargentii, commonly known as Sargent's cherry or North Japanese hill cherry, is a species of cherry native to Japan, Korea, Sakhalin (Russia), and China.

items.name: Japanese crab apple
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, well-drained loam enriched with well-rotted manure to prevent UK clay compaction.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish deep roots.
Prune lightly in late winter to remove crossed branches, keeping the natural weeping shrub shape.
Watch for apple scab in wet UK springs, clearing fallen leaves to stop the fungal spores overwintering.
Underplant with spring-flowering bulbs like Narcissus to attract early pollinators to the blossoms.
items.description: Malus floribunda, common name Japanese flowering crabapple, Japanese crab, purple chokeberry, or showy crabapple, originates from Japan and East Asia. It may be a hybrid of M. toringo with M. baccata, in which case it would be written as Malus × floribunda.

items.name: Malus 'John Downie'
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained loam enriched with well-rotted manure, keeping the graft union above soil level.
Water deeply weekly during the first two dry summers to establish roots in unpredictable UK weather.
Prune in late winter to remove congested branches and maintain an open canopy for maximum sunlight.
Monitor leaves in damp UK springs for apple scab and promptly remove fallen foliage to stop spread.
Harvest the orange-red crab apples in October when they soften slightly, ideal for traditional jelly.

items.name: European mountain-ash
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acid to neutral soil, adding leaf mould to mimic UK woodland conditions.
Water deeply once a week during the first two dry summers to establish a deep, resilient root system.
Prune only in late winter to avoid sap bleeding and reduce the risk of devastating fireblight fungus.
Watch for apple scab in damp UK summers, clearing fallen leaves to prevent the fungal spores overwintering.
Underplant with wood anemones or wild daffodils which thrive in the light shade of its open canopy.
items.description: Sorbus aucuparia, commonly called rowan and mountain-ash, is a species of deciduous tree or shrub in the rose family.

items.name: Common whitebeam
items.growersTips:
Plant in well-drained chalk or loam, ensuring the root flare sits exactly level with the soil surface.
Water newly planted whitebeam deeply once a week during dry UK spells in its first two summers.
Prune only dead or crossing branches in late winter to prevent fireblight bacteria entering wounds.
Watch for leaf-mining moths in summer, removing affected leaves to keep the canopy healthy.
Underplant with wild marjoram or field scabious to attract pollinators to the whitebeam flowers.
items.description: Aria edulis, the whitebeam or common whitebeam, is a species of deciduous tree in the family Rosaceae.

items.name: Warty birch
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist well-drained acid to neutral soil, avoiding shallow chalk to prevent leaf chlorosis.
Prune only between late autumn and midwinter to prevent the sap from bleeding heavily from cuts.
Water deeply during dry summer spells in the first two years to establish the shallow root system.
Watch for birch aphid and rust in damp UK summers, treating early to prevent premature leaf drop.
Grow dwarf cultivars like Trost's Dwarf in large pots using loam-based John Innes No 3 compost.
items.description: Betula pendula, commonly known as silver birch, warty birch, European white birch, or East Asian white birch, is a species of tree in the family Betulaceae, native to Europe and parts of Asia, though in southern Europe, it is only found at higher altitudes. Its range extends into Siberia, China, and southwest Asia in the mountains of northern Turkey, the Caucasus, and northern Iran. It has been introduced into North America, where it is known as the European white birch or weeping birch and is considered invasive in some states in the United States and parts of Canada.

items.name: Betula utilis
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil, incorporating leaf mould to mimic woodland.
Water deeply weekly during dry UK summers for the first two years to establish the shallow roots.
Prune only during late autumn to midwinter to prevent the sap from bleeding heavily from cuts.
Scrub the white bark gently with warm water and a sponge in autumn to remove green algae and moss.
Underplant with shade-loving spring bulbs like bluebells and anemones that thrive in dappled light.
items.description: Betula utilis, the Himalayan birch or bhojpatra, is a deciduous tree native to the Western Himalayas, growing at elevations up to 4,500 m (14,800 ft). The Latin specific epithet utilis means "useful", and refers to the many uses of the different parts of the tree. The white, paper-like bark was used in ancient times as a writing surface for manuscripts of Sanskrit literature. It is still used as paper for the writing of mantras, with the bark placed in an amulet and worn for protection. Selected varieties are used for landscaping throughout the world, even while some areas of its native habita

items.name: Common hawthorn
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root hawthorn in November to March at the same depth as the soil mark on the stem.
Water newly planted hawthorn deeply once a week during dry spells in its first UK spring and summer.
Prune established hawthorn hedges in July or August to keep shape without losing spring blossoms.
Watch for hawthorn shield bugs and leaf miners in June, but avoid spraying to support UK wildlife.
Mix organic compost into heavy UK clay soils before planting to prevent winter waterlogging.
items.description: Crataegus monogyna, known as common hawthorn, whitethorn, one-seed hawthorn, or single-seeded hawthorn, is a species of flowering plant in the rose family, Rosaceae. It grows to about 10 metres tall, producing hermaphrodite flowers in late spring. The berry-like pomes contain a stone-encased seed.

items.name: Crataegus laevigata
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn using a mycorrhizal fungi dip to help roots establish in heavy UK clay soils.
Prune in late winter by removing crossing branches to maintain an open crown and prevent mildew.
Water deeply every two weeks during the first dry summer, then leave to rely on UK rainfall.
Watch for hawthorn leaf blight in wet UK summers, clearing fallen leaves to stop reinfection.
Grow underplanted with wild garlic or bluebells which thrive in its dappled deciduous shade.
items.description: Crataegus laevigata, known as the Midland hawthorn, English hawthorn, woodland hawthorn, or mayflower, is a species of hawthorn native to western and central Europe, from Great Britain and Spain, east to Romania and Ukraine. The species name is sometimes spelt C. levigata, but the original orthography is C. lævigata.

items.name: Eastern Redbud
items.growersTips:
Plant in a south-facing, sheltered spot to protect young spring buds from harsh UK frosts and winds.
Incorporate well-rotted grit and organic matter to ensure heavy clay soils drain freely in winter.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells for the first two years to establish taproots.
Prune only in late spring after flowering to avoid bleeding sap and losing next year's blooms.
Watch for coral spot disease by promptly pruning out dead wood with sterilised shears in summer.
items.description: Cercis canadensis, the eastern redbud, is a large deciduous shrub or small tree, native to eastern North America from southern Michigan south to central Mexico, west to New Mexico, but able to thrive as far west as California and as far north as southern Ontario. It is the state tree of Oklahoma and the official city tree of Huntington Beach. The prevalence of the so-called "Columbus strain" has seen the residents of Columbus, Wisconsin, embrace the plant in their city's identity. Known as the "Redbud City," the town hosts "Redbud Day" annually the Saturday before Mother's Day, organizing a va

items.name: Cercis siliquastrum
items.growersTips:
Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, adding grit to heavy clay to prevent winter root rot.
Water deeply once a week during the first two dry summers to establish the deep taproot system.
Prune only in late summer to avoid bleeding sap and reduce the risk of coral spot fungus.
Watch for scale insects and apply organic winter wash to the bare bark in December or January.
Plant in its final spot when young as the sensitive taproot resents being moved once established.
items.description: Cercis siliquastrum, European Cercis, commonly known as the Judas tree or Judas-tree, is a small deciduous species of redbud in the flowering plant family Fabaceae which is noted for its prolific display of deep pink flowers in spring. It is native to Southern Europe and Western Asia.

items.name: Hazel pine
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moist, acidic to neutral soil to prevent chlorosis and ensure vibrant autumn colour.
Saturate the root ball weekly during dry UK summers for the first three years to establish roots.
Prune only in late winter to remove crossing branches before the sap rises and causes bleeding.
Shelter from strong, cold UK winds to protect the delicate, star-shaped leaves from wind scorch.
Mulch annually in spring with composted pine needles or compost to maintain the required soil acidity.
items.description: Liquidambar styraciflua, commonly known as the American sweetgum among other names, is a deciduous tree in the genus Liquidambar native to warm temperate areas of eastern North America and tropical montane regions of Mexico and Central America. Sweetgum is one of the main valuable forest trees in the southeastern United States, and is a popular ornamental tree in temperate climates. It is recognizable by the combination of its five-pointed star-shaped leaves and its hard, spiked fruits. It is currently classified in the plant family Altingiaceae, but was formerly considered a member of the Ham

items.name: Stewartia pseudocamellia
items.growersTips:
Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, adding ericaceous compost to the planting hole.
Position in a sheltered spot with morning sun and afternoon shade to prevent leaf scorch.
Water deeply with rainwater during dry summer spells to keep the shallow root system moist.
Prune minimally in late winter only to remove dead wood or crossing branches to preserve shape.
Mulch annually in spring with leaf mould or pine needles to maintain soil acidity and moisture.
items.description: Stewartia pseudocamellia, also known as Korean stewartia, Japanese stewartia, or deciduous camellia, is a species of flowering plant in the family Theaceae, native to Japan and Korea.

items.name: Potato
items.growersTips:
Chit seed tubers in a cool, bright frost-free room from February to give crops a head start.
Plant tubers 12cm deep in mid-spring, spacing rows 60cm apart to allow room for earthing up.
Draw soil up around growing stems to block light, preventing green toxic tubers and frost damage.
Water tubers deeply once they reach marble size in June to prevent common scab and boost yields.
Watch for potato blight in warm, wet summer weather and cut infected foliage to ground level.
items.description: The potato is a starchy tuberous vegetable native to the Americas that is consumed as a staple food in many parts of the world. Potatoes are underground stem tubers of the plant Solanum tuberosum, a perennial in the nightshade family Solanaceae.

items.name: Onion
items.growersTips:
Plant autumn sets in October or spring sets in April, keeping the bulb tip just visible at the surface.
Water only during dry spells in summer, then stop watering completely once the foliage turns yellow.
Cover the crop with fine insect mesh immediately after planting to block the destructive onion fly.
Mulch with garden compost in autumn to create the free-draining, fertile soil these bulbs require.
Plant mint or chamomile nearby to deter pests, but keep them far away from any beans or peas.
items.description: The onion, also known as the bulb onion or common onion, is a vegetable that is the most widely cultivated species of the genus Allium. The shallot is a botanical variety of the onion which was classified as a separate species until 2011. The onion's close relatives include garlic, scallion, leek, and chives.

items.name: Garlic
items.growersTips:
Plant cloves in autumn by late November so winter cold triggers the essential bulb splitting process.
Plant cloves pointed end up at a depth of eight centimetres to protect them from hard winter frosts.
Stop watering completely in June when leaves begin to yellow to prevent the bulbs from rotting.
Snip off curly flower scapes from hardneck varieties in May to redirect energy into bulb growth.
Watch for rust fungus in damp spring weather and immediately remove affected leaves to stop spread.
items.description: Garlic is a species of bulbous flowering plants in the genus Allium. Its close relatives include the onion, shallot, leek, chives, Welsh onion, and Chinese onion. Garlic is native to Central Asia, northeastern Iran and the foothills of Himalayas. It has naturalized in many other parts of the world, including Mediterranean Europe and China. There are two subspecies and hundreds of varieties of garlic.

items.name: Bird's nest
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at a depth of three millimetres directly outdoors from April to July.
Grow in poor to moderately fertile well-drained soil to prevent the taproot from splitting.
Water sparingly once established as this drought-tolerant native dislikes waterlogged UK winter soil.
Watch for carrot fly and deter them by interplanting with strong-smelling companion plants like alliums.
Leave the dried seed heads over winter to provide shelter for beneficial UK garden insects.
items.description: Daucus carota, whose common names include wild carrot, European wild carrot, bird's nest, bishop's lace, carrot flower, and Queen Anne's lace, is a flowering plant in the family Apiaceae. It is native to temperate regions of the Old World with a number of regional subspecies, and is naturalised widely elsewhere. Carrots cultivated as a food crop are cultivars of the domesticated subspecies Daucus carota subsp. sativus.

items.name: Sea beet
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in spring 1cm deep in free-draining sandy soil to mimic its native UK shingle habitat.
Water young plants weekly but let established beds dry out to develop the characteristic salty taste.
Pick the outer leaves continuously from March to October to prevent the plant from bolting to seed.
Protect young spring shoots from slugs and snails using beer traps or grit barriers in damp weather.
Grow alongside sea kale or wild cabbage in a dedicated coastal-style bed using poor, gritty soil.
items.description: Beta vulgaris (beet) is a species of flowering plant in the subfamily Betoideae of the family Amaranthaceae. It is a perennial plant usually growing up to 120 centimetres (4 ft) tall.

items.name: Pea
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in mid-spring 3cm deep in flat trenches to avoid wet UK soil rotting early plantings.
Support young vines immediately with hazel twigs or pea sticks to prevent wind damage on damp days.
Water heavily only when flowering and podding starts, targeting the roots to prevent powdery mildew.
Protect emerging shoots from slugs and birds using fine netting or cloches during cool UK springs.
Harvest pods regularly from the bottom up to encourage the plant to keep producing more sweet peas.
items.description: Pea is a pulse or fodder crop, but the word often refers to the seed or sometimes the pod of this flowering plant species. Peas are eaten as a vegetable.

items.name: Snap bean
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April to protect tender young seedlings from late UK spring frosts and slugs.
Plant out in late May after hardening off, spacing dwarf types thirty centimetres apart in full sun.
Water heavily at the base once flowers appear to ensure succulent pods and prevent flower drop.
Construct a sturdy wigwam support using two-metre bamboo canes for climbing varieties like Cobra.
Harvest pods every few days when they are young and snap easily to encourage continuous cropping.
items.description: Phaseolus vulgaris, the common bean, is a herbaceous annual plant. Its botanical classification, along with other Phaseolus species, is as a member of the legume family, Fabaceae. It forms a green-leaved vine which produces beans inside of pods.

items.name: Lactuca sativa crispa
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds shallowly at five millimetres deep every two weeks from March to July for continuous crops.
Water early in the morning directly at the base to prevent downy mildew in damp UK summer weather.
Protect young leaves from slugs using beer traps or copper tape during wet British spring nights.
Plant alongside chives or garlic to deter aphids and mask the scent of tender salad leaves.
Sow bolt-resistant cultivars like Lollo Rossa in midsummer to handle sudden UK heatwaves.
items.description: Lettuce is an annual plant of the family Asteraceae mostly grown as a leaf vegetable. The leaves are most often used raw in green salads, although lettuce is also seen in other kinds of food, such as sandwiches, wraps and soups; it can also be grilled. Its stem and seeds are sometimes used; celtuce is one variety grown for its stems, which are eaten either raw or cooked. In addition to its main use as a leafy green, it has also gathered religious and medicinal significance over centuries of human consumption. Europe and North America originally dominated the market for lettuce, but by the late

items.name: Spinach
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 1.5cm deep in moist, nitrogen-rich soil, spacing rows 30cm apart for optimal leaf spread.
Grow bolt-resistant cultivars like Medania or perpetual spinach to survive dry UK summer spells.
Water the soil directly and consistently at the base to prevent downy mildew in damp UK weather.
Protect young spring seedlings from slugs using beer traps or organic ferric phosphate pellets.
Sow in late August under cloches for a continuous harvest of hardy winter leaves through to spring.
items.description: Spinach is a leafy green flowering plant native to Central and Western Asia. It is of the order Caryophyllales, family Amaranthaceae, subfamily Chenopodioideae. Its leaves are a common vegetable consumed either fresh, cooked or after storage. The taste differs considerably between cooked and raw: the high oxalate content may be reduced by blanching.

items.name: Fast plants
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds 1cm deep in multi-purpose compost from April to July for reliable UK summer harvests.
Water consistently at the base to prevent bolting during dry spells or sudden UK summer heatwaves.
Protect young seedlings from flea beetles using fine insect mesh immediately after sowing outdoors.
Plant alongside mint or sage to deter cabbage white butterflies from laying eggs on the leaves.
In wet UK autumns, harvest the leafy greens early as annuals before winter frosts rot the crowns.
items.description: Brassica rapa is an annual to biennial plant species native to Eurasia that is from the Brassicaceae family. The B. rapa subspecies oleifera is an oilseed commonly known as turnip rape, field mustard, bird's rape, and keblock.

items.name: Rapeseed
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds in late August or September at a depth of one to two centimetres for overwintering.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into heavy clay soils to improve drainage before autumn sowing.
Net young plants immediately to protect them from wood pigeon damage during UK winter months.
Apply a nitrogen-rich organic fertiliser in early spring to boost rapid leafy growth and flowering.
Monitor closely for cabbage stem flea beetle damage on seedlings during dry autumn spells.
items.description: Rapeseed, also known as rape and oilseed rape and canola, is a yellow-flowered member of the Brassicaceae family.

items.name: Capsicum annuum
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in February or March using a heated propagator to offset the cool UK spring.
Pot on into peat-free compost once the first true leaves appear, burying the stem up to those leaves.
Move plants to a greenhouse or sunny patio only after late May frosts have completely passed.
Pinch out the growing tip when plants reach twenty centimetres high to encourage a bushy habit.
Water consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot, avoiding wetting the foliage.
items.description: Capsicum annuum is a flowering plant in the family Solanaceae (nightshades), native to the northern regions of South America and to southwestern North America. The plant produces berries of many colors including red, green, and yellow, often with pungent taste. It is one of the oldest cultivated crops, with domestication dating back to around 6,000 years ago in regions of Mexico. The genus Capsicum has over 30 species but Capsicum annuum is the primary species in its genus, as it has been widely cultivated for human consumption for a substantial amount of time and has spread across the world.

items.name: Watermelon
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in April at 2cm deep in 9cm pots using a heated propagator set to 21C.
Grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel, or plant outdoors in June against a south-facing brick wall.
Water the soil deeply around the base, keeping the foliage dry to prevent powdery mildew.
Pinch out the main growing tip after five leaves to encourage lateral fruiting side-shoots.
Raise developing fruits off the damp soil using a slate, tile, or straw to prevent rotting.
items.description: The watermelon is a species of flowering plant in the family Cucurbitaceae, that has a large, edible fruit. It is a scrambling and trailing vine-like plant, and is widely cultivated worldwide, with more than 1,000 varieties.

items.name: Cardoon
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March at 1.5cm deep then plant out in May after the last frost in full sun.
Incorporate well-rotted manure into free-draining soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK clay.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent shallow sprinkles.
Watch for black bean aphid infestations on young stems and blast them off with a sharp hose spray.
Wrap the stems in cardboard for four weeks in autumn to blanch them and reduce their bitterness.
items.description: The cardoon, also called the artichoke thistle, is a thistle in the family Asteraceae. It is a naturally occurring species that also has many cultivated forms, including the globe artichoke. It is native to the Mediterranean region, where it was domesticated in ancient times and still occurs as a wild plant.

items.name: Artichoke plant
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in February at ten millimetres deep to ensure a long enough UK growing season.
Plant out in May into free-draining soil enriched with compost to prevent winter root rot in wet clay.
Water deeply once a week during dry summer spells rather than giving frequent light sprinkles.
Cover the crown with a thick straw mulch in late autumn to protect it from severe UK winter frosts.
Cut back the main flower stem to ground level in autumn after harvesting to encourage new side shoots.
items.description: The artichoke is a variety of a species of thistle cultivated as food.

items.name: Rosmarinus officinalis
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining gritty soil with added horticultural grit to prevent winter root rot in UK wet.
Prune immediately after spring flowering by cutting back green stems by a third to prevent woodiness.
Grow in full south-facing sun against a brick wall to radiate heat and shelter from cold UK winds.
Water newly planted rosemary weekly in summer, then leave established plants entirely to UK rainfall.
Choose the cultivar Miss Jessopps Upright for tight spaces or Prostratus to cascade over dry walls.
items.description: Salvia rosmarinus, synonym Rosmarinus officinalis, commonly known as rosemary, is a shrub with fragrant, evergreen, needle-like leaves and purple or sometimes white, pink, or blue flowers. It is a member of the mint family, Lamiaceae. The species is native to the Mediterranean region. It has numerous cultivars, and its leaves are commonly used as a flavoring.

items.name: Thymus vulgaris
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining grit-heavy soil to prevent winter root rot in wet UK winters.
Prune hard by cutting back by half immediately after flowering in late summer to prevent woodiness.
Water newly planted thyme sparingly and only during prolonged dry spells once established.
Grow near brassicas to deter cabbage white butterflies with the strong aromatic foliage.
Select the cultivar Compactus for small UK rock gardens to ensure a neat cushion-like habit.
items.description: Thymus vulgaris is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae.

items.name: Rosemary
items.growersTips:
Plant in free-draining soil mixed with grit to survive wet UK winters and prevent root rot.
Prune immediately after flowering in late spring by cutting back green shoots to keep it bushy.
Water newly planted rosemary weekly in summer, but leave established UK plants entirely to rain.
Grow in a terracotta pot raised on feet to protect roots from waterlogging during winter frosts.
Take semi-ripe cuttings in August to propagate and replace old woody plants that lose their vigor.
items.description: Salvia rosmarinus, synonym Rosmarinus officinalis, commonly known as rosemary, is a shrub with fragrant, evergreen, needle-like leaves and purple or sometimes white, pink, or blue flowers. It is a member of the mint family, Lamiaceae. The species is native to the Mediterranean region. It has numerous cultivars, and its leaves are commonly used as a flavoring.

items.name: Dill
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds directly from April to July as dill has a taproot and hates transplant shock.
Sow in a sunny, sheltered spot to prevent the tall, hollow stems from blowing over in UK wind.
Water the soil consistently at the base to prevent powdery mildew in humid British summers.
Sow in small batches every three weeks for a continuous supply of fresh leaves until the first frost.
Plant near cabbages to repel pests but keep away from fennel to prevent cross-pollination.
items.description: Dill is an annual herb in the celery family Apiaceae. Native to North Africa and West Asia, dill is grown widely in Eurasia, where its leaves and seeds are used as a herb or spice for flavouring food.

items.name: Parsley
items.growersTips:
Pour boiling water over the soil before sowing in spring to speed up notoriously slow germination.
Sow in deep pots or root trainers to avoid disturbing the sensitive taproot when transplanting.
Water the soil around the base in the morning, keeping leaves dry to prevent septoria leaf spot.
Keep plants in light shade during hot UK summers to stop them bolting and going to seed prematurely.
In autumn cover plants with a cloche to harvest fresh leaves through the damp British winter.
items.description: Parsley, or garden parsley, is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae that is native to the Balkans. It has been introduced and naturalized in Europe and elsewhere in the world with suitable climates, and is widely cultivated as a herb and a vegetable.

items.name: Garlic chives
items.growersTips:
Sow seeds indoors in March or plant bulbs 5cm deep in free-draining soil after the last spring frosts.
Water deeply once a week during dry UK summers rather than daily dampening to prevent bulb rot.
Cut back the white star-shaped flowers in August before they set seed to stop invasive self-sowing.
Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent fungal rust disease.
Grow them alongside carrots to deter the carrot rust fly with their strong onion-like scent.
items.description: Allium tuberosum is a species of plant native to the Chinese province of Shanxi, and cultivated and naturalized elsewhere in Asia and around the world. It has a number of uses in Asian cuisine.

items.name: Marjoram
items.growersTips:
Grow in free-draining gritty soil as wet winter clay will rot the roots of this Mediterranean herb
Sow seeds indoors in March then transplant outside in May after the last frost at 5mm deep
Water young plants moderately but let established marjoram dry out completely between waterings
Prune back hard in late summer after flowering to encourage fresh leaf growth before winter
Bring potted marjoram into a cold frame or unheated greenhouse to survive wet UK winter freezes
items.description: Marjoram is a cold-sensitive perennial herb or undershrub with sweet pine and citrus flavours. In some Middle Eastern countries, marjoram is synonymous with oregano, and there the names sweet marjoram and knotted marjoram are used to distinguish it from other plants of the genus Origanum. It is also called pot marjoram, although this name is also used for other cultivated species of Origanum.

items.name: Lovage
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, fertile soil as its taproot can grow up to one metre deep.
Sow seeds in spring or autumn at a depth of one centimetre in a cold frame or directly outdoors.
Water young plants weekly during dry UK summers to keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy.
Cut the plant back to ground level in late autumn after the first frost to encourage spring growth.
Watch for celery leaf miner damage in early summer and pinch off affected leaves immediately.
items.description: Lovage is a perennial plant, the sole species in the genus Levisticum in the family Apiaceae, subfamily Apioideae. It is native to Afghanistan and Iran.

items.name: Common bilberry
items.growersTips:
Plant in highly acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, mixing pine needles or sulphur into the bed.
Water only with stored rainwater, keeping the soil constantly damp but never waterlogged.
Grow in partial shade to mimic UK woodland edges, avoiding hot, dry, south-facing positions.
Prune in late winter by removing dead wood and one-fifth of old stems to boost berry production.
Protect ripening summer berries from birds using tight-mesh netting secured at the ground level.
items.description: Vaccinium myrtillus is a holarctic species of shrub with edible fruit of blue color, known by the common names bilberry, blaeberry, wimberry, and whortleberry. It is more precisely called common bilberry or blue whortleberry to distinguish it from other Vaccinium relatives.

items.name: Redcurrant
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root bushes in deep, fertile soil from November to March, keeping the graft union clear.
Prune in winter by removing old wood and shortening new shoots to create an open, goblet-shaped bush.
Mulch annually with well-rotted manure in spring to retain moisture and suppress weeds in dry spells.
Net the bushes in June to protect ripening trusses from birds and watch for sawfly larvae damage.
Grow underplanted with chives or marigolds to deter aphids and attract pollinators to the blooms.
items.description: The redcurrant or red currant is a member of the genus Ribes in the family Grossulariaceae. It is native to western Europe. The species is widely cultivated and has escaped into the wild in many regions.

items.name: Ribes uva-crispa
items.growersTips:
Grow in a u-shaped cordon to maximise sunlight and make harvesting the thorny branches much easier
Mulch in late winter with well-rotted manure to feed the shallow roots and retain summer moisture
Prune in July by shortening side shoots to five leaves to encourage fruit spurs for next summer
Net the bushes in May to protect ripening berries from bullfinches and hungry local UK garden birds
Watch for sawfly larvae in mid-spring and handpick them immediately before they defoliate the shrub
items.description: Ribes uva-crispa, commonly known as the gooseberry or European gooseberry, is a species of flowering shrub native to Europe, northwestern Africa, and southwestern Asia. It belongs to the family Grossulariaceae, which includes currants and gooseberries. The plant is cultivated for its edible fruit, which is used in culinary applications ranging from desserts to preserves.

items.name: Rubus fruticosus
items.growersTips:
Prune two-year-old floricanes to the ground in autumn and tie in new green primocanes for next year.
Plant bare-root cultivars like Loch Ness 8cm deep in moisture-retentive, acidic to neutral clay loam.
Apply a 10cm mulch of well-rotted manure in March to retain moisture during dry UK summer spells.
Net the ripening berries in July to protect the harvest from blackbirds and spotted wing drosophila.
Train vigorous canes horizontally along wires spaced 45cm apart to maximise sunlight in UK gardens.
items.description:
Rubus fruticosus L. is the ambiguous name of a European blackberry species in the genus Rubus. The name has been interpreted in several ways:The species represented by the type specimen of Rubus fruticosus L., which is also the type specimen of the genus Rubus. This specimen is considered to match the species R. plicatus, in Rubus subgenus Rubus, section Rubus.
Various species consistent with Carl Linnaeus' original description of the species, which was based on a mixture of specimens now considered to match Rubus ulmifolius and R. plicatus
a species aggregate Rubus fruticosus agg. that includ

items.name: Loganberry
items.growersTips:
Plant in autumn in well-drained soil enriched with well-rotted manure, keeping the crown at soil level
Train vigorous new canes in a fan shape on wires, keeping them separate from this year's fruiting wood
Prune in autumn by cutting fruited canes to the ground and tying in the new green canes for next year
