Protect ripening berries from birds in July using fine netting and watch for raspberry beetle grubs
Water deeply at the base weekly during dry summer spells to prevent fruit shrivelling in UK heatwaves
items.description: The loganberry is a hybrid of the North American blackberry and the European raspberry, accidentally bred in 1881 by James Harvey Logan, for whom they are named. It is cultivated for its edible fruit.

items.name: Plum tree
items.growersTips:
Prune in midsummer to avoid silver leaf disease, never in winter when damp spores infect cuts.
Plant bare-root trees in November with the graft union kept strictly 10cm above the soil level.
Apply a thick mulch of well-rotted manure in March, keeping it clear of the main woody stem.
Thin out young green fruits in May to a hand-width apart to prevent heavy branches from snapping.
Hang pheromone traps in May to monitor plum fruit moth and protect the developing summer crop.
items.description: Prunus domestica is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. A deciduous tree, it includes many varieties of the fruit trees known as plums in English, though not all plums belong to this species. The greengages and damsons also belong to subspecies of P. domestica.

items.name: Apricot tree
items.growersTips:
Grow self-fertile cultivars like Tomcot on dwarfing Vixen rootstock to suit small UK gardens.
Plant in a sheltered south-facing spot against a brick wall to trap heat and protect early blossom.
Cover the canopy with fleece in February to protect delicate early flowers from late spring frosts.
Prune only in May or June to prevent silver leaf disease and bacterial canker entering wet cuts.
Water deeply once a week during fruit swell in dry spells to prevent the developing apricots dropping.
items.description: Prunus armeniaca is the most commonly cultivated apricot species. The native range is somewhat uncertain due to its extensive prehistoric cultivation. Genetic studies indicate Central Asia is the center of origin. It is extensively cultivated in many countries and has escaped into the wild in many places. The specific epithet armeniaca refers to the country of Armenia.

items.name: Peach
items.growersTips:
Train peaches as fans against south-facing walls to maximise UK sun and protect early spring blossom.
Cover trees with fleece from January to May to prevent rain-borne peach leaf curl fungal spores.
Thin fruits in June to leave one peach every fifteen centimetres so the tree is not overloaded.
Water deeply weekly during dry spells in summer to prevent fruit drop and ensure juicy peaches.
Prune in spring or summer after bud burst to avoid silver leaf disease, never during winter.
items.description: The peach is a deciduous tree that bears edible juicy fruits with various characteristics. Most are simply called peaches, while the glossy-skinned, non-fuzzy varieties are called nectarines. Though from the same species, they are regarded commercially as different fruits.

items.name: Pyrus communis
items.growersTips:
Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, well-drained loam in a sheltered, south-facing UK spot for sun.
Prune in winter when dormant to establish a strong central leader and remove congested branches.
Water deeply every fortnight during dry summer spells, especially while the young tree establishes.
Watch for pear midge in spring; pick and burn deformed, blackened fruitlets before larvae escape.
Mulch annually in early spring with well-rotted manure, keeping it clear of the main woody stem.
items.description: Pyrus communis, the common pear, is a species of pear native to central and eastern Europe, and western Asia.

items.name: Apple tree
items.growersTips:
Plant bare-root trees in moist, well-drained soil between November and March, keeping graft union clear.
Prune established bush trees in winter, removing dead, diseased, and crossing wood to open the center.
Thin out excess young fruitlets in June to prevent biennial bearing and ensure larger, healthier crops.
Apply grease bands to the trunk in October to stop wingless female winter moths climbing up to lay eggs.
Mulch annually in early spring with well-rotted manure, keeping it clear of the main trunk base.
items.description: An apple is the round, edible fruit of an apple tree. Fruit trees of the orchard or domestic apple, the most widely grown in the genus, are cultivated worldwide. The tree originated in Central Asia, where its wild ancestor, Malus sieversii, is still found. Apples have been grown for thousands of years in Eurasia before they were introduced to North America by European colonists. Apples have cultural significance in many mythologies and religions.

items.name: Quince
items.growersTips:
Plant your quince in a sheltered, south-facing spot to maximize UK summer sun for fruit ripening.
Prune in winter during dormancy to remove congested branches and open the canopy for air circulation.
Water deeply during dry summer spells while the fruit is swelling to prevent premature fruit drop.
Mulch annually in spring with well-rotted manure, keeping it clear of the main woody stem base.
Watch for quince leaf blight in wet UK summers and prune out infected wood immediately to control it.
items.description: The quince is the sole member of the genus Cydonia in the Malinae subtribe of the Rosaceae family. It is a deciduous tree that bears hard, aromatic bright golden-yellow pome fruit, similar in appearance to a pear. Ripe quince fruits are hard, tart, and astringent. They are eaten raw or processed into jam, quince cheese, or alcoholic drinks.

items.name: Fig
items.growersTips:
Restrict root growth by planting in a buried 40cm pot to force energy into fruit rather than leaves.
Prune in late winter to shape, then pinch out new shoot tips at five leaves in June to boost yield.
Protect tiny pea-sized young overwintering figs with fleece from November to March against UK frost.
Water container-grown figs deeply and consistently during summer fruit-swell to prevent fruit drop.
Plant against a south or west-facing brick wall to maximize heat absorption in the cool UK climate.
items.description: The fig is the edible fruit of Ficus carica, a species of tree or shrub in the flowering plant family Moraceae, native to the Mediterranean region, and to western and southern Asia. It has been cultivated since ancient times and is now widely grown throughout the world. Ficus carica is the type species of the genus Ficus, which comprises over 800 tropical and subtropical plant species.

items.name: White water-lily
items.growersTips:
Plant in a heavy clay loam using a mesh aquatic basket to prevent the rhizome from floating away.
Submerge the container gradually, starting at 20cm deep and lowering to 1m as the plant matures.
Position in full sun in still water, away from splashing garden fountains or artificial waterfalls.
Divide the congested rhizomes in late spring every four years to maintain vigorous flowering.
Watch for water-lily beetle larvae in summer and wash them off into the pond for fish to eat.
items.description: Nymphaea alba – commonly called the white water lily, European white water lily, or white nenuphar – is an aquatic flowering plant in the family Nymphaeaceae. It is native to North Africa, temperate Asia, Europe, and tropical Asia.

items.name: Nymphaea odorata subsp. tuberosa
items.growersTips:
Plant this vigorous white water lily in a large aquatic basket at a final depth of 45 to 90cm.
Use heavy clay loam soil topped with pea gravel to prevent the tuberous roots from floating up.
Divide the spreading tubers every three years in late spring to maintain flowering and control size.
Position in full sun in still water as UK summer warmth is essential to trigger the white blooms.
Watch for water lily beetle larvae in summer and wash them off into the pond for fish to eat.
items.description: Nymphaea odorata, also known as the American white waterlily, fragrant water-lily, beaver root, fragrant white water lily, white water lily, sweet-scented white water lily, and sweet-scented water lily, is an aquatic plant belonging to the genus Nymphaea. It can commonly be found in shallow lakes, ponds, and permanent slow moving waters throughout North America where it ranges from Central America to northern Canada. It is also reported from Brazil and Guyana.

items.name: Blue flag iris
items.growersTips:
Plant this moisture-lover in wet soil or shallow pond margins up to ten centimetres deep in full sun.
Divide the rhizomes, not bulbs, every three years in late summer to maintain vigorous UK flowering.
Cut back the dying foliage to the ground in autumn to prevent the common iris rust fungus overwintering.
Watch for iris sawfly larvae in May and handpick them immediately to prevent severe leaf damage.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris in boggy areas to provide contrasting early spring yellow blooms.
items.description: Iris versicolor or Iris versicolour is also commonly known as the blue flag, harlequin blueflag, larger blue flag, northern blue flag, and poison flag, plus other variations of these names, and in Great Britain and Ireland as purple iris.

items.name: Iris laevigata
items.growersTips:
Grow in heavy clay or boggy soil at a planting depth of up to fifteen centimetres of standing water.
Position in full sun to ensure reliable flowering during the typical British midsummer wet season.
Propagate by dividing the rhizomes, not bulbs, in late summer after the flowering period has ended.
Cut back dead foliage to the ground in autumn to prevent rot in damp UK winter conditions.
Plant alongside Caltha palustris to create a vibrant colour contrast in pond margins.
items.description: Iris laevigata, known as Japanese iris, rabbit-ear iris, or shallow-flowered iris, is a species of flowering plant in the family Iridaceae, native to Japan. It is related to other members of Iris subgenus Limniris, including other species of Japanese irises.

items.name: Caltha palustris
items.growersTips:
Plant this native marginal in heavy clay or wet soil at the pond edge up to ten centimetres deep.
Water container-grown specimens daily with rainwater during dry UK summers to prevent soil drying.
Cut back faded foliage to the base in July to encourage a fresh flush of leaves and autumn flowers.
Watch for powdery mildew in late summer and improve air circulation by thinning congested clumps.
Divide established clumps in early autumn or after flowering in May to maintain vigour and spread.
items.description: Caltha palustris, known as marsh-marigold and kingcup, is a small to medium sized perennial herbaceous plant of the buttercup family, native to marshes, fens, ditches and wet woodland in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. It flowers between April and August, dependent on altitude and latitude, but occasional flowers may occur at other times.

items.name: Purple loosestrife
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive soil or bog gardens at a depth where the crown sits just at ground level
Water deeply twice a week in dry UK summers to mimic its natural damp canal-side habitat
Cut stems back to the ground in late winter before new spring shoots emerge to maintain a tidy clump
Deadhead spent flower spikes in August to prevent heavy self-seeding in nearby damp garden borders
Grow alongside moisture-loving UK native companions like Marsh Marigold and Yellow Iris in wet soil
items.description: Lythrum salicaria or purple-loosestrife is a flowering plant belonging to the family Lythraceae. It should not be confused with other plants sharing the name loosestrife that are members of the genus Lysimachia in the family Primulaceae. This herbaceous perennial plant is native to temperate regions of Europe, Asia, northern Africa, and eastern Australia.

items.name: Pontederia cordata
items.growersTips:
Plant in heavy clay loam in a aquatic basket lined with hessian to prevent soil leaching in ponds.
Submerge the crown between ten and thirty centimetres below the water surface to survive UK winters.
Cut back dead stems and foliage to the base in late autumn before they rot and foul the pond water.
Divide congested clumps in spring using a sharp spade to maintain vigor and control its spread.
Grow alongside Caltha palustris to provide early spring colour before the pickerel weed emerges.
items.description: Pontederia cordata, common name pickerelweed (USA) or pickerel weed (UK), is a monocotyledonous aquatic plant native to the Americas. It grows in a variety of wetlands, including pond and lake margins across an extremely large range from eastern Canada south to Argentina. A few examples include northern rivers, the Everglades and Louisiana.

items.name: Water mint
items.growersTips:
Grow in a submerged pot up to fifteen centimetres deep in a garden pond to contain aggressive roots.
Plant in heavy clay or wet boggy soil in full sun to partial shade to mimic its native UK habitat.
Cut stems back to the base in autumn after flowering to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh growth.
Check leaves regularly in spring for the metallic blue mint beetle and handpick them to prevent damage.
Divide the root clump every three years in spring to maintain plant vigour and control its spread.
items.description: Mentha aquatica is a perennial flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae. It grows in moist places and is native to much of Europe, northwest Africa and southwest Asia.

items.name: Narrow-leaved hosta
items.growersTips:
Plant in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil at a depth where the crown sits just level with the surface
Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry UK summers, keeping the narrow, lance-shaped leaves dry
Apply organic slug pellets or beer traps in early spring as the delicate pointed shoots emerge
Divide congested clumps in late autumn or early spring to maintain the neat, mounding growth habit
Cut back the yellowing foliage to the ground in November to prevent overwintering pests in the crown
items.description: Hosta lancifolia, the narrow-leaved plantain lily or narrow-leaved hosta, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae. It is native to the southern Russian Far East and Japan, and it has been introduced to the northeastern United States and Bulgaria. A perennial cultigen reaching 0.5 m (20 in), it is available from commercial nurseries. Hardy in USDA zones 3 through 8, it is recommended for shady situations.

items.name: Rough horsetail
items.growersTips:
Plant in a submerged sealed container to stop the highly invasive rhizomes from invading UK clay.
Keep soil constantly wet or waterlogged, mimicking native UK bog conditions using stored rainwater.
Cut dead brown stems to the base in late winter to make room for bright green spring growth.
Plant alongside moisture-loving Caltha palustris to mask the bare lower stems of the horsetail.
Grow the robust robustum cultivar to better withstand harsh, cold winds in northern UK gardens.
items.description: Equisetum hyemale, commonly known as rough horsetail or scouring rush, is an evergreen perennial herbaceous pteridophyte in the horsetail family Equisetaceae native to Eurasia and Greenland. It was formerly widely treated in a broader sense including a subspecies in North America, but this is now treated as a separate species, Equisetum praealtum.
